title: A History of the Lyre
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: A poem that traces a woman's heart through its joys and griefs, told as the history of her lyre.

title: A Last Confession
author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
blurb: A dramatic monologue in blank verse: a dying exile tells his confessor of the girl he loved and how that love ended in murder.

title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Hermia flees Athens with Lysander rather than wed the man her father has chosen, and Helena, who loves the spurned Demetrius, follows them into a wood ruled by the quarrelling fairy king and queen. There Oberon's errand-boy Puck mistakes his victims, sending the lovers into a night of misplaced desire while Titania wakes to adore Bottom the weaver, now wearing an ass's head. By morning the couples are rightly matched, and the weddings at Theseus's court are crowned by the workmen's clumsy play of Pyramus and Thisbe.

title: A Mother's Tale
author: Walter Savage Landor
blurb: A narrative in blank verse that opens with the speaker's claim that she never knew but one who died for love.

title: The Abbot of Muchelnaye
author: Henry Alford
blurb: A narrative poem in three cantos, in nine-line stanzas, of an abbot of Muchelney in Somerset and the wife he lost and finds again.

title: Achilleid
author: Statius
blurb: Statius’s unfinished epic of Akhilleus’s youth, from Thetis hiding her son among the maidens of Scyros to Akhilleus’s own account of his boyhood training under Chiron.

title: Achilles in Scyros
subtitle: A drama in a mixed manner
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's drama in a mixed manner, first published in 1890. Thetis has hidden her son Achilles on Scyros, disguised as the girl Pyrrha among the daughters of King Lycomedes; Ulysses and Diomede arrive to find the hero whom the Greeks need at Troy, and Deidamia and a chorus of Scyrian maidens complete the cast.

title: Leucippe and Clitophon
subtitle: A Greek Romance in Eight Books
author: Achilles Tatius
blurb: Clitophon of Tyre falls in love with his cousin Leucippe, and the two flee together, only to suffer shipwreck, capture by Egyptian brigands, apparent deaths, abductions and a trial for chastity at Ephesus before they are reunited and married.

title: The Adventures of Kurroglou
author: Köroğlu
blurb: Köroğlu is the bandit-minstrel hero of the Turkic and Persian oral destan, the robber-poet whose adventures with his horse Kyrat and his band at Chamly-bill are told by the aushiks. The cycle mixes prose narrative with his improvised songs, here given in Alexander Chodzko's English version of 1842, collected from Persian reciters in thirteen Meetings.

title: Ælla: A Tragycal Enterlude
subtitle: or Discoorseynge Tragedie, wrotenn bie Thomas Rowleie
author: Thomas Chatterton
blurb: Chatterton's most admired Rowley forgery, a tragedy supposedly written by the fifteenth-century priest Thomas Rowley for William Canynge of Bristol. Ælla, lord of Bristol castle, marries Birtha, then is called away to repel a Danish raid. His friend Celmonde, secretly in love with Birtha, abducts her in the woods, and the Danes who capture them lead to a deadly end for all three. The minstrels' songs, including 'O! synge untoe mie roundelaie', sit within the play.

sections.title: Scene VII. Another Part of the Wode

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: Prose translation
author: Virgil
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into plain English prose by John Conington.

title: Eneados (Douglas)
subtitle: The xiii. Bukes of Eneados of the famose poete Virgill translatet into Scottish metir
author: Virgil
blurb: Gavin Douglas's Middle Scots translation of the Aeneid, finished in 1513 and first printed in London in 1553, the first complete translation of the Aeneid into any form of English, with his own prologue to each book and Vegio's thirteenth book.

title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English heroic couplets by John Dryden.

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: Prose translation
author: Virgil
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas in twelve books, rendered by J. W. Mackail into measured, Biblical-toned English prose.

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: The Aeneids of Virgil, done into English verse by William Morris
author: Virgil
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into long rhymed fourteeners by William Morris.

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: Translated into English blank verse
author: Virgil
translator: trans. James Rhoades (Longmans, Green, 1893–96; one-volume edition 1907)
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English blank verse by James Rhoades.

title: The First Four Books of the Aeneid (Stanyhurst)
subtitle: Thee first foure bookes of Virgil his Aeneis translated intoo English heroical verse
author: Virgil
blurb: An extravagant attempt to naturalise Latin hexameter in English, famous for its coinages and its defiant spelling, covering Aeneas's storm-tossed landing, the fall of Troy, his wanderings and the tragedy of Dido.

title: Certain Books of the Aeneid (Surrey)
subtitle: Certain bokes of Virgiles Aenaeis turned into English meter
author: Virgil
translator: trans. Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey (printed 1557)
blurb: Surrey's blank-verse rendering of Virgil's account of the fall of Troy (Book II) and of Dido's love and death (Book IV), the poem that gave English its first unrhymed iambic pentameter.

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: Translated into English verse by E. Fairfax Taylor
author: Virgil
translator: trans. E. Fairfax Taylor (Everyman's Library, 1907; reprinted 1910)
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English Spenserian stanzas by E. Fairfax Taylor.

title: The Aeneid
subtitle: Translated into English verse
author: Virgil
blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English blank verse by Theodore C. Williams.

title: The Speeches of Aeschines
subtitle: Against Timarchus, On the Embassy and Against Ctesiphon
author: Aeschines the Orator
blurb: The three surviving speeches of Aeschines, the Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes: his prosecution of Timarchus (345 BC), his defence on the embassy to Philip (343 BC) and his attack on Ctesiphon over the crown awarded to Demosthenes (330 BC).

title: Three Hundred Aesop's Fables
subtitle: Literally translated from the Greek
author: Aesop
blurb: The classic English collection of the fables ascribed to Aesop, the Greek storyteller of the sixth century BC: talking beasts, birds and gods, each ending in a short moral.

title: Agamemnon
subtitle: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
blurb: Browning's famously literal rendering of the play, in which Klutaimnestra, after ten years' waiting, welcomes Agamemnon home from Troia and murders him, with the captive prophetess Kassandra, in the palace at Argos. Browning keeps the Greek names in their Greek spelling.

title: Agamemnon
subtitle: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
blurb: Clytemnestra waits through ten years for her husband Agamemnon to return from Troy, and greets him with purple tapestries and fair words. The captive prophetess Cassandra foresees the murder that awaits them both in the palace; Clytemnestra kills the king in his bath, and takes up the rule of Argos with her lover Aegisthus.

title: Agamemnon
author: Seneca
blurb: The ghost of Thyestes rises to urge on the doom of the house of Atreus. In Argos, Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, her lover and Thyestes' son, plot to kill her husband on his return from Troy. Agamemnon arrives in triumph with the captive prophetess Cassandra, who foresees his death and her own; he is cut down in the palace, and Electra sends the boy Orestes away to safety before the queen turns on her.

title: Ajax
subtitle: Aias
author: Sophocles
blurb: Denied the armour of the dead Akhilleus, which is awarded to Odysseus, Ajax plans to murder the Greek chiefs; Athena drives him mad and he slaughters the army’s flocks instead. Waking to his shame, he deceives his captive-wife Tecmessa and the sailors of Salamis and falls on his sword, and his half-brother Teucer must then defend his body against Menelaus and Agamemnon until Odysseus secures his burial.

title: Ajax
subtitle: Aias
author: Sophocles
blurb: After the arms of the dead Akhilleus are given to Odysseus, Ajax sets out by night to kill the Greek leaders, but Athena clouds his mind and he butchers the army's cattle instead. Waking to his disgrace, he takes leave of his captive Tecmessa and the sailors of Salamis and dies on his own sword, and his half-brother Teucer must then defend the body against Menelaus and Agamemnon until Odysseus secures its burial.

title: Albion's England
subtitle: A continued historie of the same kingdome, from the originals of the first inhabitants thereof (1597)
author: William Warner
blurb: William Warner's fourteener history of Britain from Noah and Brutus to the Tudors, in the 1597 edition.

title: Alcestis
author: Euripides
blurb: Apollo has won Admetus, king of Pherae, the gift that he may escape his death if another dies in his place. Only his wife Alcestis agrees. As she dies, Herakles arrives as a guest, learns the truth, and wrestles Death at her tomb to bring her back.

title: Alcestis
author: Euripides
blurb: Apollo has won Admetus, king of Pherae, the gift that he may escape his death if another dies in his place. Only his wife Alcestis agrees. As she dies, Herakles arrives as a guest, learns the truth, and wrestles Death at her tomb to bring her back.

title: The Alchemist
author: Ben Jonson
blurb: During a plague outbreak in London, Lovewit leaves his house in the care of his butler Face, who lets it to the con man Subtle and his accomplice Dol Common. Posing as an alchemist, Subtle fleeces a lawyer's clerk, a tobacconist, the greedy knight Sir Epicure Mammon and two Puritans of Amsterdam with promises of the philosopher's stone, until the master returns and the scheme collapses. Jonson's fast, savage comedy of London greed.

title: Alciphron
subtitle: A Fragment
author: Thomas Moore
blurb: Moore's verse retelling of The Epicurean: an Athenian philosopher's letters from Egypt, ending with the letter of the High Priest Orcus.

sections.title: Letter I: From Alciphron at Alexandria to Cleon at Athens
Letter II: From the Same to the Same
Letter III: From the Same to the Same
Letter IV: From Orcus, High Priest of Memphis, to Decius, the Praetorian Prefect

title: Alexandra
author: Lycophron
blurb: A riddling monologue in which a slave reports the prophecies of Cassandra, foretelling the fall of Troy and the wanderings of the Greek and Trojan heroes.

title: All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: John Dryden
blurb: Dryden's blank-verse retelling of the last day of Antony and Cleopatra, set in Alexandria after Actium. Ventidius, Dolabella and Octavia pull Antony back toward Rome and duty, while Cleopatra and her eunuch Alexas draw him back to love. Jealousy and a false report of her death drive him to fall on his sword; Cleopatra follows him in death, and the lovers are laid together before Caesar arrives.

title: Morte Arthure
subtitle: The alliterative Morte Arthure
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: An alliterative Middle English romance of about 4,350 long lines, preserved in Robert Thornton's manuscript, telling the end of King Arthur's reign: the Roman emperor Lucius demands tribute, Arthur crosses to the Continent and kills the giant of Mont-Saint-Michel, defeats the Romans and sets out for Rome, but is recalled by Mordred's treason, loses Gawain at the landing, and meets Mordred in a last battle before he is carried to Avalon. It is one of the finest English alliterative poems and a source for Malory.

title: All's Well That Ends Well
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Helena, the orphaned daughter of a famous physician, loves Bertram, the young Count of Rossillon, who is far above her in rank and will not look at her. When she cures the dying King of France with her father's remedy, she asks for Bertram as her reward, but he flees to the Florentine wars rather than accept her. She follows him, and by a bed-trick and a stolen ring she fulfils the impossible conditions he sets, while his braggart companion Parolles is exposed as a coward and a liar. This so-called problem comedy makes a bitter, unsettled mirror of the marriage plot, and its title is shadowed by doubt about whether all can truly be well.

title: Alma: or, the Progress of the Mind
subtitle: A Poem in Three Cantos
author: Matthew Prior
blurb: Prior's tetrameter conversation between Matthew and Richard, in the manner of Hudibras, on the seat of the soul: Alma, the mind, climbs through the body from the toes to the head.

title: America: A Prophecy
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's prophecy of the American Revolution, in which the fiery spirit Orc rises against Albion's Angel and the Thirteen Colonies break free.

title: Amis and Amiloun
subtitle: A verse rendering
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: Two Lombard knights, born on the same night and alike as twins, swear brotherhood. When Amis is accused by a treacherous steward and must face trial by combat, Amiloun takes his place, and pays for it with leprosy; years later Amis, in turn, must sacrifice his own children to cure his friend.

title: The Roman History
subtitle: Books XIV–XXXI, Yonge translation, 1862
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
blurb: Ammianus Marcellinus's history of the Roman Empire from AD 353 to the disaster at Adrianople in AD 378, in the surviving Books XIV to XXXI, in C. D. Yonge's English prose of 1862.

title: Amours de Voyage
author: Arthur Hugh Clough
blurb: An epistolary novel in hexameters, set in Rome during the French siege of 1849, in which the doubting Claude and the Trevellyn sisters write home and fail to find one another.

title: Andreas
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The apostle Andrew's perilous sea voyage to rescue Matthew from the cannibalistic Mermedonians, told in a style deliberately recalling Beowulf's heroic diction.

title: Andreas (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The apostle Andrew's perilous sea voyage to rescue Matthew from the cannibalistic Mermedonians, told in a style deliberately recalling Beowulf's heroic diction, in the original Old English.

title: Andromache
author: Euripides
blurb: Andromache, Hector’s widow and now the concubine of Neoptolemus, shelters at the shrine of Thetis while his jealous wife Hermione and her father Menelaus plot to kill her and her son. Peleus rescues them, but Orestes has arranged Neoptolemus’s murder at Delphi.

title: Andromache
author: Euripides
blurb: Taken to Thessaly as the spoil of Akhilleus' son Neoptolemus, the Trojan captive Andromache clings to the altar of Thetis while Neoptolemus' jealous Spartan wife Hermione and her father Menelaus plot the death of her and her child. Old Peleus comes to her rescue, but Hermione, terrified of her husband's return, is carried off by Orestes, who contrives that Neoptolemus is killed at Delphi. Arthur Way renders the play in English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
blurb: Antigone defies Creon’s edict and buries her brother Polynices, who died attacking Thebes. Condemned to be walled up alive, she hangs herself; Creon’s son Haemon, her betrothed, and then Creon’s wife Eurydice take their own lives, and the king is left to his ruin.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
blurb: Thebes has fallen to Creon, who forbids burial of the traitor Polyneices on pain of death. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, appealing to the unwritten laws of the gods, and is sentenced to a living tomb. Jebb's plain prose follows the quarrel of niece and king through to the suicides of Antigone, Haemon and Eurydice, and Creon's broken closing lament.

title: The Tragedy of Antony and Cleopatra
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Mark Antony, one of the three rulers of Rome, lingers in Alexandria in the arms of Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, until news of his wife's death and of Pompey's rising calls him home. He marries Caesar's sister Octavia to mend the peace, but soon returns to Cleopatra and is destroyed by Octavius Caesar's forces at Actium. Believing Cleopatra dead, Antony falls on his sword; she, refusing to be led in triumph through Rome, takes her own life with an asp.

title: The Library and Epitome
subtitle: The Library of Greek Mythology
author: Apollodorus
blurb: A systematic handbook of Greek myth, from the birth of the gods and the families of the heroes to the Trojan War and the homecomings, with the Epitome preserving the lost end of the text.

title: The Roman History: The Civil Wars
subtitle: The Civil Wars, Books I–V
author: Appian of Alexandria
blurb: Appian's account of Rome's civil wars from the Gracchi to the triumph of Octavian, in Horace White's English prose of 1899.

title: The Roman History: Preface and Foreign Wars
author: Appian of Alexandria
blurb: Appian's history of Rome's wars against other peoples, from the kings and Italy to Spain, Carthage, Illyria, Syria and Mithridates, arranged by nation.

sections.title: Of Sicily and the Other Islands

title: The Golden Asse
subtitle: The Metamorphoses of Apuleius, in Adlington's Tudor translation
author: Apuleius
blurb: Lucius, a curious young man of Thessaly, is turned into an ass by a witch's ointment and endures many masters and adventures, including the tale of Cupid and Psyche, until the goddess Isis restores him.

title: The Argonautica
author: Apollonius of Rhodes
blurb: Jason and the Argonauts sail to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, and Medea's love for him decides the quest, in the Hellenistic epic told in four books.

title: The Tale of the Argonauts
author: Apollonius of Rhodes
blurb: Jason and the Argonauts sail to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, and Medea's love for him decides the quest, in Arthur Way's rhymed English verse version of the Hellenistic epic.

title: Aria da Capo
subtitle: A Play in One Act
author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
blurb: At a black-and-white Harlequinade supper, Pierrot and Columbine play at love and boredom until the masque of Tragedy, Cothurnus, orders them off the stage to make room for a pastoral scene. Two shepherds, Thyrsis and Corydon, build a wall of coloured ribbons between their pastures, quarrel over a pool and a mine of jewels, and destroy each other. When the bodies are dragged away, Pierrot and Columbine resume their supper from the beginning: a one-act verse play against war and indifference, first performed in 1919.

title: The Acharnians
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 425 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: When the Assembly will not make peace, the countryman Dicaeopolis makes a private treaty with Sparta, wins round the furious old men of Acharnae with a speech made in a beggar's rags borrowed from Euripides, and opens a market of his own, while the general Lamachus marches off to war and comes home wounded as Dicaeopolis sits down to feast.

title: Aristophanes' Apology
subtitle: Including a Transcript from Euripides, Being the Last Adventure of Balaustion
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Balaustion's account of the fall of Athens and a debate with Aristophanes on poetry, containing Browning's version of Euripides' Herakles.

title: The Birds
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 414 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Two Athenians, sick of the law-courts, persuade the birds to build a walled city in the air, Cloudcuckoobury, which starves the gods of sacrifice until Zeus sends envoys and Peisthetaerus wins his sceptre and a royal bride.

title: The Clouds
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 423 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Strepsiades, ruined by the debts of his horse-mad son, enrols in Socrates's Thinking-Shop to learn the Unjust Logic and cheat his creditors, but his son learns it too, with disastrous results.

title: The Ecclesiazusae
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 393 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Praxagora, at the head of a band of Athenian women who have borrowed their husbands' cloaks and put on false beards, carries a motion in the Assembly handing the city over to the women, and then decrees that property and love shall be held in common, with riotous results for her husband Blepyrus, a stingy citizen and a young man hunted down by three old hags.

title: The Frogs
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 405 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Dionysus, sick of the dearth of good poets in Athens, travels to Hades with his slave Xanthias to bring Euripides back from the dead, and ends by judging a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides for the tragic throne, in which their verses are weighed in the scales.

title: The Knights
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 424 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Two harassed slaves of old Demus, the Athenian people, plot to topple their fellow slave Paphlagon, a thinly veiled Cleon, by pitting against him a Sausage-seller who is even coarser, louder and more shameless than he.

title: The Plutus
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 388 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Chremylus, a good man who has stayed poor, follows a blind beggar home on the advice of Apollo's oracle and finds him to be Wealth himself. With his slave Cario he sets out to cure the god's sight so that the honest may prosper, braves the arguments of Poverty, has Wealth healed at the temple of Asclepius, and sees the world turned upside down: an informer is stripped, an old woman is dropped by her young lover, and Hermes and the priest of Zeus come begging for a living.

title: The Wasps
subtitle: A comedy first produced at Athens in 422 BC
author: Aristophanes
blurb: Philocleon, an old Athenian addicted to sitting on juries, is kept shut up at home by his son Bdelycleon, who tries to cure him by holding a mock trial in the house (the dog Labes is charged with stealing a cheese) and by teaching him the manners of a gentleman, with riotous results.

title: The Athenian Constitution
subtitle: The Constitution of Athens, in sixty-nine parts
author: Aristotle
blurb: The one surviving 'constitution' of the 158 that Aristotle's school compiled: a history of Athenian government from Draco and Solon to the fall of the Thirty and the restored democracy, followed by an account of how the city's offices and law courts worked in Aristotle's own day.

title: Categories
subtitle: Categoriae, in fifteen chapters
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's short treatise on the ten kinds of thing that can be said of anything: substance, quantity, quality, relation and the rest, with the logic of opposites, priority and change.

title: On the Soul (De Anima)
subtitle: Three books on the nature and faculties of the soul
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on the soul: its definition as the first actuality of a natural body, the nutritive, sensitive, imaginative and intellectual powers, the five senses and the common sense, and the active and passive intellect.

title: Metaphysics
subtitle: Metaphysica, in fourteen books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on first philosophy, the study of being as being, of substance, form and matter, potency and act, and of the unmoved mover.

title: Nicomachean Ethics
subtitle: Ethics in ten books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on the good life: happiness as activity in accordance with virtue, the moral and intellectual virtues, justice, pleasure, friendship and the contemplative life.

title: On Generation and Corruption
subtitle: Two books on coming-to-be and passing-away
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on coming-to-be and passing-away: the difference between generation and alteration, growth, contact and action, and the doctrine of the four elements and their contrary qualities.

title: On Interpretation
subtitle: De Interpretatione, in fourteen chapters
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's short treatise on the logic of statements: nouns and verbs, affirmation and denial, contradictory and contrary propositions, the sea-fight and the truth of statements about the future, and propositions of possibility and necessity.

title: On the Heavens (De Caelo)
subtitle: Four books on the world, the heavenly bodies and the elements
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on the cosmos: the finite, spherical and eternal heaven, the motion and nature of the stars, the shape and position of the earth, and the weight and lightness of the four elements.

title: Physics
subtitle: Eight books on nature, change, place, time and the first mover
author: Aristotle
translator: trans. R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye (1930)
blurb: Aristotle's lectures on nature: the principles of natural things, the four causes, chance and purpose, the analysis of motion, the infinite, place, void and time, the continuity of change, and the argument for an eternal first mover.

title: Poetics
subtitle: On the art of poetry, tragedy and epic, in twenty-six chapters
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's short treatise on poetic art: imitation, the structure of tragic plot, character, diction, and the comparison of epic with tragedy.

XXVI. A general estimate of the comparative worth of Epic Poetry and Tragedy.

title: Politics
subtitle: A Treatise on Government, in eight books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on the city and its constitutions: the household and the state, the best regime, citizenship, the kinds of government, revolutions and their causes, and the education of the citizen.

title: Posterior Analytics
subtitle: Analytica Posteriora, in two books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's theory of scientific knowledge: demonstration from necessary first principles, the knowledge of causes, the nature of definition, and how the first principles of a science are themselves grasped.

title: Prior Analytics
subtitle: Analytica Priora, in two books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's founding work of formal logic: the theory of the syllogism, its three figures and valid moods, the conversion of propositions, premisses of necessity and possibility, and the practical business of finding and testing arguments.

title: Rhetoric
subtitle: On the art of persuasion, in three books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's treatise on rhetoric: the modes of persuasion, the emotions and characters of audiences, the lines of argument, and the choice and arrangement of style.

title: On Sophistical Refutations
subtitle: De Sophisticis Elenchis, in thirty-four chapters
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's analysis of sophistical arguments: the thirteen kinds of fallacy, verbal and non-verbal, how each is detected and solved, and the art of the questioner and the answerer.

title: Topics
subtitle: Topica, in eight books
author: Aristotle
blurb: Aristotle's handbook of dialectical argument: the four predicables (definition, property, genus, accident), the commonplaces for establishing and overthrowing a thesis, and the art of questioning and answering.

title: The Anabasis of Alexander
subtitle: The History of Alexander’s Campaigns, in seven books
author: Arrian
blurb: Arrian’s account of the campaigns of Alexander the Great, from his accession to his death at Babylon, in E. J. Chinnock’s English prose of 1884.

title: The Art of Preserving Health
subtitle: A Poem
author: John Armstrong
blurb: A blank-verse didactic poem in four books on air, diet, exercise and the passions, as ingredients of a healthy life.

title: As You Like It
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Banished from her uncle's court, Rosalind flees to the Forest of Arden disguised as the youth Ganymede, with her cousin Celia and the clown Touchstone, and meets the lovesick Orlando, whom she teaches to woo her in mock courtship. Among exiled lords, shepherds and rustic couples, mistaken loves are sorted out, the usurping duke is turned from his purpose, and the play ends in four weddings and Rosalind's epilogue.

title: The Ascent of Man
author: Mathilde Blind
blurb: Mathilde Blind's evolutionary long poem, in three parts, tracing life and the human soul from the primeval waters through the Pilgrim Soul's quest to the consoling leading of Sorrow.

sections.title: Part III: The Leading of Sorrow

title: The Assumption of Our Lady
subtitle: Middle English text of Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27.2 (to l. 240), continued from British Library MS Harley 2382, ed. J. R. Lumby (1866), re-ed. G. H. McKnight (1901)
author: Anonymous
blurb: A Middle English verse legend of the death of the Virgin: warned by an angel, Mary takes leave of John, the apostles are miraculously gathered, and Christ comes to bear her soul and body up to heaven.

title: At the Hawk's Well
subtitle: A play for dancers
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: Cuchulain, a young hero, climbs a barren hillside in search of a well whose waters give immortality. An Old Man has waited beside the dry well for fifty years, and warns him that the guardian, possessed by a hawk-woman of the Sidhe, will lure him away just when the water rises. Three masked Musicians open and close the play with songs and the folding of a black cloth.

title: Atalanta in Calydon
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
blurb: A tragedy on the Greek model: the hunt of the Calydonian boar, the doom of Meleager, and the choruses that made Swinburne's name.

title: The Deipnosophists, Volume I: Books 1–5
subtitle: Or, The Banquet of the Learned
author: Athenaeus
blurb: A learned banquet in Rome, c. 200, told as a conversation: the guests of the host Larensius talk through food, wine, parasites, cooks and cups, quoting hundreds of lost Greek poets and comedians as they go. Books 1–5 cover the first feasts and the long preserved fragments of the Greek comic poets.

title: The Deipnosophists, Volume II: Books 7–11
subtitle: Or, The Banquet of the Learned
author: Athenaeus
blurb: The banquet of the learned goes on: Books 7–11 hold the long catalogue of fishes and the sayings of the comic poets about them, then ham, vegetables and fruit, the riddles and drinking games of the symposium, and the great survey of cups and goblets.

title: The Deipnosophists, Volume III: Books 12–15
subtitle: Or, The Banquet of the Learned
author: Athenaeus
blurb: The banquet of the learned continues: Book XII on luxury and the pleasures of peoples, Book XIII on women, love and the courtesans of Greece, Book XIV on cakes, music and the dessert course, and Book XV on garlands, perfumes and the songs of the table, all threaded with quotations from lost Greek poets and comedians.

title: Atta Troll
subtitle: A Summer Night's Dream
author: Heinrich Heine
blurb: Heine's mock-heroic satire in twenty-seven cantos, written in 1841 and published in 1847: a dancing bear escapes from his master at Cauterets in the Pyrenees, and the pursuit becomes a burlesque of the political poets and doctrinaire radicals of the day.

title: Aucassin and Nicolete
subtitle: The Song-Story of Aucassin and Nicolete
author: Anonymous (Old French)
blurb: The tale of the Count of Biaucaire's son, who would rather lose his knighthood than his love for the Saracen slave girl Nicolete, told in alternating sung verse and spoken prose.

title: Select Letters
subtitle: Letters of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo
author: Augustine of Hippo
blurb: Sixty-two letters of Augustine, from his early philosophical correspondence to his years as bishop of Hippo, in the Loeb translation of James Houston Baxter.

Letter 50: To the Magistrates of Sufes
Letter 66: Note against Crispinus the Schismatic

Letter 268: To the Members of Christ

title: Aurora Leigh
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
blurb: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel in nine books of blank verse, telling in the first person the life of Aurora Leigh, a poet who must choose between art and love, and her relation to her cousin Romney, a social reformer.

title: The Avowynge of King Arther
subtitle: The Avowing of King Arthur, Sir Gawan, Sir Kaye, and Sir Bawdewyn of Bretan
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: While King Arthur hunts at Carlisle, a monstrous boar draws the Round Table into a night of vows: Arthur swears to hunt it down alone and keep watch over it, Gawain to guard a lady against all comers, Kay to defend a forest against every knight, and Baldwin never to be jealous, never to refuse a guest, and never to fear death. A north-of-England verse romance of seventy-two sixteen-line stanzas.

title: The Anturs of Arther at the Tarnewathelan
subtitle: The Awntyrs off Arthure at the Terne Wathelyn
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: While Arthur hunts near Tarn Wadling, the ghost of Queen Guinevere's mother rises from torment to warn her of the fate that awaits the proud and the worldly, and of the fall of Arthur's realm; the court then rides to Carlisle, where the Scottish knight Sir Galeron claims Gawain's lands and the two meet in single combat. A north-of-England alliterative romance in fifty-five thirteen-line stanzas.

title: The Bacchae
author: Euripides
blurb: The god Dionysus comes in human guise to Thebes, where the young king Pentheus denies his divinity, imprisons the stranger and tries to suppress the rites of the maenads. The god drives the Theban women to the mountain, lures Pentheus to spy on them in woman's dress, and brings about a terrible end at the hands of his own mother Agave. Gilbert Murray renders the tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: The Bacchanals
subtitle: The Bacchae
author: Euripides
blurb: The Wine-god Dionysus comes in human guise to Thebes, where the young king Pentheus denies his godhead and tries to chain the stranger and suppress his rites. The god maddens the Theban women, drives them to the mountain, and lures Pentheus to spy on them in woman's dress, with a terrible end at the hands of his own mother Agave. Arthur S. Way's English verse translation, with rhymed choral odes.

title: Odes and Fragments
subtitle: A Prose Translation
author: Bacchylides
blurb: Edward Poste's prose version of the odes and fragments of the Ceian lyric poet recovered from the Egyptian papyri in 1896: victory odes for Hiero of Syracuse, dithyrambs on Theseus, and shorter pieces on Croesus, Menelaus, Deianira and Peace.

sections.title: Ode II. The Daughters of Proteus
Ode VI. Ajax, or the Trojans

title: Balaustion's Adventure
subtitle: Including a Transcript from Euripides
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A young Rhodian woman recounts how she saved a shipload of Athenians at Syracuse by reciting Euripides' Alkestis, which Browning renders in full within her narrative.

title: The Ballad of the White Horse
author: G. K. Chesterton
blurb: Chesterton's ballad of King Alfred and the battle of Ethandune, in eight books framed by a verse dedication to his wife: the Vision of the Virgin, the gathering of the chiefs, the harp in the Danish camp, the woman and the cakes, and the three stages of the battle.

title: The Baron's Little Daughter
author: Cecil Frances Alexander
blurb: A long narrative poem from Cecil Frances Alexander's collected Poems (1896).

title: The Barons' Wars
subtitle: In the Reign of Edward the Second (Books II–VI)
author: Michael Drayton
blurb: Drayton's verse chronicle of the civil wars under Edward II, in ottava rima — this edition preserves Books II through VI.

title: The Battaile of Agincourt
author: Michael Drayton
blurb: Drayton's account, in 315 eight-line stanzas, of Henry V's French campaign and the victory at Agincourt, opening with the dispute over the Salic law.

title: Homer's Battle of the Frogs and Mice
subtitle: after the pseudo-Homeric Batrachomyomachia
author: Thomas Parnell
blurb: Parnell's mock-heroic version of the Battle of the Frogs and Mice: a mouse drowns on a frog's back, and the two nations go to war while the gods look on.

title: Becket
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
blurb: Henry II raises his friend and Chancellor Thomas Becket to the see of Canterbury, hoping for an ally in the Church; Becket instead defends the Church's rights against the Crown. Through the quarrel at Northampton, exile in France, a patched-up reconciliation and the King's hidden love for Rosamund, the two old friends move toward the murder of the Archbishop in his own cathedral.

title: The Beggar’s Opera
author: John Gay
blurb: A ballad opera in three acts. The thief-taker and receiver Peachum learns that his daughter Polly has secretly married the highwayman Macheath, and resolves to have him hanged. Macheath is betrayed, locked in Newgate and courted by the jailer’s daughter Lucy, while the play sets the manners of the criminal world beside those of the fashionable one. A framing dialogue between a Beggar, who claims to be the author, and a Player brings about the reprieve that the Beggar says the form demands.

title: Bella Gorry
subtitle: The Pazon's Story
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: The Pazon's story, in blank verse, of Bella Gorry, who lived in a clay-walled cottage on the sandy coast near the Point of Ayre.

title: Beowulf
author: Beowulf Poet
blurb: The Geatish hero Beowulf crosses the sea to rid the Danish hall of Heorot of the monster Grendel, then Grendel's vengeful mother, and in old age faces a dragon guarding a cursed hoard — the oldest surviving epic in English.

sections.title: Prelude of the Founder of the Danish House

title: Beowulf (Hall)
subtitle: An Anglo-Saxon Epic Poem
author: Beowulf Poet
blurb: Hall renders the poem in close alliterative verse that keeps the four-stress line and heaps up compound words in the manner of the Old English original.

title: The Story of Beowulf (Kirtlan)
subtitle: Translated from Anglo-Saxon into Modern English Prose
author: Beowulf Poet
blurb: Kirtlan tells the story in plain modern English prose, following the Old English closely but without any attempt at verse or archaism.

title: The Tale of Beowulf (Morris & Wyatt)
subtitle: Sometime King of the Folk of the Weder Geats
author: Beowulf Poet
translator: trans. William Morris and A. J. Wyatt (1895)
blurb: Morris translates in a deliberately archaic diction, thick with Old English words and inverted syntax, so that the poem reads as if it had been composed in the saga-age English of his imagination.

title: Beowulf (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Beowulf Poet
blurb: The Geatish hero Beowulf crosses the sea to rid the Danish hall of Heorot of the monster Grendel, then Grendel's mother, and in old age faces a dragon guarding a cursed hoard, in the original Old English of the oldest surviving epic in English.

title: Betsy Lee
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, First Series: I
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A Manx fisherman tells, in rhymed dialect couplets, how he courted Betsy Lee and lost her; the first of Brown's Fo'c's'le Yarns.

title: Beware of Smooth Water
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: A light comedy of courtship in a Spanish household, where Don Alonso's daughters Clara and Eugenia, a nephew, gallants and servants cross one another's purposes. FitzGerald thinks it written for the 1649 wedding of Philip IV, and it closes on its own moral: beware of all smooth waters.

title: The Song Celestial
subtitle: Bhagavad Gita (from the Mahabharata)
author: Vyasa
blurb: On the field of Kurukshetra, as two armies stand ready, the warrior Arjuna lets fall his bow, and his charioteer, the god Krishna, answers his despair in eighteen chapters on duty, devotion and the self. Arnold renders the Sanskrit in blank verse, shifting into lyrical measures where the original does. The Gita is attributed by tradition to Vyasa.

title: Bird Parliament
subtitle: abridged from the Mantiq al-Tair
author: Farid al-Din Attar
blurb: An abridged English version of Attar's Sufi allegory in which the birds of the world gather to choose a king, are led by the hoopoe through seven valleys, and the few that survive the journey find that the Simorgh they seek is the mirror of themselves.

title: The Birth of the War-God
subtitle: Kumarasambhava
author: Kalidasa
blurb: Kalidasa's Sanskrit epic of the courtship of Shiva and Uma and the birth of Kumara, god of war, in seven cantos, in Griffith's rhymed couplets.

Canto III: The Death of Love

title: Black Marigolds (Chaurapanchasika)
subtitle: A free interpretation of the Chaurapanchasika
author: Bilhana
blurb: Fifty stanzas, each beginning "Even now", in which a condemned lover remembers his princess, in E. Powys Mathers's free-verse rendering of the poem attributed to the Kashmiri poet Bilhana.

title: A Blot in the 'Scutcheon: A Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Mildred Tresham, sister of the proud Earl Tresham, has secretly taken Lord Mertoun as her lover, and when he comes openly to ask for her hand the family honour seems about to be satisfied. Thorold Tresham learns of the earlier nights from his old retainer Gerard and, believing his house disgraced, confronts them both. Mertoun is killed in a duel at the foot of the yew-tree avenue, Mildred dies of grief, and Thorold dies after forgiving them, leaving the blot he sought to wipe away.

title: Griselda
subtitle: A Society Novel in Rhymed Verse
author: Wilfrid Scawen Blunt
blurb: Blunt's novel in rhyming couplets of Parisian and London society in the nineteenth century, told over five chapters.

title: Satan Absolved
subtitle: A Victorian Mystery
author: Wilfrid Scawen Blunt
blurb: A satirical dialogue in verse in which Satan pleads before the assembled angels and the Lord God, set against the conduct of Christian nations.

sections.title: Part I: The Antechamber of Heaven
Part II: The Lord God Holds Audience

title: The Consolation of Philosophy
subtitle: trans. H. R. James (1897)
author: Boethius
blurb: Imprisoned at Pavia and awaiting execution, the statesman Boethius is visited by Lady Philosophy, who drives away the Muses of tragic poetry and leads him, in alternating prose argument and verse, from grief at his fall to an understanding of true happiness, the government of the world by Providence, and the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human free will.

Book II: The Vanity of Fortune's Gifts

Book IV: Good and Ill Fortune
Book V: Free Will and God's Foreknowledge

title: The Book of Ahania
author: William Blake
blurb: Fuzon's revolt against Urizen, the casting out of Ahania, and her lament over the Tree of Mystery.

title: The Book of Los
author: William Blake
blurb: Eno's lament, the binding of Urizen, and Los's forging of the Sun in the void.

title: The Book of the Duchess
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: An elegy in dream form: a sleepless narrator reads the tale of Ceyx and Alcyone, then dreams of a grieving Black Knight in a forest, whose lost lady, White, is widely taken to honour Blanche of Lancaster.

title: The Book of Thel
author: William Blake
blurb: The shepherdess Thel questions Lily, Cloud, Worm and Clay about why life fades, enters the land of the dead, and flees back to the vales of Har.

title: The Book of Urizen
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's myth of creation and fall: Urizen, the reasoning lawgiver, is cast out, bound by Los, and the material world and its religion take shape.

title: Boris Godunov
subtitle: A Drama in Verse
author: Alexander Pushkin
blurb: Pushkin's historical tragedy of the Time of Troubles. After the death of the young Tsarevich Dimitry, the boyar Boris Godunov is begged to take the crown, but a novice monk, Gregory Otrepiev, learns that he may pass himself off as the murdered prince and escapes to Poland. Backed by Polish nobles and the love of Marina, the Pretender invades Russia, while Boris, haunted by his crime, sees his power fail. Boris dies, and on the Pretender's approach Moscow turns against the family of Godunov.

sections.title: The Palace of the Kremlin (20 February 1598)
The Virgin's Field. The New Nunnery
Night. Cell in the Monastery of Chudov (1603)
Castle of the Governor. Mnishek in Sambor
A Plain near Novgorod Seversk (21 December 1604)
Open Space in Front of the Cathedral in Moscow

title: The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich
subtitle: A Long-Vacation Pastoral
author: Arthur Hugh Clough
blurb: A long-vacation pastoral in nine cantos of English hexameters, in which Oxford reading-party men and a Highland girl, Elspie, put the class question to the test of love.

title: Brand
subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
author: Henrik Ibsen
blurb: Brand, a young priest, preaches an absolute creed: all or nothing. He holds his village, his dying mother, his wife Agnes and his own child to that demand, and the cost rises with every act, until he stands alone on the ice-fields with the mad girl Gerd and the avalanche above him.

title: The Bridal of Triermain
subtitle: or, The Vale of St. John
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A verse romance in three cantos, framed as a lover's tale told to Lucy: it follows Sir Roland de Vaux of Triermain into the enchanted Castle of Saint John, where he wakes the sleeping Gyneth, King Arthur's daughter, from her spell.

title: Britannia's Pastorals
subtitle: Books I-III (Book III unfinished)
author: William Browne of Tavistock
blurb: Browne's long Spenserian pastoral of Devon shepherds and nymphs, in rhymed pentameter couplets: the love of Marina and Celandine, her rescue from Famine's cave, and the shepherds' songs, in two books (1613, 1616) and an unfinished third.

title: The Bronze Cavalier
subtitle: A poem in two cantos
author: Alexander Pushkin
blurb: Pushkin's St Petersburg tale of the clerk Evgeny, ruined by the flood of 1824, and the bronze statue of Peter the Great that pursues him, in Charles Edward Turner's 1899 English version.

title: The Bruce
subtitle: Original Older Scots text, ed. W. M. Mackenzie (1909)
author: John Barbour
blurb: Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert the Bruce and Sir James Douglas and the Scottish War of Independence, culminating in Bannockburn, with its famous praise of freedom.

title: The Buddha-karita
subtitle: The Life of the Buddha
author: Asvaghosha
blurb: The first Sanskrit court epic on the life of the Buddha, from his birth at Kapilavastu to his enlightenment and first teaching.

title: The Bustan
subtitle: The Garden of Fruit, translated from the Persian by A. Hart Edwards
author: Sa'di of Shiraz
blurb: Sa'di's Garden of Fruit (1257): ten chapters of counsel and moral tales on justice, benevolence, love, humility, resignation, contentment, education, gratitude, repentance and prayer.

sections.title: Chapter I: Concerning Justice, Counsel, and the Administration of Government

title: Cain
subtitle: A Mystery
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's biblical drama in three acts, first published in 1821. Cain, resentful of the fate bequeathed by his parents' fall, is led by Lucifer through the abyss of space and the realm of the dead, where he is shown the vastness of creation and the meaning of death. Returning to earth, he kills his brother Abel in a rage at God's favour and is marked by an angel and driven eastward from Eden.

title: Calvary
subtitle: A play for dancers
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: On the road to Calvary Christ is met first by Lazarus, who asks for the death he was denied, and then by Judas, who betrayed Him so as to be free of His power. Three Roman soldiers, who care for nothing but their dice, gamble for His cloak. The Musicians sing of the herons, swans and eagles for whom God has not died.

title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: A fellowship of pilgrims riding from Southwark to Canterbury pass the road in stories — chivalric romance, low comedy, sermon, and fable — in the original Middle English, the foundation of English narrative poetry.

title: Captain Craig
author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
blurb: A blank-verse narrative in three parts: the narrator's friendship with a ragged, philosophizing old man in Tilbury Town.

title: Captain Tom and Captain Hugh
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, First Series: III
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A dialect yarn about two Castletown sea captains who were schoolfellows, told by a seaman who warns that it is not much of a story.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 1: Epitome of Books 1–21
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 1–21, from the landing of Aeneas to the Second Punic War and after, as preserved in the epitome of Zonaras
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the early centuries: the Trojan beginnings, the kings, the Republic and the wars against Pyrrhus and Carthage, as Zonaras epitomised the lost books, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 2: Books 36–44
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 36–44, from Pompey's eastern wars (69 B.C.) to the aftermath of Caesar's assassination (44 B.C.)
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the last years of the Republic: Pompey's eastern wars, Cicero and Catiline, Caesar's conquest of Gaul, the civil war with Pompey, Caesar's dictatorship and his assassination, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 3: Books 45–51
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 45–51, from the rise of Octavian after Caesar's murder to the death of Antony and the conquest of Egypt (44–29 B.C.)
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the years after Caesar's murder: Cicero against Antony, Mutina, the Triumvirate, Philippi, the Perusine war, Sextus Pompey, Actium and the fall of Cleopatra, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 4: Books 52–60
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 52–60, from Maecenas and Agrippa on monarchy and the settlement of Augustus to the reign of Claudius (29 B.C. – A.D. 54)
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the principate of Augustus and his successors: the debate of Agrippa and Maecenas, the settlement of 27 B.C., Augustus's later years, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 5: Books 61–76
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 61–76, from the death of Claudius and the reign of Nero to the reign of Septimius Severus (A.D. 54 – 211)
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the later first and the second century: Nero, the year of the four emperors, the Flavians, Trajan and Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Pertinax and Septimius Severus, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English of 1905.

title: Dio's Rome, Volume 6: Books 77–80
subtitle: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, Books 77–80, from the accession of Caracalla to the reign of Alexander Severus and the close of the History (A.D. 211–229)
author: Cassius Dio
blurb: Dio's Roman History for the reigns of Caracalla, Macrinus, Elagabalus and Alexander Severus, ending with Dio's own account of his retirement, in Herbert Baldwin Foster's English.

title: The Castle of Indolence: An Allegorical Poem
subtitle: Written in imitation of Spenser
author: James Thomson
blurb: Thomson's Spenserian allegory of a wizard's enchanted castle of sloth and the knight of arts and industry who overthrows it.

title: Cavender's House
subtitle: A Poem
author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
blurb: Blank-verse narrative in three parts: Cavender returns after twelve years to his shuttered, darkened house and is confronted there by the presence of Laramie.

title: The Chase
author: William Somervile
blurb: A blank-verse poem in four books on hunting, from the breeding of hounds to the pursuit of the hare, the stag and the fox.

title: Chastelard: A Tragedy
author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
blurb: The first play of Swinburne's Mary Stuart trilogy. At the court of Mary, Queen of Scots, the French poet Chastelard, who has followed her from France, is bound to her by a desperate passion. Hidden in her bedchamber, he is discovered, spared, and then caught there a second time. He is condemned to death at St Andrews, and goes to the scaffold unrepentant, while the Queen, who has used and tempted him, looks on.

title: The Chester Plays
subtitle: A Collection of Mysteries Founded upon Scriptural Subjects, Formerly Represented by the Trades of Chester at Whitsuntide
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: The twenty-five pageants of the Chester cycle, the Whitsun mystery plays acted by the craft guilds of Chester, run from the fall of Lucifer and the Creation through Noah's Flood, Abraham, the Nativity and the Passion to the Harrowing of Hell, the Resurrection and Doomsday. Each play was staged on a wagon by a different guild, in rhymed stanzas full of alliteration, with stage directions in Latin.

sections.title: II. The Creation and Fall, and Death of Abel
IV. The Histories of Lot and Abraham
VII. The Play of the Shepherds
IX. The Offering and Return of the Three Kings
X. The Slaughter of the Innocents
XII. The Temptation, and the Woman Taken in Adultery
XXII. The Emission of the Holy Ghost

title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage
author: Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's Spenserian travelogue in four cantos follows a world-weary young pilgrim through Portugal, Spain, Greece, Belgium, the Rhine and Italy, turning from personal gloom to meditations on liberty, ruin and the sublime.

title: Childe John
subtitle: János vitéz
author: Sándor Petőfi
blurb: Petőfi's Hungarian folk epic in twenty-seven cantos: the shepherd boy Jancsi (Childe John) is parted from his sweetheart Helen and goes out into the world through war, giants and witches, until he wins her back and a fairy kingdom, here in English verse by William N. Loew.

title: The Children of Herakles
author: Euripides
blurb: Hunted from city to city by the vengeful king Eurystheus, the old warrior Iolaus shelters the children of the dead Herakles at the altar of Zeus in Marathon. Demophon of Athens takes up their cause, but an oracle demands the sacrifice of a noble maiden before victory can be won, and Herakles' daughter Makaria offers her own life. Arthur Way renders the play in English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Christ I
subtitle: The Advent Lyrics
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: A sequence of lyric meditations, based on the liturgical O Antiphons of Advent, anticipating the coming of Christ.

title: Christ I (Old English)
subtitle: The Advent Lyrics: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The Old English verse of the Advent Lyrics: a sequence of lyric meditations, based on the liturgical O Antiphons of Advent, anticipating the coming of Christ.

title: Christ II
subtitle: The Ascension
author: Cynewulf
blurb: Cynewulf's account of Christ's Ascension into heaven, drawing on a homily of Gregory the Great, and of the gifts of grace bestowed on humankind.

title: Christ II (Old English)
subtitle: The Ascension: Old English text
author: Cynewulf
blurb: The Old English verse of Cynewulf's account of Christ's Ascension into heaven, drawing on a homily of Gregory the Great, and of the gifts of grace bestowed on humankind.

title: Christ III
subtitle: Judgment Day
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: A vision of the Last Judgment: Christ's sudden return, the terror of sinners and the joy of the blessed, closing the Exeter Book's Christ sequence.

title: Christ III (Old English)
subtitle: Judgment Day: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The Old English verse of a vision of the Last Judgment: Christ's sudden return, the terror of sinners and the joy of the blessed, closing the Exeter Book's Christ sequence.

title: Christ and Satan
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The last poem of the Junius Manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, Christ's Harrowing of Hell and Ascension, and finally Satan's temptation of Christ in the wilderness.

title: Christ and Satan (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The Old English verse of the Junius Manuscript in the Krapp and Dobbie edition: the last poem of the Junius Manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, Christ's Harrowing of Hell and Ascension, and finally Satan's temptation of Christ in the wilderness.

title: The Christian Captives
subtitle: A Tragedy in Five Acts in a mixed manner
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's tragedy in five acts, first published in 1890. In a castle garden by the sea, Almeh, daughter of the King of Fez, meets the Christian captives of the Moorish court, among them the Portuguese princes Ferdinand and Enrique; a chorus of the captives sings Latin hymns and speaks in turn.

title: Christmas Rose
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, First Series: II
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A dialect yarn that begins on a Christmas-time evening at the school in the year of the great storm of 'hunder-thirty-nine' and ends with the mystery of who or what the Christmas Rose was.

title: Christs Victorie and Triumph
subtitle: in Heaven, and Earth, over, and after Death
author: Giles Fletcher the Younger
blurb: A Spenserian poem in four parts on the redemption of man, from Mercy's plea in heaven to Christ's temptation, his death on the cross and his resurrection and ascension.

title: Chronicle of England
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A rhymed chronicle of about 1,040 lines in couplets, from the coming of Brutus and the giants of Albion through the British kings Lud, Bladud and Arthur and the Saxon and Danish kings to the Norman Conquest and the Plantagenets, closing with the death of Piers Gaveston under Edward II.

title: Chronicle of the Cid
author: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
blurb: Robert Southey’s English compilation of the medieval Spanish chronicles and ballads recounting the life and legend of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid.

title: On the Ends of Good and Evil (De Finibus)
subtitle: Five dialogues on the supreme good: the Epicurean, Stoic and Peripatetic accounts examined
author: Cicero
blurb: Written in 45 BC, De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum sets the leading Hellenistic schools against one another on the question of what the highest good is. Torquatus defends Epicurus and Cicero replies (Books I and II); Cato expounds the Stoic view (III) and Cicero answers it (IV); Piso sets out the Peripatetic and Old Academic position (V). C. D. Yonge's literal translation (Bohn, 1853), with Cicero's chapter numbers kept at the head of paragraphs.

title: On Duties (De Officiis)
subtitle: Three books to his son Marcus: moral goodness, expediency, and the conflict between the two
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's last major work, written in 44 BC for his son Marcus, then studying at Athens: a Stoic-inspired guide to what is morally right, what is expedient, and how to choose when the two seem to clash. Walter Miller's translation for the Loeb Classical Library, with the chapter numbers kept as plain leading numbers.

title: On the Orator (De Oratore)
subtitle: Three books on the making of the perfect orator, in dialogue between Crassus, Antonius and their friends
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's dialogue on eloquence, written in 55 BC and set in 91 BC at the Tusculan villa of the orator Lucius Crassus. Crassus and Marcus Antonius, with Scaevola, Catulus, Cotta and Sulpicius, discuss what the perfect orator must know: his learning, the invention and arrangement of his matter, the use of wit, and the style and delivery of his speech. J. S. Watson's translation, with the chapter numbers kept as plain leading numbers.

title: The Letters of Cicero, Volume I
subtitle: Letters from 68 to 52 BC, including the letters of the exile
author: Cicero
blurb: The first volume of Shuckburgh's chronological translation of Cicero's correspondence: letters to Atticus, to his brother Quintus and to friends, from his candidacy for the praetorship to the year before the civil war, including the letters written in exile.

sections.title: Letters in Exile and After (58–52 BC)

title: The Letters of Cicero, Volume II
subtitle: Letters from 51 to 49 BC, from Cicero's journey to Cilicia to the outbreak of the civil war
author: Cicero
blurb: The second volume of Shuckburgh's chronological translation of Cicero's correspondence, carrying on the numbering of the first: Cicero's journey to Cilicia and his governorship of the province, the letters of his return to Italy, and the correspondence of the opening months of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, to Atticus, to Tiro, to Terentia, to Caelius, to Appius Claudius Pulcher and to many others.

sections.title: Letters of 50 BC: The Proconsulate and the Return
Letters of 49 BC: The Outbreak of the Civil War

title: The Letters of Cicero, Volume III
subtitle: Letters from 48 to 44 BC, from Pompey's camp in Epirus to the eve of Caesar's murder
author: Cicero
blurb: The third volume of Shuckburgh's chronological translation of Cicero's correspondence, carrying on the numbering of the second: the letters from Pompey's camp in Epirus and the long wait at Brundisium after Pharsalia, through the years of Caesar's dictatorship, Cicero's retirement to his villas, his divorce, the death of his daughter Tullia and his consolation in philosophical writing, down to the winter of 44 BC. Addressed to Atticus, Terentia, Tiro, Varro, Papirius Paetus, Servius Sulpicius, Cassius and many others.

sections.title: Letters of 48 BC: Epirus and Brundisium
Letters of 47 BC: Brundisium and the Return to Italy
Letters of 46 BC: Rome under Caesar
Letters of 45 BC: Tullia's Death and the Philosophical Works
Letters of 44 BC: The Months before the Ides of March

title: The Letters of Cicero, Volume IV
subtitle: Letters from the Ides of March 44 BC to July 43 BC, from Caesar's murder to the eve of the second triumvirate
author: Cicero
blurb: The fourth and last volume of Shuckburgh's chronological translation of Cicero's correspondence, carrying on the numbering of the third: the letters written after Caesar's assassination on the Ides of March 44 BC. They follow Cicero's retreat to his country villas, his growing quarrel with Antony and the Philippics, the war at Mutina, and the last anxious exchanges with Brutus, Cassius, Decimus Brutus, Plancus and Lepidus, down to the summer of 43 BC. Addressed to Atticus, Tiro, Cornificius and many others, with letters to Cicero from the generals and the conspirators themselves.

sections.title: Letters of 44 BC: After the Ides of March
Letters of 44 BC: The Break with Antony
Letters of 43 BC: The Philippics and Mutina
Letters of 43 BC: Decimus Brutus, Plancus, Lepidus and the Last Letters

title: On Divination (De Divinatione)
subtitle: A dialogue on whether the future can be foretold: Quintus defends divination, and Cicero answers him
author: Cicero
blurb: Written in 44 BC, shortly before Caesar's death, De Divinatione is the companion to Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods. In Book I his brother Quintus defends every kind of divination, from the entrails of victims and the flight of birds to dreams and prophetic frenzy, on Stoic grounds. In Book II Cicero, speaking as an Academic sceptic, takes the argument apart, while still upholding the religious institutions of Rome. C. D. Yonge's literal translation (Bohn, 1853), with Cicero's chapter numbers kept at the head of paragraphs and the verses he cites set as indented blocks.

title: On Friendship (Laelius de Amicitia)
subtitle: A dialogue on the nature and laws of friendship
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's dialogue on friendship, written in 44 BC and dedicated to Atticus. The aged Laelius, mourning his friend Scipio Africanus, tells his sons-in-law what friendship is, why it rests on virtue, and what its limits and duties are. Shuckburgh's translation, with the chapter numbers kept as plain leading numbers.

title: On Old Age (Cato Maior de Senectute)
subtitle: A dialogue in which Cato the Elder, in his eighty-fourth year, defends old age before Scipio and Laelius
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's late dialogue, addressed to Atticus, in which the aged Marcus Cato answers four charges against old age: that it withdraws us from active employments, weakens the body, deprives us of pleasures, and stands near to death.

title: On the Commonwealth (De Re Publica, with the Dream of Scipio)
subtitle: Six books on the best constitution, in dialogue between Scipio Aemilianus and his friends
author: Cicero
translator: trans. Francis Barham (1841), revised by C. D. Yonge (1877)
blurb: Cicero's dialogue on the state, composed in 54 BC and set in 129 BC in the garden of Scipio Aemilianus, where Scipio, Laelius, Philus and their friends debate the best form of government, the history of the Roman constitution, and whether justice is the foundation of a commonwealth. The work was lost until a palimpsest was found in the Vatican in 1822, so most of it survives in gaps and fragments; the Dream of Scipio, which closes Book VI, was preserved separately by Macrobius.

title: On the Laws (De Legibus)
subtitle: A dialogue between Marcus, his brother Quintus and Atticus on the nature of law, with a code of religious and civil statutes
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's companion to his Republic, set in the grove at Arpinum. In Book I he grounds law in nature and universal reason; in Book II he lays down and expounds the laws of religion; in Book III those of the magistrates and the constitution.

title: On the Nature of the Gods (De Natura Deorum)
subtitle: A dialogue on whether the gods exist and whether they govern the world
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero's last great dialogue on religion (45 BC) stages a debate among three friends: the Epicurean Velleius argues that the gods are blessed and care nothing for mankind, the Stoic Balbus defends providence and the divine order of the cosmos, and the Academic Cotta, speaking for Cicero's own sceptical school, dismantles both. Cicero himself, as narrator, leans to the Stoic view as the more probable.

title: The Orations of Cicero, Volume I
subtitle: For Quinctius, For Sextus Roscius, For Quintus Roscius, Against Caecilius, and the Verrine Orations
author: Cicero
blurb: The first volume of Yonge's Bohn translation of Cicero's speeches: the early pleadings for Quinctius, Sextus Roscius and the actor Quintus Roscius, the Divinatio against Caecilius, and the great prosecution of Verres, governor of Sicily, in the First Pleading and the five books of the Second.

Against Verres, Second Pleading, Book II: His Judgments in Sicily

title: The Orations of Cicero, Volume II
subtitle: For Tullius, Fonteius, Caecina, Cluentius, Rabirius, Murena, Sulla, Archias, Flaccus and Scaurus; the Manilian Law, the Agrarian Law, the Catilinarians, and the speeches after his return
author: Cicero
blurb: The second volume of Yonge's Bohn translation of Cicero's speeches: the pleadings of his consular years and after, among them the Manilian Law, the three speeches on the Agrarian Law, the four Catilinarians, and the defences of Murena, Archias, Flaccus and Sulla, with the two speeches after his return from exile.

After his Return, to the People

title: The Orations of Cicero, Volume III
subtitle: On his House, the Haruspices, Plancius, Sestius, Vatinius, Caelius, the Consular Provinces, Balbus, Piso, Milo, Postumus, Marcellus, Ligarius and King Deiotarus
author: Cicero
blurb: The third volume of Yonge's Bohn translation of Cicero's speeches: the orations of his years after exile, among them the plea for his house, the defences of Sestius, Caelius, Plancius and Milo, the invective against Piso, and the three speeches before Caesar for Marcellus, Ligarius and King Deiotarus.

sections.title: On the Answers of the Haruspices

title: The Orations of Cicero, Volume IV: The Philippics
subtitle: The fourteen speeches against Marcus Antonius
author: Cicero
blurb: The fourth volume of Yonge's Bohn translation of Cicero's speeches: the fourteen Philippics of 44 and 43 BC, in which Cicero, after Caesar's murder, attacks Marcus Antonius in the Senate and before the people and urges war to save the republic, the work that cost him his life.

title: Tusculan Disputations
subtitle: Five books on death, pain, grief, the passions and the happy life
author: Cicero
blurb: Cicero, in 45 BC, recounts five days of conversation at his villa near Tusculum, in which he argues against a pupil on the great questions of the philosophical life: why death is not an evil, how pain may be borne, how grief and the other passions of the mind may be cured, and why virtue alone suffices for a happy life. The speaker's verse quotations from Ennius, Homer, the tragedians and others are given in Yonge's English renderings.

title: The Civile Wars betweene the Two Houses of Lancaster and Yorke
subtitle: Eight books in ottava rima (1609 text)
author: Samuel Daniel
blurb: Samuel Daniel's historical epic of the Wars of the Roses, from the deposition of Richard II to the marriage of Henry VII and Elizabeth of York, in eight books of eight-line stanzas. The first four books appeared in 1595; the 1609 edition corrected and continued the poem. Each book opens with a short verse argument.

title: Clarel: A Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land
author: Herman Melville
blurb: Melville’s long narrative poem of a pilgrimage in Palestine, the longest poem in American literature: a young divinity student, Clarel, joins a company of pilgrims who travel from Jerusalem through the Judean wilderness to Mar Saba, the Dead Sea and Bethlehem, debating faith and doubt as they go. It runs to some eighteen thousand lines, chiefly in rhymed octosyllabic couplets with lyric interludes, in four parts: Jerusalem (44 cantos), The Wilderness (39), Mar Saba (32) and Bethlehem (35, the last an Epilogue).

title: Cleanness
subtitle: Clannesse
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: A homily in some 1,800 alliterative lines on purity, in which God rejects those who come unclean to his presence. It tells the parable of the wedding feast and retells three Old Testament judgements: the Flood, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Belshazzar's feast with the profaned vessels of the Temple.

title: The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians
subtitle: A letter from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth
author: Clement of Rome
blurb: A letter sent from the Church at Rome to the Church at Corinth, urging reconciliation after a rebellion against its presbyters; traditionally written by Clement, bishop of Rome, about AD 96.

title: The Second Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians
subtitle: An early Christian homily traditionally ascribed to Clement
author: Clement of Rome
blurb: An early Christian sermon on repentance and the keeping of the baptismal vow, handed down with the First Epistle under the name of Clement of Rome; the attribution is traditional and the work is generally thought to be by another hand.

title: Cligés
subtitle: Cligés
author: Chrétien de Troyes
blurb: A Greek prince of Arthur's line and his love for Fenice, framed as an answer to the Tristan story.

title: The Cloud-Messenger
subtitle: Meghaduta
author: Kalidasa
blurb: An exiled Yaksha begs a passing rain-cloud to carry a message of love across India to his wife in the Himalayas.

title: Dipsychus
subtitle: A verse drama in two parts
author: Arthur Hugh Clough
blurb: In Venice a young man, scrupulous and unsure of his faith, is shadowed by a cynical Spirit who urges him to enjoy the world, take a profession and make terms with the way things are. Dipsychus answers in blank verse, lyric and song, and at last yields in part, with reservations.
