Hymn XV — To Heracles The Lion-Hearted
Hymn XXIII — To The Son Of Cronos, Most High
Hymn XXV — To The Muses And Apollo
Hymn XXX — To Earth The Mother Of All

title: The Homeric Hymns
author: Homer
blurb: George Chapman’s verse versions of the Homeric Hymns, the anonymous invocations to the Greek gods that antiquity ascribed to Homer, published around 1624 as the companion to his Iliad and Odyssey.

sections.title: Hymn XIV — To The Mother Of The Gods
Hymn XV — To Heracles The Lion-Hearted
Hymn XXIII — To The Son Of Cronos, Most High
Hymn XXV — To The Muses And Apollo
Hymn XXX — To Earth The Mother Of All
A Hymn to Men of Hospitality

title: The Homeric Hymns
author: Homer
blurb: Andrew Lang’s prose version of the thirty-three Homeric Hymns, the anonymous invocations to the Greek gods that antiquity ascribed to Homer. Lang numbers them in his own order, so his Hymn IV is the long Hymn to Demeter. Square brackets in the text are Lang’s own, marking passages of doubtful authenticity; his essays, notes and illustrations are omitted.

sections.title: XIII. To the Mother of the Gods
XXIV. To the Muses and Apollo
XXIX. To Earth, the Mother of All

title: The Hop-Garden
subtitle: A Georgic in Two Books
author: Christopher Smart
blurb: Smart's georgic in blank verse on the cultivation of hops in his native Kent, in the manner of Virgil and in the Miltonic style, first printed in his Poems on Several Occasions.

title: The House of Fame
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: A dream vision in three books in which the narrator is carried by a golden eagle to the palace of Fame, where rumour, reputation and the whims of the goddess decide which names endure.

title: Hudibras
subtitle: In Three Parts, Written in the Time of the Late Wars
author: Samuel Butler
blurb: Samuel Butler's mock-heroic satire on the Puritans and the Civil War, in which the knight Sir Hudibras and his squire Ralpho ride out to reform the world and are beaten, jailed and humbled in galloping octosyllabic couplets.

sections.title: An Heroical Epistle of Hudibras to Sidrophel
An Heroical Epistle of Hudibras to His Lady
The Lady's Answer to the Knight

title: The Tale of Alleyne
subtitle: from Moral Tales in Verse, vol. I (London, 1797)
author: Thomas Hull
blurb: A verse tale in two parts from Hull’s Moral Tales, preceded by a separate verse introduction.

title: The Tale of Cadwal
subtitle: from Moral Tales in Verse, vol. II (London, 1797)
author: Thomas Hull
blurb: A verse tale in two parts from Hull’s Moral Tales, preceded by a separate verse introduction.

title: The Tale of Edward and Orra
subtitle: from Moral Tales in Verse, vol. II (London, 1797)
author: Thomas Hull
blurb: A verse tale in four parts; the author’s note says its events occurred in a private London family about the middle of the eighteenth century.

title: The Tale of Foscue
subtitle: from Moral Tales in Verse, vol. I (London, 1797)
author: Thomas Hull
type: Narrative poem, in the manner of the old English ballad
blurb: A tale in two parts, written in imitation of the old English ballad; the source note says its hero, a Farmer-General, belongs to the years around 1761.

title: Richard Plantagenet
subtitle: A Legendary Tale, Now First Published
author: Thomas Hull
blurb: A legendary tale in two parts: the bricklayer Richard Plantagenet tells, in his old age, the story of his birth to the knight who has given him his land at Eastwell (London, 1774).

title: The Humours of the Court
subtitle: A Comedy in Three Acts
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's comedy in three acts, first published about 1893. The action fills three days at Belflor, the residence of the Countess Diana, where the Duke of Milan appears as Ricardo and her secretary Frederick, the major-domo Sir Gregory and his daughter Laura figure in the courtly intrigues.

title: Hymns to the Night
subtitle: Hymnen an die Nacht, translated from the German
author: Novalis (Friedrich von Hardenberg)
blurb: Six meditations on night, sleep and death, written after the death of the poet's betrothed, in George MacDonald's English.

title: Idylls of the King
subtitle: In Twelve Books
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
blurb: Tennyson's cycle of twelve idylls retelling the rise and fall of King Arthur's court, from The Coming of Arthur to The Passing of Arthur, framed by a dedication to Prince Albert and an epilogue to Queen Victoria.

title: Epistles
subtitle: The seven letters of Ignatius of Antioch
author: Ignatius of Antioch
blurb: Seven letters written by the bishop of Antioch while under guard on the road to martyrdom at Rome.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: Theodore Alois Buckley’s literal prose translation of Homer’s Iliad, keeping close to the Greek and marking its own additions in square brackets.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: Samuel Butler’s brisk, plain-spoken prose translation of Homer’s epic of the wrath of Akhilleus and the last year of the siege of Troy.

title: The Iliad
subtitle: The Iliads of Homer, translated by George Chapman
author: Homer
blurb: George Chapman’s Iliad, the first complete English translation of the poem from the Greek, whose rolling fourteeners Keats praised in his sonnet “On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer.”

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
translator: trans. William Cowper (1791; Southey’s edition, New York 1860)
blurb: William Cowper’s blank-verse translation of the Iliad, first published in 1791, here in the 1860 New York edition of Robert Southey’s text.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: The Earl of Derby, three times Prime Minister, rendered Homer’s epic of the wrath of Akhilleus into stately Victorian blank verse.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: Thomas Hobbes's rhymed-quatrain translation of the Iliad, first published in 1676 when the philosopher of the Leviathan was in his late eighties, here in the 1676 London edition of William Crook.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
translator: trans. Andrew Lang, Walter Leaf and Ernest Myers (1911)
blurb: The prose translation of the Iliad by Walter Leaf, Andrew Lang and Ernest Myers, in a deliberately archaic, Authorised-Version-flavoured English, here in the 1911 revised edition.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: A. T. Murray’s literal prose translation of the wrath of Akhilleus and the last year of the siege of Troy, from the Loeb Classical Library of 1924.

title: The Iliad
author: Homer
blurb: Alexander Pope’s celebrated heroic-couplet translation of the Iliad, one of the great achievements of Augustan English verse.

title: The Iliad (Way)
author: Homer
blurb: Arthur S. Way’s rhymed verse translation of the Iliad, in long swinging anapaestic lines, published in two volumes in 1886 and 1888.

title: In a Balcony
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A short drama in one scene. Norbert, a young statesman, has won the Queen's favour and asks Constance, her cousin and companion, to let him claim her hand as his reward. Constance advises a cautious approach; the Queen, hearing him speak, mistakes whom he loves, and the evening ends in discovery.

title: In the Name of Time
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: Michael Field
blurb: A tragedy in five acts set in eighth-century Francia and Italy. Carloman, Frankish Mayor of the Palace, is torn between his wife Geneviva and his vow to renounce the world, and leaves for Rome and Monte Cassino to take the monastic habit while his brother Pepin works toward the crown. Written by Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper, who published as Michael Field, it was issued posthumously in 1919.

title: Indian Idylls
subtitle: from the Sanskrit of the Mahabharata
author: Vyasa
blurb: Eight episodes from the Mahabharata in Sir Edwin Arnold's English verse, from the love of Savitri and the tale of Nala and Damayanti to the last journey of the Pandavas and Yudhisthira's entry into heaven.

title: The Inferno (Carlyle)
subtitle: Prose translation by John Aitken Carlyle, revised by H. Oelsner (Temple Classics)
author: Dante Alighieri
translator: trans. John Aitken Carlyle (1849), revised by H. Oelsner (Temple Classics, 1900)
blurb: Dante's journey through Hell in John Aitken Carlyle's plain, literal prose, revised for the Temple Classics by Hermann Oelsner, whose added words are kept in square brackets.

title: The Inferno (Sibbald)
subtitle: Translated by James Romanes Sibbald
author: Dante Alighieri
blurb: Dante's journey through Hell, in James Romanes Sibbald's Victorian terza rima, the form and rhyme of the original kept.

title: The Inferno (Wright)
subtitle: Translated by Ichabod Charles Wright
author: Dante Alighieri
blurb: Dante's journey through Hell in Ichabod Charles Wright's rhymed tercets, the three-line stanza of the original kept.

title: Iolanthe
subtitle: Or, The Peer and the Peri
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: The fairy Iolanthe, banished for marrying a mortal, is reunited with her son Strephon, a half-fairy shepherd who loves Phyllis, a ward of Chancery. When the Lord Chancellor and the peers of the realm contest Phyllis's hand, and Strephon enters Parliament, the Fairy Queen's magic turns the House of Lords upside down.

title: Ion
author: Euripides
blurb: At Delphi, the temple servant Ion does not know that he is the son of Apollo and Creusa, the Athenian queen who exposed him as a newborn. When she and her husband Xuthus come to the oracle, a false answer, a poisoned cup and a recognition at the altar bring mother and son together. Coleridge's literal prose translation.

title: Ion
author: Euripides
blurb: At Delphi, a temple servant named Ion, once a foundling left in the sanctuary of Apollo, meets the childless Athenian queen Kreusa and her husband Xuthus. A muddled oracle, a failed poisoning and an ark of hidden tokens bring mother and son to recognise one another. Arthur Way renders Euripides' play in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Iphigeneia at Aulis
author: Euripides
blurb: At Aulis the Greek fleet lies windbound, and the seer Kalchas declares that the goddess Artemis will release the winds only if Agamemnon sacrifices his daughter. Lured to the camp with the promise of a marriage to Akhilleus, Iphigeneia must choose between her mother's grief and her own willing death. Arthur Way renders Euripides' last tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Iphigeneia in Taurica
author: Euripides
blurb: Snatched from the altar at Aulis by Artemis, Iphigeneia serves as priestess in the savage land of the Taurians, where every Greek who lands is sacrificed to the goddess. When two strangers are seized on the shore, she finds that one of them is her brother Orestes, and together they plot an escape with the goddess's image. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy of recognition in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Iphigenia in Tauris
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
blurb: Goethe's verse drama in five acts. Iphigenia, saved from sacrifice at Aulis and made priestess of Diana among the Taurians, longs for Greece. When her brother Orestes, pursued by the Furies, arrives with his friend Pylades as captives destined for the altar, she must choose between truth and escape, and between loyalty to the king who sheltered her and the call of her family.

title: Speeches
author: Isaeus
blurb: Eleven speeches and a large fragment of a twelfth by the Athenian orator Isaeus, nearly all of them inheritance cases, in Forster's Loeb translation.

title: Discourses, Volume I
subtitle: To Demonicus, To Nicocles, Nicocles or the Cyprians, Panegyricus, To Philip, Archidamus
author: Isocrates
blurb: Six of the discourses of the Athenian orator Isocrates, from the first volume of Norlin's Loeb edition: three on kingship and conduct, the Panegyricus, and the appeals to Philip and Archidamus.

title: Discourses, Volume II
subtitle: On the Peace, Areopagiticus, Against the Sophists, Antidosis, Panathenaicus
author: Isocrates
blurb: Five of the discourses of the Athenian orator Isocrates, from the second volume of Norlin's Loeb edition: the appeals On the Peace and the Areopagiticus, the prospectus Against the Sophists, the Antidosis (his defence of his life's work as a teacher), and the Panathenaicus.

title: Italy
subtitle: A Poem
author: Samuel Rogers
blurb: Samuel Rogers's travel poem in blank verse, published in two parts in 1822 and 1828, in which a pilgrim from the north passes through the Alps, Lombardy, Venice, Florence, Rome and Naples, telling the local legends as he goes.

title: Jenny
author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
blurb: A dramatic monologue spoken at dawn by a young man over the sleeping prostitute whose head rests on his knee.

title: Jerusalem
subtitle: The Emanation of the Giant Albion
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's longest prophetic poem, in four chapters, in which the sleeping giant Albion is called back to Jerusalem, his lost Emanation, and to the forgiveness of sins.

title: Jerusalem Delivered
subtitle: Gerusalemme Liberata
author: Torquato Tasso
blurb: Tasso's epic of the First Crusade and the siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon, in twenty books of ottava rima, in Edward Fairfax's English version.

title: Jerusalem Delivered
subtitle: Translated into English Spenserian Verse by J. H. Wiffen
author: Torquato Tasso
blurb: Tasso's epic of the First Crusade and the siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon, in twenty books, in J. H. Wiffen's English version in nine-line Spenserian stanzas (1824–25).

title: The Jew of Malta
author: Christopher Marlowe
blurb: Barabas, the richest Jew of Malta, is stripped of his wealth by Governor Ferneze to pay the tribute owed the Turks, and sets out on a course of revenge that costs him his daughter Abigail, a convent of nuns, two friars and his own accomplices. Prefaced by Machiavel in person, Marlowe's savage comedy of greed, religion and policy ends with Barabas boiled in the very cauldron he prepared for the Turkish prince.

sections.title: Prologue to the Stage, at the Cock-pit
Epilogue to the Stage, at the Cock-pit

title: Joan of Arc, an Epic Poem
subtitle: In Ten Books (first edition, 1796)
author: Robert Southey
blurb: Southey's youthful republican epic in ten books of blank verse, written in 1793 and published in 1796: Joan of Arc heals the wounded Dunois, wins over Charles VII and the besieged city of Orleans, and in visions of Heaven and Hell sees the crimes of kings and the hope of a freer world.

title: The Book of Job
subtitle: Authorized Version of the book of Job.
author: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
blurb: A long poetic dialogue between Job and his friends, set within a prose frame.

title: Job the White
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Third Series: 2
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A sequel to The Manx Witch, in dialect verse, which Brown published in The New Review in December 1895.

title: Clifton
subtitle: a Poem, in Two Cantos
author: Henry Jones
blurb: Henry Jones's topographical poem on Clifton and the Hotwells near Bristol, praising its spa, its houses and its company in heroic couplets.

title: The Isle of Wight
subtitle: a Poem, in Three Cantos
author: Henry Jones
blurb: Henry Jones's topographical poem in three cantos on the Isle of Wight, its scenery and towns, written in heroic couplets.

title: Against Apion
subtitle: Josephus's defence of the antiquity of the Jewish people against Apion and other Greek detractors, in two books
author: Flavius Josephus
blurb: Josephus's reply to the slanders of Apion, Manetho, Apollonius Molon and others, setting out the antiquity of the Jews and the excellence of their law, in William Whiston's English of 1737.

title: The Antiquities of the Jews
subtitle: The Jewish Antiquities, in twenty books, from the Creation to the twelfth year of Nero
author: Flavius Josephus
blurb: Josephus's history of the Jewish people from the Creation to the eve of the revolt against Rome, in twenty books, in William Whiston's English of 1737.

title: The Wars of the Jews; or, The History of the Destruction of Jerusalem
subtitle: The Jewish War, in seven books, from the capture of Jerusalem by Antiochus Epiphanes to the fall of Masada
author: Flavius Josephus
blurb: Josephus's eyewitness account of the Jewish revolt against Rome (AD 66–73), from the siege of Jotapata to the burning of the Temple and the end at Masada, in William Whiston's English of 1737.

title: The Life of Flavius Josephus
subtitle: Josephus's autobiography, written about AD 100 as an appendix to the Antiquities
author: Flavius Josephus
blurb: Josephus's account of his priestly descent, his schooling among the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, his command in Galilee during the revolt against Rome, and his later life, in William Whiston's English of 1737.

title: Judas Maccabaeus
subtitle: A Play in Five Acts
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: A verse play on the Jewish revolt against the Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes. Antiochus, with the renegade High-Priest Jason, tries to force Greek gods on Jerusalem; a mother and her seven sons endure martyrdom; Judas Maccabaeus rallies the Jews, defeats the general Nicanor and retakes the Temple; and the play closes with the death of Antiochus.

title: Judith
author: Anonymous (Old English)
translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
blurb: A retelling, in the Nowell Codex alongside Beowulf, of the apocryphal Book of Judith: the widow Judith beheads the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes and delivers her people, recast in the heroic idiom of Old English verse.

title: Judith (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: A retelling, in the Nowell Codex alongside Beowulf, of the apocryphal Book of Judith, in the original Old English: the widow Judith beheads the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes and delivers her people, recast in the heroic idiom of Old English verse.

title: Juliana
author: Cynewulf
blurb: One of Cynewulf's four signed poems: the passion of the virgin martyr Juliana of Nicomedia, who resists both an unwanted marriage to a pagan prefect and torture by a demon sent to break her faith.

title: Juliana (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Cynewulf
blurb: The Old English verse of one of Cynewulf's four signed poems: the passion of the virgin martyr Juliana of Nicomedia, who resists both an unwanted marriage to a pagan prefect and torture by a demon sent to break her faith.

title: The Civil War
subtitle: Commentaries on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, 49–48 BC, in three books (De Bello Civili)
author: Julius Caesar
translator: trans. W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn (1869)
blurb: Caesar's own account of the outbreak of the war with Pompey and the Senate: the crossing of the Rubicon, the Italian and Spanish campaigns, the siege of Massilia, and the struggle in Illyricum, Africa, Epirus and Thessaly down to the eve of the Alexandrian war.

title: The Gallic War
subtitle: Commentaries on the war in Gaul, 58–52 BC, in eight books (De Bello Gallico)
author: Julius Caesar
translator: trans. W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn (1869)
blurb: Caesar's own account of his campaigns against the Gauls, Germans and Britons, from the Helvetian migration to the siege of Alesia and the final pacification of Gaul, with Hirtius's continuation.

title: The Tragedy of Julius Caesar
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Rome's leaders fear that Julius Caesar, fresh from his triumph over Pompey's sons, will make himself king. Cassius draws the honourable Brutus into a conspiracy, and the conspirators stab Caesar in the Capitol on the Ides of March. Brutus justifies the killing to the crowd, but Mark Antony's funeral speech turns the people against the assassins and they are driven from the city. Brutus and Cassius quarrel, then are overwhelmed by Antony and Octavius at Philippi, where both die by their own hands.

title: The Kalevala
subtitle: The Epic Poem of Finland
author: Elias Lönnrot
blurb: Fifty runes of Finnish folk song gathered into one epic: the birth of the sage Wainamoinen, the rivalry of Finns and the people of Pohjola for the Sampo, the doomed Kullervo, and the hero's departure as a new age arrives.

subtitle: The Land of the Heroes
author: Elias Lönnrot
blurb: Kirby's 1907 English version of the Finnish national epic in fifty runos, from the birth of the sage Väinämöinen through the forging and theft of the Sampo and the doomed Kullervo to the hero's departure as Marjatta's child is made King of Carelia.

title: The Kasîdah of Hâjî Abdû El-Yezdî
author: Sir Richard Francis Burton
blurb: A philosophical quatrain-sequence in which a desert traveller, Haji Abdu, reflects on faith, fate and the vanity of creeds. Burton's own composition, offered as a rendering from the Persian.

title: Keep Your Own Secret
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: At the court of Parma the Prince, his secretary Don Cesar and the courtier Don Felix each hide a love from the rest, and every secret confided to the wrong ear tangles the plot further. The comedy ends with Nisida's hand placed in Felix's and a moral against trusting even a friend with a secret.

title: King Arthur
subtitle: Books I to XII
author: Edward Bulwer Lytton
blurb: Bulwer Lytton’s twelve-book romantic epic in Spenserian stanzas, following Arthur and the wizard Merlin through the three labours of Fable-land.

title: King Horn
subtitle: Middle English text of Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27.2, ed. J. R. Lumby (1866), re-ed. G. H. McKnight (1901)
author: Anonymous
blurb: The earliest surviving English verse romance: the exiled prince Horn, cast adrift as a boy after Saracens kill his father, wins the love of Rymenhild, proves himself in Ireland, and returns to reclaim his kingdom.

title: The Life and Death of King John
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: King John holds the English crown against the claim of his nephew Arthur, whom France backs, and the play follows the quarrel through the siege of Angiers, the bargained marriage of Louis and Blanche, and the grief of Arthur's mother Constance. Philip Faulconbridge, the Bastard, acknowledged as Richard Lionheart's son, becomes the play's sardonic commentator on politics and 'commodity'. Arthur dies leaping from the castle walls, the barons turn against John, and the king is poisoned at Swinstead Abbey, leaving England to young Henry.

title: The Tragedy of King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: King Lear, old and weary of rule, divides his kingdom among his daughters according to their professions of love, banishing the plain-spoken Cordelia and Kent. Goneril and Regan soon strip him of his retinue and turn him out into the storm, where he goes mad upon the heath beside his Fool and the disguised Edgar. Meanwhile Gloucester, deceived by his bastard son Edmund, is blinded for helping the king. Cordelia returns with a French army, but Lear and she are defeated, and the play ends in the deaths of Cordelia, Lear and almost all the rest.

title: King Victor and King Charles: A Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A historical tragedy of the House of Savoy. In 1730 the aged Victor Amadeus, first King of Sardinia, abdicates in favour of his timid son Charles; within a year he regrets it and tries to take the crown back, and the second half of the play follows the son's struggle to keep his throne against his father and the minister D'Ormea.

sections.title: First Year, 1730: King Victor, Part I
First Year, 1730: King Victor, Part II
Second Year, 1731: King Charles, Part I
Second Year, 1731: King Charles, Part II

title: The King’s Threshold
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: Seanchan, chief poet of Ireland, lies fasting on the steps of King Guaire’s palace because the king has stripped poets of their place at his council. His pupils, the court ladies, a monk and the king himself urge him to eat, and the poet will not give way, even for his sweetheart Fedelm. Yeats’s one-act play, drawn from an old Irish tale, argues the dignity of poetry against power.

title: Kitty of the Sherragh Vane
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series: 2
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A two-part dialect yarn set at the Sherragh Vane, a farm high up Sulby glen, with Kitty and Saul at its centre.

title: The Knight of Curtesy
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A poem of 500 lines in four-line stanzas, an English version of the story of the Chastelain de Couci and the lady of Fayel: the knight of Curtesy and the lady of Faguell love in chastity, her jealous husband sends him to fight at Rhodes, and after the knight is killed the husband serves his heart to her at table.

title: Konrad Wallenrod
subtitle: An Historical Poem
author: Adam Mickiewicz
blurb: Mickiewicz's narrative poem of 1828 in six cantos: a Lithuanian taken as a boy by the Teutonic Knights rises to be their Grand Master, and, hiding his vengeance behind a mask, leads the Order to ruin. Read in its day as a parable of Poland under Russian rule. Translated by Maude Ashurst Biggs.

title: The Kyng of Tars
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: The Christian king of Tars refuses his daughter to the Sultan of Damascus, who attacks his kingdom; to save her father's people she marries the heathen lord, and bears him a shapeless lump of flesh. Christian baptism turns the lump into a living, fair child, the Sultan renounces his gods and is himself baptised, and the converted Sultan then conquers the lands of his enemies.

title: The Lady of the Lake
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A romance of the Scottish Highlands, unfolding over six days on the shores of Loch Katrine, that made Sir Walter Scott the most popular poet in Europe.

title: Laili and Majnun
subtitle: A poem from the original Persian of Nizami, translated by James Atkinson
author: Nizami Ganjavi
blurb: The Arab tale of Qays, who is driven mad by love and called Majnun, and of Laili, who is married to another and dies of longing, as Nizami told it in the twelfth century and Atkinson first rendered it into English verse.

title: Lalla Rookh
subtitle: An Oriental Romance
author: Thomas Moore
blurb: Thomas Moore's best-selling Oriental romance: four verse tales told to a princess on her journey from Delhi to Kashmir, by the young poet Feramorz.

title: Lamentations
subtitle: Authorized Version of Lamentations.
author: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
blurb: Five laments for the fallen city of Jerusalem.

title: The Lamp and the Bell
subtitle: A Drama in Five Acts, written for the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Vassar College Alumnae Association
author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
blurb: A verse drama set in the kingdoms of Fiori and Lagoverde, in the spirit of the fairy tale of Snow-White and Rose-Red. Beatrice, 'Rose-Red', daughter of King Lorenzo, and Bianca, 'Snow-White', daughter of his second wife Octavia, are stepsisters who love each other dearly, and the play follows their bond across its five acts. It was written for the fiftieth anniversary of the Vassar College Alumnae Association, and includes the songs that Millay also gathered as Three Songs from The Lamp and the Bell.

title: Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart
subtitle: Lancelot, ou Le Chevalier de la charrette
author: Chrétien de Troyes
blurb: Lancelot braves shame and peril to rescue Queen Guinevere from Meleagant; concluded by Godefroi de Leigni.

title: Lancelot of the Laik
subtitle: A Scottish Metrical Romance
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle Scots romance in decasyllabic couplets, after the French prose Lancelot. A lovesick poet is bidden by a vision to write of Lancelot, then tells of King Arthur at Carlisle, his dreams, the war with Galiot, and Lancelot’s love for Guinevere. The manuscript breaks off in mid-battle.

title: Lancelot
subtitle: A Poem
author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
blurb: Blank-verse Arthurian narrative in nine parts: Lancelot, Gawaine, Guinevere and the fall of Arthur's kingdom, as Lancelot rides out in search of the Light.

title: The Land of Heart's Desire
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: On a May Eve in the Barony of Kilmacowen, County Sligo, young Mary Bruin, absorbed in an old book of faery tales, is called away from her husband Shawn and her household by a Faery Child who claims her for the land of heart's desire. Father Hart's crucifix and the family's blessings are set against the child's songs of a land where nobody grows old, and Mary must choose between hearth and faeryland.

title: Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland
subtitle: A Modern Poem in Twelve Chapters
author: William Allingham
blurb: Allingham's verse novel of Irish rural life: a young landlord returns to his Ulster-bordering estate and confronts agents, tenants, secret societies and evictions, in twelve chapters of heroic couplets.

sections.title: Chapter III. A Dinner at Lisnamoy House
Chapter VI. Neal at the Lough

title: The Tale of the Armament of Igor
subtitle: A Russian historical epic, A.D. 1185 (the Slovo o polku Igoreve)
author: Anonymous (The Lay of Igor's Campaign)
blurb: The only surviving epic of medieval Kievan Rus', telling of Prince Igor Svyatoslavic's ill-fated raid on the Polovtsy in 1185, his defeat and capture, the lament of his wife Yaroslavna, and his escape home.

title: The Lay of the Cid
subtitle: Cantar de Mio Cid
author: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
translator: trans. R. Selden Rose and Leonard Bacon (1919)
blurb: The anonymous twelfth-century Castilian epic of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, in three cantares: his banishment, the marriage of his daughters, and the affront of Corpes.

sections.title: Cantar I: The Banishment of the Cid
Cantar II: The Marriage of the Cid's Daughters
Cantar III: The Affront of Corpes

title: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
subtitle: A Poem
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A verse romance of Border feud, magic and thwarted love in sixteenth-century Branksome Hall, framed as the song of the last of the old minstrels.

title: Le Bone Florence of Rome
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of about 2,190 lines in twelve-line stanzas: Florence, daughter of the emperor Otes of Rome, is sought in marriage by the aged emperor Garcy, and after her father's death she marries the knight Emere. In his absence she is slandered, driven out and sold at sea, and at last becomes a nun at Beverfayre, where she heals her husband and her enemies.

title: The Legend of Good Women
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: Commanded by the God of Love to atone for Troilus and Criseyde, the poet dreams a Prologue among daisies and then tells nine legends of women who were faithful in love and betrayed by men.

sections.title: IV. The Legend of Hypsipyle and Medea

title: The Legends of Saint Patrick
author: Aubrey de Vere
blurb: Fifteen narrative poems on the conversion of Ireland, from the infant baptism of Patrick to his dying Confession, drawn from the ancient Lives of the saint.

sections.title: The Disbelief of Milcho, or, Saint Patrick’s One Failure

title: Leoline and Sydanis
subtitle: A Romance of the Amorous Adventures of Princes
author: Sir Francis Kynaston
blurb: Kynaston's rhyme-royal romance of the Welsh prince Leoline and the Princess Sydanis, enchanted lovers parted by sorcery and reunited after many adventures, first printed in 1642 with the Cynthiades.

title: The Lesser Testament
subtitle: Le Lais, translated by John Payne
author: François Villon
blurb: Written at Christmas 1456, as Villon prepared to leave Paris, this is a comic will in which he bequeaths his imaginary property, and his scorn, to friends, enemies and officials of the city.

title: The Libation-Bearers
subtitle: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
blurb: Orestes, banished since boyhood, comes back to his father's tomb at Argos and meets his sister Electra there among the women bearing offerings for the dead. At Apollo's bidding he kills his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus to avenge Agamemnon, and is driven out of his wits by the avenging Furies.

title: Liberty
subtitle: A Poem in Five Parts
author: James Thomson
blurb: Thomson's blank-verse vision in five parts, in which the Goddess of Liberty traces her course from ancient Greece and Rome through the dark ages to her settled home in Britain.

sections.title: Part I: Ancient and Modern Italy Compared

title: The Life and Death of Jason
subtitle: A Poem
author: William Morris
blurb: Morris's first long narrative poem, in seventeen books of rhymed couplets: Jason's boyhood among the Centaurs, the voyage of the Argo, the winning of the Golden Fleece with Medea's help, and the tragedy of their later life at Iolchos and Corinth.

title: A Life-Drama
subtitle: In Thirteen Scenes
author: Alexander Smith
blurb: The poem that made Smith’s name: the story of the young poet Walter, his ambition, loves and disillusion, told in blank verse and lyric in thirteen scenes.

title: The Light of Asia
author: Sir Edwin Arnold
blurb: Arnold's blank-verse life of the Buddha, narrated by a devout Buddhist, from the prince's birth through the Great Renunciation to his enlightenment and teaching.

title: The Light of the World
subtitle: or, The Great Consummation
author: Sir Edwin Arnold
blurb: Arnold's blank-verse life of Christ, told by Mary Magdalene to a visiting Indian sage in her house at Magdala, from the Nativity to the Resurrection.

sections.title: Book V. The Love of God and Man

title: Lilian
author: Cecil Frances Alexander
blurb: A long narrative poem from Cecil Frances Alexander's collected Poems (1896).

title: The History of Rome, Books XXVII–XXXVI
subtitle: Ab Urbe Condita, from Hannibal in Italy to the war with Antiochus
author: Livy
blurb: Livy's narrative of the later Second Punic War, from the death of Marcellus and Scipio's victories in Spain, through the defeat of Hannibal at Zama, to the Macedonian and Syrian wars, in the English translation of Cyrus R. Edmonds.

title: The History of Rome, Books XXXVII–XLV, with the Epitomes
subtitle: Ab Urbe Condita, from the war with Antiochus to the fall of Perseus, with the summaries of the lost later books
author: Livy
blurb: Livy's narrative of the war with Antiochus, the Macedonian wars and the defeat of King Perseus at Pydna, down to 167 BC, in the English translation of W. A. McDevitte, followed by the epitomes of the lost books that carried the history on to the death of Drusus in 9 BC.

title: The History of Rome, Books I–VII
subtitle: Books I–VII: Ab Urbe Condita, from Aeneas and the founding of the city, through the kings and the early Republic, to the Gallic sack and the struggles of the orders
author: Livy
translator: trans. Rev. Canon William Masfen Roberts (1912-1924)
blurb: Livy's narrative of Rome from Aeneas and the foundation of the city, through the kings and the early Republic, the Decemvirate and the destruction of Rome by the Gauls, to the wars on the frontiers, in the English translation of Canon W. M. Roberts.

title: The History of Rome, Books VIII–X, XXI–XXIV
subtitle: Books VIII–X, XXI–XXIV: Ab Urbe Condita, the Samnite wars, then Hannibal in Italy from Saguntum to the fall of Syracuse
author: Livy
translator: trans. Rev. Canon William Masfen Roberts (1912-1924)
blurb: Livy's account of the Samnite wars down to 293 BC (Books VIII–X), followed, after the lost Books XI–XX, by the opening of the Second Punic War: Saguntum, the Trebia, Cannae, Hannibal at Capua and the fall of Syracuse, in the English translation of Canon W. M. Roberts.

title: The History of Rome, Books XXV–XXXI
subtitle: Books XXV–XXXI: Ab Urbe Condita, from the fate of Capua and Scipio in Spain to the end of the Hannibalic War and the Second Macedonian War begun
author: Livy
translator: trans. Rev. Canon William Masfen Roberts (1912-1924)
blurb: Livy's narrative of the later Second Punic War, from the fall of Capua and Scipio's campaigns in Spain and Africa to the close of the Hannibalic War, and the opening of the Second Macedonian War, in the English translation of Canon W. M. Roberts.

title: The History of Rome, Books XXXII–XXXVIII
subtitle: Books XXXII–XXXVIII: Ab Urbe Condita, from the Second Macedonian War to the war with Antiochus and the trial of Scipio
author: Livy
translator: trans. Rev. Canon William Masfen Roberts (1912-1924)
blurb: Livy's narrative of the Second Macedonian War, the settlement of Greece, the war against Antiochus in Greece and Asia, and the arraignment of Scipio Africanus, in the English translation of Canon W. M. Roberts.

title: The History of Rome, Books XXXIX–XLV
subtitle: Books XXXIX–XLV: Ab Urbe Condita, from the Bacchanalia to the fall of Macedonia
author: Livy
translator: trans. Rev. Canon William Masfen Roberts (1912-1924)
blurb: Livy's narrative from the suppression of the Bacchanalia and the quarrel of Perseus and Demetrius, through the Third Macedonian War, to Pydna and the fall of Macedonia, in the English translation of Canon W. M. Roberts.

title: The History of Rome, Books I–VIII
subtitle: Ab Urbe Condita, from the founding of the city to 293 BC
author: Livy
blurb: Livy's narrative of Rome from Aeneas and the foundation of the city, through the kings and the early Republic, to the Samnite wars, in the English translation of D. Spillan.

title: The History of Rome, Books IX–XXVI
subtitle: Ab Urbe Condita, from the Samnite wars to the fall of Capua
author: Livy
translator: trans. D. Spillan and Cyrus R. Edmonds (1849-50)
blurb: Livy's narrative from the Caudine Forks and the later Samnite wars, through the Pyrrhic and First Punic wars (known for Books XI–XX only from short epitomes), to Hannibal's invasion and the fall of Capua in the Second Punic War, in the English translation of D. Spillan and Cyrus R. Edmonds.

title: On the Sublime
subtitle: Peri Hupsous
author: Longinus
blurb: The Greek treatise on what makes writing great, by an anonymous first-century critic traditionally called Longinus, with quoted passages of Homer, Sappho, Plato and Demosthenes.

title: Daphnis and Chloe
subtitle: A Pastoral Novel
author: Longus
blurb: Two foundlings, a boy suckled by a goat and a girl nursed by a ewe, are raised by humble herdsmen on Lesbos, and as the seasons turn they discover love, with the help of pirates, rivals, shepherds and Pan, until their birth is revealed and they marry.

title: The Lord of the Isles
subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A verse romance of the Scottish Wars of Independence, from Robert the Bruce's return to the Hebrides in 1307 to his victory at Bannockburn, woven round the story of Edith of Lorn.

title: Love is Enough, or The Freeing of Pharamond: A Morality
subtitle: A Morality
author: William Morris
blurb: Morris's verse morality, played before a newly wedded Emperor and Empress, tells of King Pharamond, who leaves his throne to seek Love and finds that Love is enough. The play is framed by the peasant couple Giles and Joan and by lyric interludes sung by the Music.

Pharamond: In the King's Chamber of Audience

Pharamond: On a Highway in a Valley
Love, Holding a Crown and Palm-Branch
Giles and Joan: After the Play
Giles and Joan: The Way Home

title: Love's Labour's Lost
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: The King of Navarre and his three lords swear off women, wealth and sleep for three years of study, only for the Princess of France and her ladies to arrive on an embassy and overturn the oath. Berowne, Longaville and Dumaine each write secret love-verses and are found out in turn, and the lords disguise themselves as Muscovites to woo the ladies, who mock them. A pageant of the Nine Worthies is interrupted by news of the French king's death, and the ladies set the lovers a year's penance, ending with the songs of Spring and Winter.

title: The Loves of the Angels
subtitle: A Poem
author: Thomas Moore
blurb: Moore's 1823 poem in which three fallen angels, conversing on a hillside at evening, each tell the story of the mortal woman for whose love he lost heaven.

title: The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Volume I
subtitle: Satires and dialogues, from The Vision to the Voyage to the Lower World
author: Lucian
translator: trans. H. W. and F. G. Fowler (1905)
blurb: Fifteen pieces by the Syrian satirist of the Antonine age: his autobiographical Vision, the dialogues of gods, sea-gods and the dead, and the comic fantasies in which Charon, Hermes and Zeus show up the follies of philosophers, priests and the rich.

sections.title: Trial in the Court of Vowels

title: The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Volume II
subtitle: The Dependent Scholar to Lexiphanes: essays, dialogues, declamations and The True History
author: Lucian
translator: trans. H. W. and F. G. Fowler (1905)
blurb: Seventeen pieces by the Syrian satirist of the Antonine age: the essays on the dependent scholar and on writing history, the philosophical dialogue Hermotimus, the oracle-monger Alexander, the dance-essay Of Pantomime, and The True History, the travellers' tale of a voyage to the moon.

sections.title: A Slip of the Tongue in Salutation

title: The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Volume III
subtitle: The Life of Demonax to The Fly: biography, dialogues, essays and lectures
author: Lucian
translator: trans. H. W. and F. G. Fowler (1905)
blurb: Nineteen pieces by the Syrian satirist of the Antonine age: the Life of Demonax, the two Portrait-Study essays, Toxaris on friendship, the Zeus dialogues, Icaromenippus and its flight to heaven, The Parasite, Anacharsis, and the comic lectures on Dionysus, Heracles, the Fly and the book-collector.

sections.title: The Parasite, a Demonstration That Sponging Is a Profession
Anacharsis, a Discussion of Physical Training
Remarks Addressed to an Illiterate Book-Fancier

title: The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Volume IV
subtitle: Slander, a Warning to The Purist Purized: essays, dialogues, the Peregrine and the Saturnalia
author: Lucian
translator: trans. H. W. and F. G. Fowler (1905)
blurb: Fifteen pieces by the Syrian satirist of the Antonine age: the essays on Slander, the Hall and Patriotism, the voyage-and-wishes dialogue The Ship, the Dialogues of the Hetaerae, the death of the Cynic Peregrine, the Saturnalia with its festival laws and letters, the quarrelsome philosophers' banquet of A Feast of Lapithae, and the comic assemblies of The Gods in Council and The Purist Purized.

title: Lucifer
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: Joost van den Vondel
blurb: Vondel's Lucifer (1654) stages the revolt in Heaven. When the herald Gabriel announces that God means to set man, still unborn in Paradise, above the angels, the proud Lucifer and his followers, Belzebub, Belial and Apollion among them, resolve to rebel. Michael leads the loyal host against them, the rebels are cast down into hell, and the angels' chorus closes the play with the promise of a Redeemer. The Dutch poet's drama has long been compared with Milton's Paradise Lost.

title: Lucile
author: Robert Bulwer-Lytton, Earl of Lytton (Owen Meredith)
blurb: A verse novel in twelve cantos: the Comtesse de Nevers, once the lover of Lord Alfred Vargrave, calls him to Luchon on the eve of his marriage, and a story of renunciation and loyalty unfolds.

title: Luria: A Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A tragedy of Renaissance Florence. Luria, a Moorish general serving the Republic against Pisa, wins his campaign but learns that the Florentine commissary Braccio has already prepared the charges that will destroy him once the war is over. Loyal to the end, he chooses his own way out.

title: The Lusiad, or Portugals Historicall Poem
subtitle: Os Lusíadas
author: Luís de Camões
blurb: Camões's national epic of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the story of Portugal, in ten cantos of ottava rima, first Englished by Sir Richard Fanshawe in 1655.

title: The Lusiad; or, The Discovery of India
subtitle: Os Lusíadas
author: Luís de Camões
translator: trans. William Julius Mickle (1776), rev. E. Richmond Hodges (1877)
blurb: Camões's national epic of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the story of Portugal, in ten books, rendered into English heroic couplets by William Julius Mickle.

title: The Lusiads
subtitle: Os Lusíadas
author: Luís de Camões
blurb: Camões's national epic of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the story of Portugal, in ten cantos of ottava rima, rendered into English by Sir Richard Francis Burton.

title: Lybeaus Disconus
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: Gawain's son, raised in a forest by his mother and not knowing his own name, takes the armour of a slain knight and is knighted by King Arthur as Lybeaus Disconus, the Fair Unknown. He rides out with the lady Elene and her dwarf to free the Lady of Synadowne, defeating Maugys, Lambard, Gyffroun and other champions on the way, and at last frees the lady from her enchantment by a kiss.

title: Lycidus; or, The Lover in Fashion
subtitle: The songs
author: Aphra Behn
blurb: The verse songs of Behn's prose tale of Lycidus, a fashionable rake's account of his own voyage to the Isle of Love, with its amorous pursuits and its farewell to love.

title: Ane Dialog betuix Experience and ane Courteour
subtitle: The Monarche
author: Sir David Lyndsay
blurb: A long dialogue in Middle Scots, written in 1553, in which the old courtier-turned-sage Experience instructs a Courteour on the misery of the world, rehearsing the history of the four great monarchies from Creation to the Last Judgement and attacking idolatry and the abuses of Church and state.

title: Speeches
author: Lysias
blurb: Thirty-four law-court speeches by the Athenian speech-writer Lysias, from the murder trial of Eratosthenes to the Funeral Oration, in Lamb's Loeb translation.

title: The Tragedy of Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Returning from battle, the Scottish general Macbeth is hailed by three witches as future king. Urged on by Lady Macbeth, he murders King Duncan in his sleep and seizes the throne, then kills Banquo and Macduff's family to secure it. Haunted by guilt, and by Banquo's ghost, he falls to the English army and Macduff at Dunsinane, as Birnam Wood seems to come against him. The play ends with Malcolm proclaimed king.

title: The Madness of Herakles
author: Euripides
blurb: While Herakles is away in the Underworld on his last labour, the usurper Lykus threatens to kill his wife, sons and aged father; the hero returns in time to save them, only for Hera to send Madness upon him. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in English verse, with the choral odes in rhymed lyric measures.

title: Madoc
subtitle: A Poem, in Two Parts
author: Robert Southey
blurb: The Welsh prince Madoc sails west across the Atlantic, finds a new land, and returns to Wales for settlers; on his second voyage he wars with the Aztecs and overthrows their bloody gods.

title: Mador of the Moor
author: James Hogg
blurb: A romance of fourteenth-century Scotland in Spenserian stanzas, in five cantos with an introduction and a conclusion, of the lost Mador and a king's night in the Highlands.

title: Magnyfycence
subtitle: A Goodly Interlude and a Mery
author: John Skelton
blurb: A morality interlude in rhyme royal. The prince Magnyfycence, advised by Measure, is flattered by the courtiers Counterfet Countenaunce, Crafty Conueyaunce and Cloked Colusyon, who lead him to dismiss restraint and spend with Lyberte and Fansy. Adversity strikes him down and Poverty, Despair and Mischief bring him to the edge of self-murder, until Goodhope, Redresse and Sad Circumspeccyon raise him up and restore him to his state. Skelton's warning to the court of Henry VIII on the fall of great men.

title: Maha-bharata
subtitle: The Epic of Ancient India Condensed into English Verse
author: Vyasa
blurb: Romesh Chunder Dutt's condensed English rendering of the great Sanskrit epic of the Kuru and Pandava war, in twelve books of rhymed couplets, from the tournament at Hastina to the sacrifice of the horse. Published by J. M. Dent and Co., Aldine House, London, 1899.

sections.title: Book XII: Sacrifice of the Horse

title: The Mahabharata, Book 1: Adi Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Beginning
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 1 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta, from 1883. The Adi Parva tells how the epic came to be recited, the stories of the Bharata line, the birth and upbringing of the Kauravas and Pandavas, and the winning of Draupadi, down to the burning of the Khandava forest.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 10: Sauptika Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Sleeping Warriors
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 10 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Sauptika Parva recounts the night massacre: Ashvatthama, resolving on revenge for the dying Duryodhana, kills the sleeping Pandava camp, and the Aishika weapon is loosed and turned aside.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 11: Stri Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Women
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 11 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Stri Parva is the lament of the women: Dhritarashtra's grief and anger, Gandhari's curse, the widows moving over the field of Kurukshetra among the dead, and the funeral rites for the fallen.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 12: Santi Parva
subtitle: The Book of Peace
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 12 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Santi Parva, the longest book of the epic, opens with Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows after the war, instructing the grieving Yudhishthira on the duties of kings, on conduct in times of distress, and on the paths to liberation.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 13: Anusasana Parva
subtitle: The Book of Instructions
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 13 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Anusasana Parva gives Bhishma's further teaching on gifts, duties and the merit of deeds, ending with his death and ascent.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 14: Aswamedhika Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Horse Sacrifice
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 14 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Aswamedhika Parva tells of the horse sacrifice by which Yudhishthira, once the war is over and the kingdom secure, claims the sovereignty of the earth. Before it Krishna relates the Anugita, a philosophical discourse to Arjuna, and Arjuna follows the sacrificial horse on its wanderings, fighting its opponents.

title: Book 15: Asramavasika Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Hermitage
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 15 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Asramavasika Parva follows the old king Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti as they leave the city for a hermitage in the forest, where the dead of the war are briefly seen again, and ends with the forest fire in which they die.

title: Book 16: Mausala Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Clubs
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 16 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Mausala Parva records the destruction of the Vrishni clan, who slaughter one another with iron clubs thirty-six years after the war, and the departure of Krishna and Balarama from the world.

title: Book 17: Mahaprasthanika Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Great Journey
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 17 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. In the Mahaprasthanika Parva the Pandavas renounce the kingdom and walk north toward the Himalaya, and one by one Draupadi and four of her husbands fall by the way.

title: Book 18: Svargarohanika Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Ascent to Heaven
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 18 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Svargarohanika Parva brings the epic to its close: Yudhishthira's trial at the gates of Heaven, his sight of Hell, the reunion of the heroes, and the closing words on the merit of hearing the Mahabharata.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 2: Sabha Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Assembly Hall
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 2 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Sabha Parva tells of the building of Yudhishthira's great assembly hall, the Rajasuya sacrifice, the death of Sisupala, and the fateful game of dice.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Forest
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 3 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Vana Parva tells of the twelve years of the Pandavas' exile in the forest after the game of dice, with the tale of Nala and Damayanti, the pilgrimages, Arjuna's quest for celestial weapons, and the Yaksha's riddling questions.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 4: Virata Parva
subtitle: The Book of Virata
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 4 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Virata Parva tells of the thirteenth year of exile, when the Pandavas live in disguise at the court of King Virata, the slaying of Kichaka, and the great cattle raid and battle against the Kauravas.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 5: Udyoga Parva
subtitle: The Book of the Effort
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 5 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Udyoga Parva tells of the Pandavas' return from exile and the fruitless diplomacy that precedes the war: the embassies and Krishna's failed peace mission to the Kuru court, the counsel of Vidura and Sanat-sujata, the story of Amba, and the marshalling of the two armies at Kurukshetra.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 6: Bhishma Parva
subtitle: The Book of Bhishma
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 6 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Bhishma Parva opens the great war at Kurukshetra and holds the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna on the eve of battle; it follows the first ten days of fighting under Bhishma's command until he falls on a bed of arrows.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 7: Drona Parva
subtitle: The Book of Drona
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 7 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Drona Parva narrates the five days of battle under Drona's command: the death of Abhimanyu in the wheel formation, the slaying of Jayadratha, the night battle in which Ghatotkacha falls, and the stratagem by which Drona himself is killed.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 8: Karna Parva
subtitle: The Book of Karna
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 8 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Karna Parva narrates the two days of battle under Karna's command as Kaurava commander: the long single combats, Karna's quarrel with his charioteer Shalya, the death of Dushasana at Bhima's hands, and Karna's fall to Arjuna when his chariot wheel sinks in the earth.

title: The Mahabharata, Book 9: Shalya Parva
subtitle: The Book of Shalya
author: Vyasa
translator: trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published by Pratap Chandra Roy, 1883–1896)
blurb: Book 9 of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English prose translation of the Mahabharata, published in parts by Pratap Chandra Roy, Calcutta. The Shalya Parva tells of the last day of the great battle: Shalya's brief command and death at Yudhishthira's hands, the fall of Shakuni, Duryodhana's flight and hiding in the lake, Baladeva's pilgrimage along the Sarasvati, and the mace duel in which Bhima breaks Duryodhana's thigh.

title: Malcolm's Katie
subtitle: A Love Story
author: Isabella Valancy Crawford
blurb: A blank-verse love story of Max and Katie, set among Canadian settlers, which begins with the gift of a silver ring and ends in a home on the cleared land.

title: The Man in the Panther's Skin
subtitle: A Georgian epic, translated in prose
author: Shota Rustaveli
blurb: Rustaveli's Georgian national epic of c. 1200: the knight Tariel, clad in a panther's skin, and Avt'handil, who sets out to find him, search for the lost Nestan-Daredjan, in a tale of love, loyalty and chivalry.

title: Manfred
subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's Faustian drama of a Count in the high Alps, tormented by guilt over the death of Astarte, who summons the spirits of the universe, refuses to bow to Arimanes, and defies the demons who come for his soul.

title: Meditations
subtitle: The Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
author: Marcus Aurelius
blurb: The private notebook of the Stoic emperor, twelve books of reflections on duty, mortality and the governing mind.

title: Mari Magno; or, Tales on Board
author: Arthur Hugh Clough
blurb: Tales told by passengers on an Atlantic steamer, on the subject of love and marriage: here the traveller’s own tale and the lawyer’s second.

sections.title: My Tale: A la Banquette; or, a Modern Pilgrimage

title: Marien’s Pilgrimage
subtitle: A Fire-Side Story
author: Mary Howitt
blurb: Howitt’s story of a child, Marien, who wanders across the world on a mission of Christian love, told in twelve parts.

title: Marino Faliero, Doge of Venice
subtitle: An Historical Tragedy
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's tragedy in five acts, first published in 1821, on the fourteenth-century Doge of Venice. Marino Faliero, an old man whose appeal for justice against the patrician Michel Steno's insult is dismissed by the Forty as a trifling punishment, is drawn by the plebeian leader Israel Bertuccio into a conspiracy to overthrow the aristocratic Council. The plot is betrayed, the conspirators are condemned by the Council of Ten, and the Doge is sentenced to death and beheaded on the Giants' Staircase.

title: Marmion
subtitle: A Tale of Flodden Field
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A verse romance of treachery and doomed love set against the Scottish army's march to its catastrophic defeat at Flodden in 1513.

title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's satirical prophetic book, engraved in the early 1790s, overturns the moral order of Heaven and Hell: Energy is Eternal Delight, and the Devil's party speaks for Genius and Imagination. Blending verse, aphorism, parable and prose, it sets the Proverbs of Hell beside five Memorable Fancies and closes with A Song of Liberty, a visionary salute to the revolutions of his age.

title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
subtitle: A letter of the Church of Smyrna
author: The Apostolic Fathers
blurb: The earliest surviving account of a Christian martyrdom, written by the Church of Smyrna to the Church of Philomelium: the arrest, trial and burning of the aged bishop Polycarp.

title: Mary Quayle
subtitle: The Curate's Story
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: The Curate's Story: a tale in English verse that opens with a climb up Barrule on the north-east side of the Isle of Man.

title: The Masnavi (abridged), Books I–VI
subtitle: The Spiritual Couplets, abridged and translated by E. H. Whinfield
author: Jalal al-Din Rumi
blurb: Rumi's great Persian Sufi teaching poem in six books, here in E. H. Whinfield's abridged English version, opening with the lament of the reed-flute torn from its reed-bed and moving through tales of the prince and the handmaid, the lion and the beasts, the harper and 'Omar, and the elephant in the dark room.

title: The Masque of Pandora
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: A masque on the Greek myth. Hephaestus fashions Pandora from clay and Zeus gives her life; Hermes carries her to Epimetheus, brother of the chained Prometheus, who warns against receiving gifts from the gods. Pandora, given a mysterious casket, cannot resist opening it, and all the evils fly out into the world, while Hope alone remains. Choruses of Graces, Fates, Furies, Dreams and Eumenides comment on the action.

sections.title: III. Tower of Prometheus on Mount Caucasus

title: Maud
subtitle: A Monodrama
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
blurb: A young man, embittered by his father's ruin and death, finds love and hope in Maud, then loses her in a duel, and passes through madness toward a stern new purpose.

title: A Continuation of Lucan's Historicall Poem
subtitle: till the death of Iulius Caesar
author: Thomas May
blurb: Thomas May's own seven-book English epic in heroic couplets, written to carry Lucan's unfinished story of the civil war on from Caesar at Alexandria to his assassination.

title: The Mayor of Zalamea
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: Soldiers of Philip II are quartered at Zalamea, and the Captain dishonours the daughter of Pedro Crespo, a prosperous farmer. Crespo, newly made Mayor, arrests the Captain and has him judged and executed, and the King upholds his justice. The one play in the volume FitzGerald says was already well known.

title: Measure for Measure
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Duke Vincentio of Vienna pretends to leave the city and, disguised as a friar, hands his strict deputy Angelo the enforcement of laws long neglected. Angelo condemns Claudio to death for fathering a child out of wedlock, then offers to spare him if Claudio’s sister Isabella, a novice nun, will yield herself to him. Isabella refuses, and the Duke, watching in disguise, contrives a bed-trick that substitutes Angelo’s abandoned betrothed Mariana, and finally unmasks himself in a public reckoning of justice and mercy.

title: Medea
author: Seneca
blurb: On the day of her husband Jason’s wedding to Creusa, the princess of Corinth, the Colchian sorceress Medea is ordered into exile by King Creon. She wins one day’s grace and spends it on vengeance: she sends the bride a poisoned robe and crown that burn her and her father to death. Then, to wound Jason beyond healing, she kills the two sons she has borne him before his eyes and escapes through the air in a chariot drawn by dragons.

title: Medea
author: Euripides
blurb: Abandoned in Corinth by Jason, who has taken the king's daughter as his new bride, the sorceress Medea plans a vengeance that will cost her what she loves most. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: The Arbitrants
subtitle: Epitrepontes; or, Those Who Submit their Case to Arbitration
author: Menander
blurb: Charisius has left his young wife Pamphila after a child she exposed was born too soon, not knowing that he himself is the father; a charcoal-burner, a slave and a harp-girl bring the exposed child and its ring to light. The play survives in part, from the Cairo papyrus.

title: Fragments
subtitle: Selections from the unidentified minor fragments
author: Menander
blurb: Sayings, speeches and one-liners quoted from lost comedies, with the translator's captions, as selected in Allinson's Loeb volume.

sections.title: Fragments Assigned with Doubt to Menander

title: The Girl from Samos
subtitle: Samia
author: Menander
blurb: On the day of a wedding, Demeas takes the baby nursed by Chrysis, the Samian girl he keeps, to be his adopted son Moschion's, and in a fit of rage drives her from the house; the neighbour Niceratus is soon drawn in. The play survives in part, from the Cairo papyrus.

title: The Shorter Play-Fragments
subtitle: The Hero and the fragments of sixty-seven other comedies
author: Menander
blurb: What survives of Menander's other comedies in Allinson's Loeb volume: a scene of The Hero, the longer passages of The Farmer, The Flatterer, The Hated Man and The Ghost, and the sayings and fragments quoted from dozens of lost plays.

The Woman Possessed with a Divinity
The Women who Would Drink Hemlock

title: The Shearing of Glycera
subtitle: Perikeiromene; or, The Girl Who Gets Her Hair Cut Short
author: Menander
blurb: The soldier Polemon, jealous after seeing Moschion kiss Glycera, cuts off her hair; she takes refuge in the house next door, where birth-tokens reveal that she and Moschion are brother and sister and that Pataecus is their father. The play survives in part, from the Cairo papyrus.

title: The Merchant of Venice
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: To fund his friend Bassanio's courtship of the heiress Portia, the merchant Antonio borrows three thousand ducats from the moneylender Shylock, pledging a pound of his own flesh against default. When Antonio's ships are lost, Shylock demands his bond in open court, and Portia, disguised as a young lawyer, turns the letter of the law against him. Beside the trial run the riddle of the three caskets, the elopement of Shylock's daughter Jessica, and the comedy of the rings.

title: Merlin
subtitle: A Poem
author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
blurb: Blank-verse Arthurian narrative in seven parts: the ruin of Camelot and the old enchanter Merlin, held by Vivian in the forest of Broceliande.

title: The Mesnevi, Book the First
subtitle: Translated and versified by James W. Redhouse
author: Jalal al-Din Rumi
blurb: The first book of Rumi's great Persian Sufi teaching poem, opening with the lament of the reed-flute torn from its reed-bed, and moving through tales of the prince and the handmaid, the parrot and the oilman, and the lion and the beasts, each tale unfolding a lesson of love and the soul's return to God.

sections.title: Tale I: The Prince and the Handmaid
Tale II: The Oilman and the Parrot
Tale III: The Jewish King, Persecutor of the Christians
Tale IV: Another Jewish King, Persecutor of Christians
Tale V: The Lion and the Beasts
Tale VII: The Merchant and the Parrot
Tale IX: The Poor Scenite Arab and his Wife
Tale X: Patience and Perseverance under a Teacher
Tale XI: The Lion’s Hunt, in Company
Tale XII: Joseph and the Mirror
Tale XIII: The Prophet’s First Amanuensis
Tale XIV: The Chinese and Roman Artists

title: Metamorphoses
author: Ovid
blurb: Ovid’s vast narrative poem in fifteen books, retelling the myths of transformation from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar.

title: Metamorphoses (Golding)
author: Ovid
blurb: Ovid’s vast narrative poem in fifteen books, retold in Arthur Golding’s rollicking English fourteeners of 1567. This is the translation Shakespeare knew.

title: Metamorphoses (Howard)
subtitle: in English blank verse
author: Ovid
blurb: Ovid's fifteen books of transformations in the English blank verse of J. J. Howard, a Georgian version printed privately in 1807, with its period elisions intact and the poet's bolder passages deliberately chastened for general readers.

title: Metamorphoses (More)
author: Ovid
blurb: Ovid’s vast narrative poem in fifteen books, in Brookes More’s American blank verse of 1922, with the translator’s own headings for each tale.

title: The Meters of Boethius
subtitle: trans. W. J. Sedgefield (1900)
author: King Alfred
translator: trans. Walter John Sedgefield, King Alfred's Version of the Consolations of Boethius (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1900)

title: Metrical Legends of Exalted Characters
author: Joanna Baillie
blurb: Joanna Baillie's three verse legends of William Wallace, Christopher Columbus and Lady Griseld Baillie, with four shorter ballads of the supernatural.

sections.title: The Legend of Lady Griseld Baillie
Lord John of the East: A Ballad
Malcom's Heir: A Tale of Wonder
The Elden Tree: An Ancient Ballad

title: M'Fingal
subtitle: A Modern Epic Poem, in Four Cantos
author: John Trumbull
blurb: Hudibrastic satire on a Tory squire in revolutionary Massachusetts.

title: Michael Angelo
subtitle: A Fragment
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: A dramatic poem on the last decades of Michelangelo in Rome, published after Longfellow's death. In scenes of dialogue and monologue it sets the aged sculptor and painter beside Vittoria Colonna and Julia Gonzaga, Benvenuto Cellini, Titian, Vasari and the Popes, and follows him from the Last Judgment to the labour on St. Peter's and the Dead Christ.

sections.title: Part First, I: Prologue at Ischia
Part First: Monologue: The Last Judgment
Part First, IV: Borgo delle Vergine at Naples

Part Second, IV: Fra Sebastiano del Piombo
Part Third, II: Vigna di Papa Giulio
Part Third, IV: In the Coliseum
Part Third, V: Macello de' Corvi
Part Third, VI: Michael Angelo's Studio
Part Third, VII: The Oaks of Monte Luca
Part Third, VIII: The Dead Christ

title: The Mighty Magician
subtitle: Taken from Calderón's El Mágico Prodigioso
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: In Antioch the scholar and magician Cipriano sells his soul to the Devil to win the Christian Justina, who resists every spell. Cipriano is converted, and he and Justina are martyred together while Lucifer is left to confess his defeat. This is a different play and a different translation from Shelley's scenes of the same drama.

title: The Mikado
subtitle: Or, The Town of Titipu
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: In the town of Titipu, Nanki-Poo, the Mikado's son, flees an arranged match with the elderly Katisha and falls in love with Yum-Yum, the ward of Ko-Ko, a cheap tailor raised to Lord High Executioner. When the Mikado orders an execution in Titipu within the month, Ko-Ko must find someone to behead, and the stratagems that follow tangle the whole town.

title: Milton
subtitle: A Poem in 2 Books
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's prophetic epic in which the dead poet Milton returns from eternity to correct his errors, set between the Preface hymn "And did those feet in ancient time" and the vision of the Great Harvest.

title: Milton
subtitle: In Four Parts
author: Edward Bulwer Lytton
blurb: A poem in four parts picturing Milton in youth, manhood and age, linked by a thread of romantic fiction drawn from his Italian journey.

title: The Minstrel
subtitle: or, The Progress of Genius
author: James Beattie
blurb: A Spenserian poem in two books tracing the growth of a young poet, Edwin, among the hills and shepherds of the Scottish countryside.

title: Mirèio
subtitle: A Provençal Poem
author: Frédéric Mistral
blurb: Mistral's Provençal pastoral epic of the farmer's daughter Mirèio and the basket-weaver Vincen, whose love is thwarted by her family and ends at the shrine of the Saints Maries.

title: Miss Kilmansegg and Her Precious Leg
subtitle: A Golden Legend
author: Thomas Hood
blurb: Hood's comic narrative of an heiress whose golden leg, bought after a riding accident, makes her fortune and her ruin: a satire on money, marriage and the worship of gold, told in eighteen sections.

title: The Moallakát
subtitle: The Seven Arabian Poems which were suspended on the Temple at Mecca
author: The Mu'allaqat Poets
blurb: Seven great odes of pre-Islamic Arabia, said to have been hung on the Kaaba at Mecca, by Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, Antara, Amr ibn Kulthum and al-Harith ibn Hilliza.

sections.title: The Poem of Amru (Amr ibn Kulthum)
The Poem of Hareth (al-Harith ibn Hilliza)

title: The Modern Traveller
author: Hilaire Belloc
blurb: A mock-heroic monologue in which the boastful explorer Mr. Rooter, interviewed by a journalist, tells of his African expeditions and of his dead companions Commander Sin and Captain Blood.

title: Much Ado About Nothing
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: In Messina, Claudio, fresh from the wars, woos Hero with the help of his prince, Don Pedro, while Hero's cousin Beatrice and the soldier Benedick trade barbed wit and swear they will never love. Friends contrive to make each believe the other is secretly in love, even as Don John, the prince's embittered bastard brother, plots to shame Hero on her wedding day. The slander is exposed by the bumbling constable Dogberry and his watch, Hero is restored, and the sparring pair are brought to marriage.

title: Hero and Leander
subtitle: The Divine Poem of Musaeus, First of All Books, translated according to the original
author: Musaeus
blurb: Chapman's rhymed-couplet version of the Greek epyllion of c. AD 500, the story of the priestess Hero and Leander, who swims the Hellespont each night to her torch.

title: Musophilus
subtitle: Containing a generall defence of all learning
author: Samuel Daniel
blurb: Samuel Daniel's long verse dialogue in defence of poetry and learning. Philocosmus, the lover of the world, scorns the poet's idle art; Musophilus, the lover of the Muses, answers him at length on fame, the worth of the English language, the dangers of ignorance and the place of learning in a commonwealth. It is dedicated, in a sonnet, to Fulke Greville.

title: Nala and Damayanti
subtitle: An episode of the Mahabharata (Vana Parva)
author: Vyasa
blurb: The story of King Nala of Nishadha and Damayanti, princess of Vidarbha: the swan messenger, the choice among the gods, the possession of Nala by the demon Kali, the dice, the desertion in the forest and the long wanderings, until husband and wife are reunited and his kingdom restored.

title: Of the Nature of Things
author: Lucretius
blurb: Lucretius's Latin didactic poem De rerum natura, an exposition of Epicurean atomism in six books, rendered into English blank verse by William Ellery Leonard.

title: Nepenthe
subtitle: A Poem in Two Cantos
author: George Darley
blurb: Darley's visionary fragment of two cantos: the first of over-joy, the second of excessive melancholy, a poet's flight across desert, river and mountain in search of the nepenthe that would cure both.

title: Lives of Eminent Commanders
subtitle: John Selby Watson translation, 1853
author: Cornelius Nepos
blurb: Cornelius Nepos's short biographies of twenty-two Greek and Carthaginian commanders, from Miltiades at Marathon to Hannibal, with a chapter on kings and lives of Cato the Elder and of his friend Atticus, in John Selby Watson's English prose of 1853.

title: Nero, Part I
subtitle: An Historical Tragedy
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's historical tragedy of the first part of Nero's reign, published in 1885: the young emperor, his mother Agrippina, his tutor Seneca and the prefect Burrus, the poisoning of Britannicus at table, and Agrippina's end at Baiae. Written in blank verse and, as Bridges says in his notes, not intended for the stage.

title: Nero, Part II
subtitle: From the death of Burrus to the death of Seneca, comprising the conspiracy of Piso
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: The second part of Bridges's history of Nero, published in 1894, carries the story from the death of Burrus to the death of Seneca, taking in the conspiracy of Piso against the emperor and its fatal consequences for Seneca, Lucan and the Stoic circle of Thrasea.

title: The New England Tragedies
subtitle: Christus: A Mystery, Part III
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: The third part of Longfellow's trilogy Christus: A Mystery, two verse plays on the religious intolerance of colonial New England. John Endicott shows the Puritan governor of Boston persecuting Quakers in 1665, whipping and hanging those who will not conform, while his own son sides with them. Giles Corey of the Salem Farms dramatises the witchcraft delusion of 1692, in which an old farmer, pressed to death for refusing to plead, becomes its martyr. The part closes with the Finale, Saint John wandering the earth, and the Interludes between the parts of the trilogy are printed after the plays.

subtitle: A Romance of London
author: Edward Bulwer Lytton
blurb: Bulwer Lytton’s satire in heroic couplets on London society, politics and literature, framed by the story of a rescued orphan girl and her benefactor.

title: A Modern Faust
subtitle: Verse sections only
author: Roden Noel
blurb: Noel's long visionary poem of a modern Faust, a pilgrim who goes from faith through doubt and disorder to a vision of order.
