title: Beatrice
subtitle: From Beatrice and Other Poems
author: Roden Noel
blurb: Roden Noel's long narrative poem in four books, following the dreamer Clement and Beatrice, whose love ends in loss, with lyric songs woven through it.

title: Livingstone in Africa
author: Roden Noel
blurb: A blank-verse narrative in seven cantos of David Livingstone's last years in Africa, his death, and the carrying of his body home, with the lyric 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' set within it.

title: Melcha
subtitle: From Songs of the Heights and Deeps
author: Roden Noel
blurb: A narrative poem in three parts about the pensive maiden Melcha, wooed by the fairy knight O'Donoghue and carried under the waters of an Irish lake as his bride.

title: Oberon
subtitle: A Poem, from the German of Wieland
author: Christoph Martin Wieland
blurb: Wieland's romance of the knight Huon of Bordeaux, sent by Charlemagne to Babylon and helped by the fairy king Oberon, who has sworn to reconcile with his queen Titania only when a faithful pair keep their vows through every trial; Sotheby's English verse version of the German epic.

title: Octavia
subtitle: Attributed to Seneca
author: Seneca
blurb: Rome, AD 62. Nero has resolved to divorce his stepsister and wife Octavia, the daughter of the murdered emperor Claudius, and to marry his mistress Poppaea. Agrippina’s ghost curses the wedding, Seneca pleads in vain for restraint, and the people rise in Octavia’s defence. Nero crushes the rising and has Octavia put aboard a ship bound for exile and death on the island of Pandataria. The only surviving Roman historical drama, it was transmitted among Seneca’s tragedies but is generally held not to be his.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
translator: trans. S. H. Butcher and A. Lang (1879)
blurb: Butcher and Lang's prose translation of Odysseus's ten-year voyage home from Troy, in a deliberately archaic, King James-like English.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
blurb: Samuel Butler’s prose translation of Odysseus’s ten-year voyage home from Troy, companion to his Iliad.

title: The Odyssey
subtitle: The Odysseys of Homer, translated by George Chapman
author: Homer
blurb: George Chapman’s Odyssey, completed in 1614–15 as the companion to his Iliad, rendering the ten-year homecoming of Ulysses in rhymed decasyllabic couplets.

title: The Odyssey
subtitle: A line-for-line translation in the metre of the original
author: Homer
blurb: H. B. Cotterill's 1911 English hexameter version of the Odyssey, which keeps to the long line of Homer's own metre and renders the poem line for line.

title: The Odyssey
subtitle: Translated by William Cowper
author: Homer
blurb: William Cowper's blank-verse translation of Homer's Odyssey, published in 1791.

title: The Odyssey
subtitle: Done into English verse by William Morris
author: Homer
blurb: William Morris's rhymed, archaising translation of Homer's Odyssey, published in 1887 in two volumes.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
blurb: A. T. Murray’s literal prose translation of Odysseus’s ten-year voyage home from Troy, from the Loeb Classical Library of 1919.

title: The Odyssey
subtitle: Translated by Alexander Pope, with William Broome and Elijah Fenton
author: Homer
translator: trans. Alexander Pope, with William Broome and Elijah Fenton (1725–1726)
blurb: Alexander Pope's heroic-couplet version of Odysseus's long voyage home from Troy, completed with the help of William Broome and Elijah Fenton.

title: The Odyssey (Way)
author: Homer
blurb: Arthur S. Way’s rhymed verse translation of the Odyssey, in long swinging anapaestic couplets; this is the third, revised edition of 1904, first published in 1880 under the pseudonym “Avia”. Books I–XXIV.

title: Oedipus at Colonus
author: Sophocles
blurb: Blind and exiled, Oedipus comes to the grove of the Eumenides at Colonos near Athens, guided by his daughter Antigone. Theseus gives him shelter and defends him against Creon and the pleas of his son Polynices, and Oedipus passes mysteriously from the sight of men, a blessing to Athens.

title: Oedipus at Colonus
author: Sophocles
blurb: Old, blind and driven from Thebes, Oedipus reaches a grove of the Eumenides near Athens and learns that here his wanderings are to end. Theseus protects him, Creon tries to carry off his daughters, and Polyneices pleads in vain for a father’s blessing, until a summons of thunder calls Oedipus away to a hidden and holy death.

title: Oedipus
author: Seneca
blurb: A plague is killing Thebes, and King Oedipus, who once saved the city by solving the Sphinx's riddle, sends Creon to Delphi to learn the cause. The god's answer is that the murderer of the old king Laius must be found and driven out. After a grim sacrifice and a summoning of Laius's ghost, the evidence closes in on Oedipus himself, and an old herdsman from Corinth completes the proof: Oedipus is the son of Laius and Jocasta. Jocasta kills herself, and Oedipus blinds himself and goes into exile.

title: Oedipus the King
author: Sophocles
blurb: A plague lies on Thebes, and Apollo declares that it will lift only when the murderer of King Laius is found. Oedipus vows to find him, and the search leads step by step to the truth about his own birth and to the fulfilment of the oracle: Jocasta hangs herself, and Oedipus blinds himself.

title: Oedipus the King
author: Sophocles
blurb: A plague lies on Thebes, and the oracle at Delphi says it will end only when the killer of the old king, Laius, is driven out. Oedipus, who rules the city, swears to find him. His questioning of the prophet Teiresias, of Creon and of Iocasta, and the testimony of two shepherds, bring him step by step to the truth about his own birth, his marriage and the man he killed at the crossroads. Jebb renders the play in prose that keeps the speeches whole.

title: The Old Bush Songs
subtitle: Comprising Bush Ballads, Songs of the Bullock Dray and the Overland Routes, Digger’s Ditties, and other Songs of Australian Life
author: A. B. Paterson (ed.)
blurb: Paterson’s collection of anonymous and half-forgotten songs of the Australian bush: shearers, stockmen, swagmen, diggers, immigrants and bushrangers.

sections.title: A National Song for Australia Felix
It’s Only a Way He’s Got
The Squatter of the Olden Time

title: Apu Ollantay: A Drama of the Time of the Incas
author: Anonymous (Quechua)
blurb: The general Ollantay, a commoner, loves Cusi Coyllur, daughter of the Inca Pachacuti, and secretly fathers her child. When Pachacuti discovers it he imprisons the princess and Ollantay rises in revolt in the fortress of Ollantaytambo. Years later, under Pachacuti's son Tupac Yupanqui, the rebels are tricked, the princess is found, and the lovers are reconciled.

title: On Baile’s Strand
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: In a great hall by the sea, a blind man and a fool wait while the High King Concobar binds the hero Cuchullain to an oath of obedience. A young stranger arrives who proves to be Cuchullain’s own unknown son, and the oath drives the father to a tragic deed on the shore. Yeats’s one-act play, taken from the Irish heroic cycle, was first staged in 1904.

title: The Only Jealousy of Emer
subtitle: A play for dancers
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: Cuchulain lies apparently dead on a fisher's litter, his ghost crouching beside him, while his wife Emer and his mistress Eithne Inguba keep watch. A Woman of the Sidhe offers to release him if Emer will give up the thing she most values, the hope of his love. Emer, whose only jealousy is for his love, must choose.

title: Orestes
author: Euripides
blurb: Six days after the murder of their mother, Orestes lies delirious in Argos while the city votes whether he and his sister Electra must die. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tense late tragedy of madness, desperate plotting and an unexpected divine rescue in English verse.

title: Orion: An Epic Poem
subtitle: In Three Books
author: Richard Henry Horne
blurb: Horne's allegorical epic of the giant hunter Orion, from his blinding by Oenopion and his cure by the rising sun to his translation among the stars, published at a farthing in 1843.

title: Orlando Furioso in English Heroical Verse
subtitle: Translated by Sir John Harington from the Italian of Ludovico Ariosto, in forty-six cantos
author: Ludovico Ariosto
blurb: Ariosto's romance epic of Charlemagne's paladins, Orlando's love-madness, and the love of Ruggiero and Bradamante, in Sir John Harington's Elizabethan ottava rima, the first complete English version.

title: Orlando Furioso
subtitle: Translated into English verse from the Italian of Ludovico Ariosto, in forty-six cantos
author: Ludovico Ariosto
blurb: Ariosto's romance epic of Charlemagne's paladins, Orlando's love-madness, and the love of Ruggiero and Bradamante, in William Stewart Rose's eight-line stanzas.

title: Osorio
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
blurb: Coleridge's first tragedy, written at Nether Stowey in 1797 for Sheridan and Drury Lane, where it was rejected that December; it was not printed until 1873. Set in Spain under Philip II, during the persecution of the Moors, it follows Albert, long believed dead, who comes back disguised as a sorcerer to face his treacherous younger brother Osorio. It is the earlier form of the play that Coleridge reworked in 1813 as Remorse.

title: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Othello, the Moor who commands Venice's forces, secretly marries Desdemona, the daughter of the senator Brabantio, and is sent to defend Cyprus against the Turks. His ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, poisons his mind with the lie that Desdemona is unfaithful to him with the lieutenant Cassio. Driven to jealous rage by a lost handkerchief and Iago's insinuations, Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed, and learns the truth too late to do anything but take his own life.

title: Otho the Great
subtitle: A Tragedy in Five Acts
author: John Keats and Charles Armitage Brown
blurb: Otho the Great, Emperor of Germany, has put down a rebellion led by his own son Ludolph and by Conrad, Duke of Franconia, who has changed sides in time to share the victory. Ludolph has meanwhile fought for his father in disguise as a mysterious Arab warrior, and is reconciled to him, only to be married at once to Conrad's sister Auranthe. Auranthe and Conrad have slandered Otho's niece Erminia to clear their own way; the Abbot Ethelbert, the Hungarian prince Gersa and the knight Albert bring the plot to light, and the play ends in the frenzy and death of Ludolph. Keats wrote the verse in 1819 to a plan drawn up by Brown.

title: Otuel
subtitle: The Auchinleck romance of the Saracen Otuel
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle English couplet romance of Charlemagne. The Saracen champion Otuel comes to Charles's court as King Garsie's envoy, fights Roland to a standstill, is converted when a white dove lights on his head, marries the emperor's daughter Belisent and helps the Christians destroy Garsie's host.

title: The Owl and the Nightingale
subtitle: A verse rendering
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: On a summer evening an Owl and a Nightingale fall to quarrelling in a hidden dell, each pouring scorn on the other's song, habits and usefulness, until they agree to put their case to Master Nicholas of Guildford and fly off to find him.

title: The Painter of His Own Dishonour
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: A nobleman-painter, Don Juan Roca, brings his bride Serafina to Naples, where the Prince of Orsino is smitten with her. Her former suitor Alvaro, long believed drowned, returns to carry her off, and Juan, in the name of his honour, kills them both. FitzGerald's free version of Calderón's El pintor de su deshonra.

title: Palestine
subtitle: A Prize Poem
author: Reginald Heber
blurb: A prize poem on the fall of Jerusalem and the promised restoration of the Holy Land, recited at Oxford in 1803.

title: The Palice of Honour
subtitle: Compylit be M. Gawine Dowglas, Bischop of Dunkeld
author: Gavin Douglas
blurb: Douglas's dream-vision of 1501, dedicated to James IV: a poet, condemned by Venus's court for slandering love, is pardoned at the intercession of Calliope and led by the Muses to the Palace of Honour, where Venus, the poets and the exemplary dead of history pass before him.

sections.title: The Author directis his Buik to the Richt Nobill and Illuster Prince Iames the Feird, King of Scottis

title: Palicio
subtitle: A Romantic Drama in Five Acts in the Elizabethan manner
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's romantic drama in five acts, in the Elizabethan manner, first published in 1890. The scene is Palermo and the hills above Monreale under the Spanish occupation of Sicily, where the brigand Giovanni Palicio, the viceroy Hugo and his court, and the lovers Margaret and Livio are drawn into a web of intrigue.

title: Master Thaddeus; or, The Last Foray in Lithuania
subtitle: A Polish Tale of the Years 1811 and 1812
author: Adam Mickiewicz
blurb: Mickiewicz's national epic of Lithuania in twelve books, a story of feuding noble families, a lost love and the coming of Napoleon's army in 1811-12, here in the first English translation, in blank verse, by Maude Ashurst Biggs.

sections.title: Book IV: Diplomacy and the Chase
Book XII: Let Us Love One Another

title: Pan Tadeusz; or, The Last Foray in Lithuania
author: Adam Mickiewicz
blurb: Mickiewicz's national epic of the last foray in Lithuania, set in 1811–12 on the eve of Napoleon's invasion of Russia: a quarrel between two noble families, a young man's return to the family estate, and a love story, in twelve books full of hunts, feasts, mushroom-gathering and nostalgia for a vanished Poland.

sections.title: Book IV: Diplomacy and the Chase
Book XII: Let Us Love One Another!

title: Paracelsus
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Browning's first acknowledged work follows the sixteenth-century physician and alchemist Paracelsus through five parts, from the aspiration that drives him from Würzburg to the long reckoning of his death in Salzburg, in a drama of the mind rather than of events.

title: Paradise Lost
subtitle: A Poem in Twelve Books
author: John Milton
blurb: Milton’s epic of the war in Heaven and the fall of man — twelve books of blank verse, from Satan’s rebellion to the expulsion from Eden.

title: Paradise Regain'd
subtitle: A Poem in Four Books
author: John Milton
blurb: The brief epic sequel: Christ in the wilderness, tempted by Satan and refusing every worldly power.

title: The Paradiso (Wicksteed)
subtitle: Prose translation by Philip H. Wicksteed (Temple Classics)
author: Dante Alighieri
blurb: Dante's ascent through the spheres of Heaven in Philip H. Wicksteed's plain, literal prose for the Temple Classics, printed in 1899 as the facing English of the Italian text.

title: The Paris Psalter (Old English)
subtitle: The metrical Psalms 51–150: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: An Old English verse rendering of Psalms 51–150, preserved in a tenth-century Paris manuscript that gives the first fifty psalms in prose.

title: The Parliament of Fowls
subtitle: The Assembly of Fowls
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: A Valentine's Day dream vision in which birds of every rank gather before Nature to choose their mates — often read as an allegory of courtship and royal marriage.

title: Parzival: A Knightly Epic
subtitle: Translated from the Middle High German of Wolfram von Eschenbach
author: Wolfram von Eschenbach
blurb: Weston's 1894 verse rendering, the first complete English Parzival, in long rhyming couplets.

title: The Passage of the Red Sea
author: Reginald Heber
blurb: A poem on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea and the overthrow of Pharaoh's host.

sections.title: The Passage of the Red Sea

title: The Pastime of Pleasure
subtitle: An Allegorical Poem
author: Stephen Hawes
blurb: Hawes's allegorical romance in rhyme royal: the young Graunde Amoure learns the seven liberal arts in the Tower of Doctrine, wins the hand of La Bell Pucell by slaying giants and monsters, and is brought through age and death to the judgement of Fame, Time and Eternity.

title: Patience
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: A retelling of the Book of Jonah in about 530 alliterative lines, preceded by a prologue on the Beatitudes of poverty and patience. The reluctant prophet flees by sea, is swallowed by the whale and is finally rebuked for his anger at God's mercy.

title: Patience
subtitle: Or, Bunthorne's Bride
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: The rapturous maidens of Castle Bunthorne all adore the fleshly poet Reginald Bunthorne, until the idyllic poet Archibald Grosvenor arrives and draws their devotion away from him. Between the two aesthetes stands Patience, the simple milkmaid, who is wooed by both and must work out what unselfish love really means.

title: Description of Greece, vol. 1 (Books I-VI)
subtitle: Attica, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia and Elis
author: Pausanias
blurb: The first half of the traveller Pausanias's Greek guidebook: Attica, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia and Elis, with their temples, statues, legends and battles, in A. R. Shilleto's English of 1886.

title: Description of Greece, vol. 2 (Books VII-X)
subtitle: Achaia, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis
author: Pausanias
blurb: The second half of the traveller Pausanias's Greek guidebook: Achaia, Arcadia, Boeotia and Phocis, with their temples, statues, legends and battles, in A. R. Shilleto's English of 1886.

title: Pearl
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: A grieving father falls asleep on the grave of his infant daughter and dreams her transfigured into a maiden of Heaven, radiant among the elect — an elegy of loss answered by consolation, in interlocking rhymed stanzas.

title: Pearl (Middle English text)
subtitle: The Pearl
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: The original Middle English text of the dream-vision elegy, in 101 twelve-line stanzas of interlocking rhyme and alliteration. A bereaved father falls asleep by the grave of his lost pearl and sees her, transfigured, across a stream in the heavenly city.

title: Peer Gynt
subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
author: Henrik Ibsen
blurb: Peer Gynt, a boastful young peasant, steals a bride, flees into the mountains and the hall of the Troll King, and goes out into the world: a rich trader in Morocco, a prophet among the Bedouin, an emperor in a Cairo madhouse. Returning old and empty-handed, he meets the Button-Moulder, who has come to melt him down, and the faithful Solveig, who has waited.

title: The Psalms of David (Psalms 44–150)
subtitle: Metrical paraphrase from the Sidney Psalter, in the 1823 printed text
author: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
blurb: The Countess of Pembroke's verse paraphrase of Psalms 44–150, each psalm in a different stanza form, completing the psalter begun by her brother Sir Philip Sidney.

title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: To make a wife of the incestuous Antiochus's daughter, Prince Pericles of Tyre must solve a deadly riddle, and having solved it he flees, beginning years of shipwreck and exile narrated by the ghostly poet Gower. He wins Thaisa at Pentapolis, loses her at sea in childbirth, and leaves their daughter Marina at Tarsus, where jealous Dionyza plots her murder and pirates carry her to a brothel in Mytilene. After a long grief he is reunited with Marina and, guided by Diana, with Thaisa at Ephesus.

title: The Persians
author: Aeschylus
blurb: At the Persian court of Susa, the elders and the queen mother Atossa wait anxiously for news of Xerxes and his vast army, gone to conquer Greece. A messenger arrives with the tale of Salamis and the ruin of the fleet, and the ghost of Darius is raised from the tomb to name the king's pride as the cause. Xerxes returns in rags to a chorus of lament.

title: Peru
subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
author: Helen Maria Williams
blurb: A poem in six cantos on the Spanish conquest of Peru, the fall of the Inca Ataliba and the sufferings of his queen Alzira, ending in an appeal against cruelty and the lust for gold.

title: The Satyricon
subtitle: Satyricon, or the Satyrical Adventures of Encolpius
author: Petronius
blurb: The surviving episodes of Petronius's comic novel of Nero's Italy, in which Encolpius and his companions drift from lodging-house to the banquet of the freedman Trimalchio, in Michael Heseltine's English prose of 1913.

title: Phaedra
author: Jean Racine
blurb: At Troezen, Phaedra, wife of the absent Theseus, wastes away with a guilty passion for her stepson Hippolytus. Word comes that Theseus is dead, and she confesses her love; then he returns alive. Her nurse Oenone accuses Hippolytus of the very crime Phaedra herself desired, and Theseus calls down Neptune's curse on his son, who is killed by a sea monster. Phaedra takes poison and admits her guilt before she dies.

title: Phaedra
subtitle: or Hippolytus
author: Seneca
blurb: Phaedra, wife of the absent Theseus, is consumed by a guilty passion for her stepson Hippolytus, an austere young huntsman who scorns love. Her nurse carries her secret to him and he recoils in horror. When Theseus unexpectedly returns, Phaedra accuses Hippolytus of attacking her. Theseus calls down a curse on his son, and a monster from the sea destroys him. Phaedra confesses the truth and kills herself.

title: The Phenomena and Diosemeia
author: Aratus of Soli
blurb: A heroic-couplet version of Aratus’s star-poem and its weather signs by John Lamb, Dean of Bristol, published in 1848.

title: Phaenomena
author: Aratus
blurb: Aratus’s hexameter account of the constellations, the celestial circles, the risings of the zodiac and the weather signs, a poem of the stars that was widely read and translated in antiquity.

sections.title: A. Constellations north of the ecliptic (Lines 19–318)
B. Constellations south of the ecliptic (Lines 319–453)
D. Circles of the celestial sphere (Lines 462–558)

title: Pharonnida
subtitle: A Heroick Poem
author: William Chamberlayne
blurb: A heroic romance in rhymed couplets, in five books of five cantos each, of love and adventure among Christians and Turks; text from the 1659 edition (EEBO-TCP), in original spelling.

title: Pharsalia
subtitle: De Bello Civili (The Civil War)
author: Lucan
blurb: Lucan’s unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey, notable for banishing the gods from its narrative entirely.

title: The Civil War (Pharsalia)
subtitle: Books I-X, Loeb translation by J. D. Duff
author: Lucan
blurb: J. D. Duff's plain prose translation of Lucan's unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, ten books ending where Lucan's text breaks off.

title: Pharsalia
subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, containing the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey
author: Lucan
blurb: Sir Arthur Gorges's 1614 rhymed translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, in octosyllabic couplets, with a verse argument before each book.

title: Pharsalia (May)
subtitle: Lucans Pharsalia: or The Civill Warres of Rome, betweene Pompey the Great, and Iulius Caesar
author: Lucan
blurb: Thomas May's rhymed heroic-couplet translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, the first complete English version in pentameter couplets, with May's own verse argument before each book.

title: Pharsalia (Rowe)
subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, translated into English verse by Nicholas Rowe
author: Lucan
blurb: Nicholas Rowe's version of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, in heroic couplets, published after the translator's death in 1718.

title: Philoctetes
author: Sophocles
blurb: Odysseus brings the young Neoptolemus to Lemnos to trick the exiled Philoctetes out of the bow of Heracles, without which Troy cannot fall. Neoptolemus, moved by pity and shame, gives the bow back, and only the appearance of the deified Heracles persuades the wounded archer to sail for Troy and healing.

title: Philoctetes
author: Sophocles
blurb: Left on desolate Lemnos for ten years with a festering wound, the archer Philoctetes is the only man who can bend the bow of Heracles, and Troy cannot fall without it. Odysseus sends young Neoptolemus to win the weapon by deceit, but the boy finds he cannot betray a suffering man, and only the voice of the deified Heracles can resolve the clash of honour and necessity.

title: The Phoenician Maidens
author: Euripides
blurb: Thebes is besieged by Polyneikes and his Argive host, and the house of Oedipus stands on the edge of its last catastrophe: Jocasta, Kreon, the blind seer Teiresias and a chorus of Phoenician maidens watch as the brothers move toward single combat. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse.

title: The Phoenix
author: Anonymous (Old English)
translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
blurb: A richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

title: The Phoenix (Old English)
subtitle: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: The Old English verse of a richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

title: The Piccolomini
author: Friedrich Schiller
blurb: At Pilsen, in the Thirty Years' War, the imperial generals gather round their commander Wallenstein while a plot against him is already being laid by Octavio Piccolomini, whose son Max loves Wallenstein's daughter Thekla. Octavio holds a secret commission to take the generalship, and father and son are drawn toward a collision of loyalties.

title: Piers Plowman
subtitle: The Vision of Piers Ploughman
author: William Langland
blurb: Falling asleep on the Malvern Hills, the dreamer Will sees a field full of folk and sets out through a sequence of visions to find Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a vast alliterative satire of church, court, and commons.

title: The Pilgrims of the Sun
author: James Hogg
blurb: A visionary poem in four books, in Spenserian stanzas, in which a Scottish girl, Mary Lee, is borne in spirit through the planets and the sun, with a dedication to Lord Byron.

title: Pippa Passes
subtitle: A Drama
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Browning's drama of New Year's Day at Asolo follows Pippa, a silk-mill girl on her one holiday, whose songs, passing unheard by, break in on four scenes of love, guilt, plot and temptation and change the lives of those who hear them.

title: The Pirates of Penzance
subtitle: Or, The Slave of Duty
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: Frederic, bound apprentice to a band of tender-hearted pirates by his nurse's mistake, is freed on his twenty-first birthday and falls in love with Mabel, daughter of Major-General Stanley. But he was born on 29 February, so his indentures have barely a quarter of their term run, and his duty to the pirates and to the law pull him apart until a call to yield in Queen Victoria's name resolves the matter.

title: Apology
subtitle: The defence of Socrates before the Athenian jury
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates' speech to the Athenian jury at his trial for impiety and corrupting the young, followed by his words after the verdict and the sentence of death. Plato's account of the philosopher's defence of the examined life.

title: Apology
subtitle: The defence of Socrates before the Athenian jury
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates' speech to the Athenian jury at his trial for impiety and corrupting the young, followed by his words after the verdict and the sentence of death. Plato's account of the philosopher's defence of the examined life.

title: Charmides
subtitle: Socrates, Charmides and Critias on temperance
author: Plato
blurb: Back from the siege of Potidaea, Socrates visits the palaestra of Taureas and meets the beautiful young Charmides. Together with Critias they ask what temperance is, and each definition in turn collapses, leaving the question open.

title: Cratylus
subtitle: The dialogue on the correctness of names
author: Plato
blurb: Hermogenes and Cratylus disagree whether names are natural or conventional; Socrates tests both views through a long run of etymologies, and ends by doubting that names can teach us the truth of things.

title: Critias
subtitle: The unfinished dialogue on ancient Athens and Atlantis
author: Plato
blurb: Critias tells how ancient Athens and the island empire of Atlantis once stood against each other, in a dialogue that breaks off in mid-speech.

title: Crito
subtitle: Socrates in prison refuses to escape
author: Plato
blurb: In the prison at dawn, Crito urges the condemned Socrates to escape. Socrates replies by questioning him on justice and, speaking for the Laws of Athens, explains why he must stay and accept his sentence.

title: Crito
subtitle: Socrates in prison refuses to escape
author: Plato
blurb: In the prison at dawn, Crito urges the condemned Socrates to escape. Socrates replies by questioning him on justice and, speaking for the Laws of Athens, explains why he must stay and accept his sentence.

title: Epinomis
author: Plato
blurb: A sequel to the Laws: the Athenian Stranger, the Cretan Cleinias and the Spartan Megillus ask what mortals must learn in order to be wise, and find the answer in number, the study of the heavens and the stars, and the piety that follows from knowing the orderly motions of the gods.

title: Euthydemus
subtitle: The dialogue on the sophists and the art of wisdom
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates tells Crito how two sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, tied a young man in knots with verbal tricks, and how he answered them by urging the young Cleinias to seek true wisdom.

title: Euthyphro
subtitle: Socrates and Euthyphro on the nature of piety
author: Plato
blurb: On the porch of the King Archon, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is about to prosecute his own father for murder, and asks him what piety really is. Each definition falls apart under questioning, and the dialogue ends without an answer.

title: Euthyphro
subtitle: Socrates and Euthyphro on the nature of piety
author: Plato
blurb: On the porch of the King Archon, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is about to prosecute his own father for murder, and asks him what piety really is. Each definition falls apart under questioning, and the dialogue ends without an answer.

title: Gorgias
subtitle: Socrates on rhetoric, justice and the good life
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates questions the rhetoricians Gorgias and Polus, and then the ambitious Callicles, on whether the orator's power is a true art or mere flattery, and whether it is better to do wrong or to suffer it. Ends with the myth of the judgment of the dead.

title: Gorgias
subtitle: Socrates on rhetoric, justice and the good life
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates questions the rhetoricians Gorgias and Polus, and then the ambitious Callicles, on whether the orator's power is a true art or mere flattery, and whether it is better to do wrong or to suffer it. Ends with the myth of the judgment of the dead.

title: Hippias Major
subtitle: The dialogue on the nature of the beautiful
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates presses the sophist Hippias of Elis to say what the beautiful itself is, and one confident definition after another gives way under his questioning.

title: Ion
subtitle: The dialogue on inspiration and the rhapsode
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion, a celebrated reciter of Homer, and argues that his gift comes not from art or knowledge but from divine inspiration, like a chain of magnets.

title: Laches
subtitle: The dialogue on courage
author: Plato
blurb: Two fathers ask two generals how their sons should be educated; Socrates turns the question to courage, and no definition survives.

title: Laws
author: Plato
blurb: Plato's last and longest dialogue: an Athenian Stranger, a Cretan and a Spartan walk from Knossos to the cave of Zeus, talking the whole way, and draw up the laws of a new colony, from education, marriage and drinking parties to crime, religion and the Nocturnal Council that is to guard the state.

title: Laws
author: Plato
blurb: Plato's last and longest dialogue: an Athenian Stranger, a Cretan and a Spartan walk from Knossos to the cave of Zeus, talking the whole way, and draw up the laws of a new colony, from education, marriage and drinking parties to crime, religion and the Nocturnal Council that is to guard the state.

title: Letters
author: Plato
blurb: Thirteen letters transmitted under Plato's name, most of them touching his dealings with Dionysius of Syracuse and with Dion, his friend and pupil. The long Seventh Letter tells the story of Plato's three Sicilian journeys and sets out, in a famous digression, his view of what can and cannot be written down about the highest matters.

title: Lysis
subtitle: The dialogue on friendship
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates, on his way to the Lyceum, is drawn into a new palaestra and questions two young friends, Lysis and Menexenus, about what a friend is; the search ends without an answer.

title: Menexenus
subtitle: Socrates recites the funeral oration he learned from Aspasia
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates mocks the Athenian funeral oration, then recites one he says Aspasia taught him: a long panegyric of Athens from its mythic origins through the Persian and Peloponnesian wars.

title: Meno
subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
author: Plato
blurb: Meno asks whether virtue can be taught; Socrates answers with a geometry lesson for a slave boy, the theory of recollection, and a search for what virtue is.

title: Meno
subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
author: Plato
blurb: Meno asks whether virtue can be taught; Socrates answers with a geometry lesson for a slave boy, the theory of recollection, and a search for what virtue is.

title: Parmenides
subtitle: The dialogue on the One and the Forms
author: Plato
blurb: Cephalus recounts how the young Socrates met the aged Parmenides and Zeno, and how Parmenides tested the theory of Forms and then led the young Aristoteles through the long exercise on the One.

title: Parmenides
subtitle: The dialogue on the One and the Forms
author: Plato
blurb: Cephalus recounts how the young Socrates met the aged Parmenides and Zeno, and how Parmenides tested the theory of Forms and then led the young Aristoteles through the long exercise on the One.

title: Phaedo
subtitle: The dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates
author: Plato
blurb: On his last day in prison Socrates talks with his friends about death, the soul and its survival, and then drinks the hemlock. Phaedo tells the story to Echecrates of Phlius.

title: Phaedo
subtitle: The dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the death of Socrates
author: Plato
blurb: On his last day in prison Socrates talks with his friends about death, the soul and its survival, and then drinks the hemlock.

title: Phaedrus
subtitle: The dialogue on love, rhetoric and the soul
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates and Phaedrus talk beneath a plane-tree by the Ilissus: three speeches on love lead to the myth of the soul's winged chariot, and then to the nature of true rhetoric and the worth of writing.

title: Phaedrus
subtitle: The dialogue on love, rhetoric and the soul
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates and Phaedrus talk beneath a plane-tree by the Ilissus: three speeches on love lead to the myth of the soul's winged chariot, and then to the nature of true rhetoric and the worth of writing.

title: Philebus
subtitle: The dialogue on pleasure and wisdom as the good
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates and Protarchus take up Philebus's claim that pleasure is the good, weighing it against mind and wisdom, and ranking the elements of the good life.

title: Protagoras
subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates meets the great sophist Protagoras at the house of Callias and asks whether virtue is one thing or many, and whether it can be taught.

title: Protagoras
subtitle: The dialogue on whether virtue can be taught
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates meets the great sophist Protagoras at the house of Callias and asks whether virtue is one thing or many, and whether it can be taught. Translated by W. R. M. Lamb for the Loeb Classical Library (Plato, vol. IV, 1924).

title: The Republic
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates and his companions in the Piraeus ask what justice is, and build in speech an ideal city and a just soul, ending with the myth of Er.

title: Sophist
subtitle: The dialogue on being and not-being
author: Plato
blurb: Theodorus brings a stranger from Elea to Socrates, and with Theaetetus he hunts the sophist through a series of divisions, which forces a reckoning with the riddle of what is not.

title: Sophist
author: Plato
blurb: Theodorus brings a stranger from Elea to Socrates, and with Theaetetus he hunts the sophist through a series of divisions, which forces a reckoning with the riddle of what is not.

title: Statesman
subtitle: The dialogue on the art of ruling, also called Politicus
author: Plato
blurb: The Eleatic Stranger, with the young Socrates, seeks the definition of the statesman by division, tells the myth of the reversed cosmos, and likens the king's art to weaving.

title: Statesman
subtitle: The dialogue on the art of ruling, also called Politicus
author: Plato
blurb: The Eleatic Stranger, with the Younger Socrates, seeks the definition of the statesman by division, tells the myth of the reversed cosmos, and likens the king's art to weaving.

title: Symposium
subtitle: The banquet at Agathon's house and the speeches in praise of Love
author: Plato
blurb: At a supper in the house of the tragic poet Agathon, the guests, Socrates among them, each deliver a speech in praise of Love; the drunken Alcibiades breaks in at the end.

title: Symposium
subtitle: The banquet at Agathon's house and the speeches in praise of Love
author: Plato
blurb: At a supper in the house of the tragic poet Agathon, the guests, Socrates among them, each deliver a speech in praise of Love; the drunken Alcibiades breaks in at the end. Translated by W. R. M. Lamb for the Loeb Classical Library (Plato, vol. III, 1925).

title: Theaetetus
subtitle: The dialogue on the nature of knowledge
author: Plato
blurb: Socrates, the midwife of ideas, questions the young Theaetetus on what knowledge is: perception, true opinion, or true opinion with an account.

title: Timaeus
subtitle: The dialogue on the making of the world, the soul and the human body
author: Plato
blurb: Timaeus tells how a good Creator shaped the ordered world, its soul and its living creatures, after Critias recalls the story of Atlantis.

title: Amphitryon
subtitle: Jupiter in Disguise
author: Plautus
blurb: Jupiter takes the shape of the Theban general Amphitryon, and Mercury that of his slave Sosia, so that the god may spend the night with Alcmena while her husband is at the wars; when the true master and servant come home, nobody in the house can tell who is who, until Jupiter shows himself and Alcmena has borne twins, Hercules and Iphiclus.

title: Aulularia; or, The Concealed Treasure
subtitle: The Pot of Gold
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of Euclio, a miser who has found a pot of gold hidden by his grandfather and cannot rest for fear of thieves, while a rich neighbour asks for his daughter's hand, a slave steals the pot, and the girl's secret comes out. The ending is lost. Molière drew on it for L'Avare.

title: Bacchides; or, The Twin-Sisters
author: Plautus
blurb: Mnesilochus asks his friend Pistoclerus to find his lost mistress Bacchis, and Pistoclerus is drawn into the house of her twin sister, also called Bacchis; the quick-witted slave Chrysalus then tricks old Nicobulus out of his gold, not once but twice, to rescue the young men from a swaggering captain. When the fathers finally see through the scheme and come to demand their sons, the two courtesans coax them in as well.

title: Captivi
subtitle: The Captives
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of two captives who swap names and clothes, so that a slave may send his master home, while the old man who owns them does not know that the slave is his own lost son.

title: Casina
subtitle: The Stratagem Defeated
author: Plautus
blurb: Two slaves, Olympio the bailiff and Chalinus the armour-bearer, are set to win the foundling girl Casina as a bride, each at the secret bidding of a rival in love: old Stalino wants her for himself, and his son for himself. His wife Cleostrata takes her son's side, the matter is settled by drawing lots, and when Stalino's man wins she and her friend Myrrhina dress up Chalinus as the veiled bride, so that the old lecher and the bailiff go off to the bridal chamber with a bearded, hard-fisted wife; the play ends in a thrashing, a pardon, and the discovery that Casina is a freeborn Athenian.

title: Menaechmi
subtitle: The Twin Brothers
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of mistaken identity: one twin, carried off as a child to Epidamnus, is mistaken for the other, who has come in search of him, so that a courtesan, a parasite, a wife and a father-in-law all take the stranger for the man they know. It was the source of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors.

sections.title: Act V, Scene I (second Act V heading)
Act V, Scene II (second Act V heading)

title: Miles Gloriosus
subtitle: The Braggart Captain
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of Ephesus in which a vainglorious soldier who has carried off an Athenian girl is outwitted by his own slave: a hole in the party wall, a twin sister who does not exist, a pretended wife next door, and a beating for the braggart in the end.

title: Mostellaria
subtitle: The Haunted House
author: Plautus
blurb: While old Theuropides is abroad, his son Philolaches squanders the estate on revels and on buying a music-girl her freedom; when the father returns unexpectedly, the quick-witted slave Tranio saves the day by claiming that the house is haunted and has been shut up, then ensnares the old man in one lie after another until the truth comes out and the young men are forgiven.

title: Pseudolus
subtitle: The Cheat
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of intrigue: the slave Pseudolus promises his young master Calidorus that he will win back the girl Phoenicium, whom the pimp Ballio has sold to a soldier, and he does it by tricking pimp, soldier's messenger and his own master alike. Cicero records that Plautus himself counted it among his best plays.

title: Rudens
subtitle: The Rope
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of shipwreck and recognition: a storm raised by the star Arcturus wrecks a procurer's ship off the coast near Cyrene and casts two girls ashore at the temple of Venus, where a fisherman hauls up in his net a wallet whose trinkets reveal that one of them is the lost daughter of the old exile who lives next door.

title: Trinummus
subtitle: The Three Pieces of Money
author: Plautus
blurb: A comedy of money and friendship, adapted from Philemon's The Treasure. While the merchant Charmides is abroad, his spendthrift son Lesbonicus sells the family house, and Charmides' friend Callicles buys it, in secret, to protect the treasure buried beneath it. To give the daughter a dowry without shaming her brother, a hired sharper is sent with a pretended letter and 'three pieces of money'; but Charmides returns just in time to meet him. The play opens with Luxury leading her daughter Poverty to the young man's door.

title: The Pleasures of Memory
subtitle: In Two Parts
author: Samuel Rogers
blurb: Samuel Rogers's best-known poem, in heroic couplets, on the association of ideas and the consolations of memory, from a revisited village to the afterlife.

title: The Natural History, Volume I: Books I–V
subtitle: Books I–V
author: Pliny the Elder
translator: trans. John Bostock and H. T. Riley (1855)
blurb: Pliny's vast encyclopaedia of the natural world, in the Bohn translation: the dedication and contents, then cosmology and the heavens (Book II) and the geography of Europe, Africa and Asia (Books III–V).

title: Letters
subtitle: Selected letters, with the correspondence with the Emperor Trajan
author: Pliny the Younger
translator: trans. William Melmoth (1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet (1878)
blurb: Pliny's polished letters to friends and statesmen, among them the eruption of Vesuvius and his ghost stories, followed by his official correspondence with the Emperor Trajan, including the exchange on the Christians of Bithynia.

sections.title: Book X: Correspondence with the Emperor Trajan

title: The First Ennead
subtitle: The Ethical Treatises
author: Plotinus
blurb: The nine ethical treatises that open Porphyry's arrangement of Plotinus, on the soul and the man, virtue, dialectic, happiness, beauty, the Good and the nature of evil.

sections.title: I.1. The Animate and the Man
I.4. On Happiness (or The Authentic Good of Life)
I.5. On Happiness and Extension of Time
I.7. On the Primal Good and its Secondary Forms
I.8. On Evil, Its Nature and Source

title: The Second Ennead
subtitle: The Psychic and Physical Treatises (II)
author: Plotinus
blurb: The nine treatises of the Second Ennead, on the heavens and the stars, matter, potentiality and actuality, quality, and the argument against the Gnostics, in Stephen MacKenna's English of 1921.

title: The Third Ennead
subtitle: The Psychic and Physical Treatises (III)
author: Plotinus
blurb: The nine treatises of the Third Ennead, on fate and providence, our tutelary spirit, love, the impassivity of the unembodied, time and eternity, and contemplation, in Stephen MacKenna's English of 1921.

sections.title: III.6. The Impassivity of the Unembodied
III.8. Nature Contemplation and the One

title: The Fifth Ennead
subtitle: The Divine Mind
author: Plotinus
blurb: The nine treatises of the Fifth Ennead, on the three divine hypostases, the knowing Intellectual-Principle, the One beyond Being, the Ideas, the Intellectual Beauty and the Authentic Existence, in Stephen MacKenna's English of 1926.

V.3. The Knowing Hypostases and the Transcendent

V.7. Is There an Ideal Archetype of Particular Beings?
V.9. The Intellectual-Principle, the Ideas and the Authentic Existence

title: Parallel Lives: Demetrius and Antony
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs two flamboyant and ill-fated men of power, Demetrius the City-besieger, successor of Alexander, and Mark Antony, the Roman general. He offers them as cautionary examples, men whose great gifts were undone by pleasure and passion. Demetrius's sieges, kingship and fall in Macedonia and Asia are set beside Antony's rise under Caesar, the triumvirate, Cleopatra, Actium and death in Alexandria.

title: Parallel Lives: Demosthenes and Cicero
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the greatest Greek orator beside the greatest Roman one. Demosthenes rises from a plundered orphanhood and a stammering tongue to lead Athens against Philip and Alexander of Macedon, and dies by poison rather than fall into Antipater's hands. Cicero climbs from a provincial family to the consulship, crushes the conspiracy of Catiline, is driven into exile, and is finally hunted down and killed on the orders of Antony.

title: Parallel Lives: Agesilaus and Pompey
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the Spartan king Agesilaus, who led Greek arms into Asia and ruled Sparta for decades, beside Pompey the Great, the Roman general whose victories over pirates and eastern kings ended in defeat by Caesar and a murder on the Egyptian shore. Both men gained great fame, and both were brought low by the fortunes of civil strife. A short comparison closes the pair.

title: Parallel Lives: Agis and Cleomenes, Tiberius and Caius Gracchus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the Spartan reforming kings Agis IV and Cleomenes III with the Roman tribunes Tiberius and Caius Gracchus, four idealists who tried to restore a lost equality of land and citizenship and died for it. The closing Comparison sets the two pairs side by side, weighing the Romans' fine upbringing against the Spartans' bolder remedies.

sections.title: Comparison of Agis and Cleomenes with the Gracchi

title: Parallel Lives: Alcibiades and Coriolanus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the brilliant, unstable Athenian Alcibiades with the Roman patrician Coriolanus. Each is a gifted soldier whose pride and anger drive him from his city into the camp of its enemies. Alcibiades' career runs from his youth under Socrates through the Sicilian expedition, exile and recall; Coriolanus' from his valour at Corioli to his banishment and his march on Rome. A short comparison weighs the two.

title: Parallel Lives: Alexander and Caesar
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the conqueror Alexander the Great with Julius Caesar, who overthrew Pompey. Declaring that he writes lives, not histories, he looks to a phrase or a jest for the signs of the soul. Alexander's youth, his campaigns from the Granicus to Babylon and his death are set beside Caesar's rise, the Gallic wars, the civil war against Pompey and the Ides of March.

title: Parallel Lives: Aratus, Artaxerxes, Galba and Otho
author: Plutarch
blurb: Four single Lives from the later part of Plutarch's series. Aratus recounts the Achaean statesman who freed Sicyon and built up the Achaean League against Macedon. Artaxerxes follows the Persian king Artaxerxes II, his rivalry with his brother Cyrus, and the intrigues of the court. Galba and Otho tell of the Roman emperors of the civil-war year that followed Nero's death.

title: Parallel Lives: Aristides and Cato the Elder
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the incorruptible Athenian Aristides, called the Just, beside Marcus Cato the Censor, the stern guardian of old Roman ways. Both men rose by character rather than birth, and both are shown as champions of probity at the cost of popularity. The pair closes with a formal comparison of the two statesmen.

title: Parallel Lives: Cimon and Lucullus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Cimon, the Athenian statesman and general who won the victories at the Eurymedon and carried the war against Persia, with Lucullus, the Roman commander who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes and then retired to a famous luxury. The two lives are closed by a short comparison of the men.

title: Parallel Lives: Dion and Brutus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Dion of Syracuse, Plato's disciple who overthrew the tyrant Dionysius, with Marcus Brutus, who led the conspiracy against Caesar. Both were pupils of Plato's philosophy, both were cut off before their aims were achieved, and each saw an ill-boding spectre before the end. Dion's exile, return and murder are set beside Brutus's part in the Ides of March and his defeat at Philippi, with a brief closing comparison.

title: Parallel Lives, Part I
subtitle: Theseus to Marcus Cato, with their Comparisons
author: Plutarch
translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
blurb: Plutarch sets the lives of Greek and Roman statesmen and soldiers side by side, reading character through deeds, sayings and small incidents, and closes most pairs with a comparison of the two men. This first part opens with the founders and lawgivers, Theseus and Romulus, Lycurgus and Numa, Solon and Poplicola, then follows the great captains and politicians of Athens and Rome, among them Themistocles, Pericles, Alcibiades, Coriolanus, Aemilius Paulus and Cato the Censor.

sections.title: Comparison of Timoleon with Aemilius Paulus
Comparison of Aristides with Marcus Cato

title: Parallel Lives, Part II
subtitle: Philopoemen to Pompey and Agesilaus, with their Comparisons
author: Plutarch
translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
blurb: The second part of the Lives pairs Greek and Roman soldiers and statesmen of the Hellenistic and late Republican ages: Philopoemen and Flamininus, the liberators and last defenders of Greece; Pyrrhus and Marius; Lysander and Sylla; Cimon and Lucullus; Nicias and Crassus, two fortunes ruined abroad; Sertorius and Eumenes, exiles who led foreign armies; and Agesilaus and Pompey. As before, Plutarch reads character through deeds and sayings, and closes most pairs with a comparison.

title: Parallel Lives, Part III
subtitle: Alexander to Cicero, with their Comparisons
author: Plutarch
translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
blurb: Here Plutarch pairs the conquerors and the statesmen who failed to save their republics: Alexander with Caesar, the honest Phocion with Cato the Younger, the reforming kings of Sparta, Agis and Cleomenes, with the tribunes Tiberius and Caius Gracchus, and finally the orator Demosthenes with Cicero. Anecdote, omen and last words are his preferred evidence of character.

sections.title: Comparison of Tiberius and Caius Gracchus with Agis and Cleomenes

title: Parallel Lives, Part IV
subtitle: Demetrius to Otho, with their Comparisons
author: Plutarch
translator: trans. John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
blurb: The last part of the Lives pairs Demetrius the Besieger with Mark Antony, Dion of Syracuse with Marcus Brutus, and closes with the single Lives of Aratus of Sicyon, the Persian king Artaxerxes, and the short-lived emperors Galba and Otho. Plutarch reads ambition, luxury and loyalty through the fates of men who rose by arms and fell to their own excess or to conspiracy, from the Hellenistic kings to the civil wars of Rome and the year of the four emperors.

title: Parallel Lives: Lycurgus and Numa
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus with Numa Pompilius, the pious second king of Rome. Both are shadowy figures whose dates and deeds are disputed, and both gave their cities the laws and institutions that shaped them. Lycurgus's austere discipline of land, table and training for war is set beside Numa's calendar, priesthoods and cult of peace, and a closing Comparison weighs the two statesmen against each other.

title: Parallel Lives: Lysander and Sulla
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the Spartan admiral Lysander, who broke Athens at Aegospotami and then overreached at home, beside Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general who won the civil war, took the dictatorship and wrote his own epitaph. The two Lives follow ambition, luck and cruelty in victory, and the closing Comparison weighs Lysander's self-restraint against Sulla's greater successes.

title: Parallel Lives: Nicias and Crassus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Nicias, the cautious Athenian general whose scruples and superstition doomed the Sicilian expedition, with Crassus, the richest man in Rome, whose greed for glory ended in the Parthian disaster at Carrhae. Warning that Thucydides has already told the Sicilian story unsurpassably, he follows with a closing comparison of the two fortunes and the two men.

title: Parallel Lives: Pelopidas and Marcellus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the Theban liberator Pelopidas beside the Roman general Marcellus, finding in both a valour that risked too much. Pelopidas overthrows the Spartan garrison of Thebes, leads the Sacred Band at Leuctra and dies fighting the tyrant Alexander of Pherae. Marcellus wins the spolia opima, takes Syracuse despite the engines of Archimedes and falls in an ambush near Hannibal's camp. A short comparison weighs the two.

title: Parallel Lives: Pericles and Fabius Maximus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the Athenian statesman Pericles, who made Athens the school of Hellas, with Fabius Maximus, the cautious Roman dictator who wore Hannibal down by delay. He opens by urging that we study virtuous lives rather than idle spectacles, then follows Pericles from the Parthenon to the plague, and Fabius from the Alps to the walls of Tarentum, closing with a formal comparison of the two.

sections.title: Comparison of Pericles and Fabius Maximus

title: Parallel Lives: Philopoemen and Flamininus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Philopoemen, the Achaean general whom he calls the last of the Greeks, with Titus Flamininus, the Roman who proclaimed freedom for Greece at the Isthmian Games after defeating Philip V of Macedon. Philopoemen reforms the Achaean army, defeats the Spartan tyrant Machanidas and dies a prisoner of the Messenians; Flamininus wins at Cynoscephalae, wars against Nabis, and brings about the flight of Hannibal. A brief comparison weighs the two.

title: Parallel Lives: Phocion and Cato the Younger
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Phocion, the austere Athenian general who was elected strategos forty-five times and yet was put to death by the city he served, with Cato the Younger, the unbending Roman Stoic who killed himself at Utica rather than live under Caesar. Both men were honest in a corrupt age and both were destroyed by it. No formal Comparison of the two survives.

title: Parallel Lives: Pyrrhus and Caius Marius
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the Epirot king Pyrrhus beside the Roman general Caius Marius. Pyrrhus, kinsman of Alexander, wins his famous costly victories against Rome in Italy and Sicily and dies in the streets of Argos. Marius, a peasant's son from Arpinum, rises to a record seven consulships, defeats Jugurtha and the Cimbri and Teutones, then is drawn into civil war with Sulla. Both are portrayed as brilliant soldiers whose restless ambition outran their fortune.

title: Parallel Lives: Sertorius and Eumenes
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs two exiles who led armies of foreigners: the Roman Sertorius, who held Spain against Sulla's successors and Pompey until his own officers murdered him, and Eumenes of Cardia, Alexander's secretary, who fought the Successors until betrayed to Antigonus. Plutarch opens with a meditation on coincidence, and closes with a short comparison of the two men's careers and deaths.

title: Parallel Lives: Solon and Publicola
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch sets the Athenian lawgiver Solon beside Publicola, the Roman who helped drive out the Tarquins and stood first among the founders of the Republic. Solon's cancelling of debts, his laws, his poems and his meeting with Croesus are matched with Publicola's consulship, his laws and his wars against Tarquin and Porsena, and a closing comparison weighs the two men.

title: Parallel Lives: Themistocles and Camillus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs the Athenian Themistocles, architect of the fleet that won Salamis, with Camillus, the Roman who saved the city from the Gauls. Each statesman is driven into exile by the ingratitude of his own people, and each is shown in the hour of the country's peril. The comparison of the pair is lost.

title: Parallel Lives: Theseus and Romulus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch pairs Theseus, the legendary founder of Athens, with Romulus, the founder of Rome. Warning that the earliest ages shade into fable, he sets the Athenian's labours against the Roman's rise from the wolf's den to the walls of the city, and closes with a formal comparison of the two founders.

title: Parallel Lives: Timoleon and Aemilius Paulus
author: Plutarch
blurb: Plutarch opens with his celebrated preface on why he writes Lives, using history as a mirror for his own conduct, and pairs two commanders whom fortune and wisdom favoured alike. Timoleon of Corinth frees Syracuse from the tyrants and defeats the Carthaginians at the Crimisus; Aemilius Paulus, a stern and upright Roman, conquers Perseus of Macedon at Pydna. A brief comparison weighs the two.

subtitle: Lays of the Gods and Lays of the Heroes, translated from the Icelandic with the stanza numbering of the standard editions
author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
blurb: The great Old Norse collection of mythological and heroic lays preserved in the Codex Regius, in Bellows's 1923 verse translation, with the Eddas' own prose links kept in place.

title: The Elder Edda
subtitle: The Poetic Edda of Sæmund
author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
blurb: The Old Norse mythological and heroic lays of the Codex Regius in Benjamin Thorpe's 1866 prose translation, with the manuscripts' own prose links kept in place.

sections.title: Fragments of the Lay of Sigurd and Brynhild

title: The Poet's Pilgrimage to Waterloo
subtitle: Proem and two parts (1816)
author: Robert Southey
blurb: Southey's account in six-line stanzas of his journey in 1815 through Flanders and Brussels to the field of Waterloo, followed by a dream-vision on the Mountain of the Muse in which he is shown the hopes of mankind after the victory.

Part II, Canto IV: The Hopes of Man

title: Politian: Scenes from an Unpublished Drama
author: Edgar Allan Poe
blurb: Poe's only drama, left unfinished, survives in five blank-verse scenes set in Rome. Politian, Earl of Leicester, loves Lalage, a ward whose betrothal to the Count Castiglione stands in the way; haunted by melancholy and fatal premonition, he is drawn toward a challenge that the scenes break off before resolving.

title: Poltava
subtitle: A poem in three cantos
author: Alexander Pushkin
blurb: Pushkin's narrative poem of Mazeppa, Kotzubei and his daughter Marie, set against the Ukrainian hetman's betrayal of Peter the Great and the battle of Poltava (1709), in Charles Edward Turner's 1899 English version.

title: Poly-Olbion
subtitle: A Chorographicall Description of Great Britain, in thirty Songs
author: Michael Drayton
blurb: Drayton's topographical poem in alexandrines on the rivers, hills, forests and history of England and Wales, in thirty Songs (Songs 1-18 printed 1612, Songs 19-30 in 1622), each opening with its verse Argument; Selden's prose Illustrations are omitted.

title: The Histories, Books I–IX
author: Polybius
blurb: Polybius's account of how Rome came to rule the Mediterranean world in barely fifty-three years, from the First Punic War to the fall of Carthage, with his famous analysis of the Roman constitution in Book VI.

title: The Histories, Books X–XL and fragments
author: Polybius
blurb: The surviving later books of Polybius's history of Rome's rise, from the recovery of Tarentum and Scipio in Spain through Cannae's aftermath, Zama, the wars with Philip, Antiochus and Perseus, to the destruction of Carthage and Corinth in 146 BC, with his reflections on historical method and his own conclusion.

title: The Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians
author: Polycarp of Smyrna
blurb: A short pastoral letter from the bishop of Smyrna to the church at Philippi, on righteousness, the duties of deacons and presbyters, and the example of the martyrs.

title: Polyeucte
author: Pierre Corneille
blurb: Polyeucte, an Armenian nobleman newly converted to Christianity, is married to Pauline, who once loved the Roman knight Severus and obeyed her father in marrying another. When Severus returns in favour with the Emperor, Polyeucte's zeal leads him to smash the pagan idols and refuse to recant, even at the pleading of his wife and father-in-law. His martyrdom in turn converts Pauline and, finally, her father Felix. Corneille's tragedy of 1643 is written in rhymed couplets.

sections.title: Act IV: Polyeucte, Cleon, Three Other Guards

title: Garrick's Looking-Glass; or, the Art of Rising on the Stage
subtitle: A Poem in Three Cantos
author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
blurb: A satirical poem in three cantos on the theatrical world of David Garrick, published in 1776 (TCP K040357).

title: Humanity, or the Rights of Nature
subtitle: A Poem in Two Books
author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
blurb: Pratt’s verse attack on the slave trade and on cruelty to the weak, in heroic couplets, published in 1788 (TCP K038048).

title: Sympathy; or, a Sketch of the Social Passion
subtitle: A Poem
author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
blurb: A two-book poem in praise of fellow-feeling as the bond of society, published in 1781 (TCP K094645).

title: Prince Arthur
subtitle: An Heroick Poem in Ten Books
author: Sir Richard Blackmore
blurb: Blackmore's first epic, in ten books of rhymed couplets, follows the British prince Arthur against the Saxons, with Lucifer and the powers of Hell working to thwart him.

title: Prince Hohenstiel-Schwangau, Saviour of Society
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A dramatic monologue in blank verse in which a disgraced ruler, a thinly veiled Napoleon III, defends his career to a woman in London.

title: The Prince's Quest
author: William Watson
blurb: A romance in ten parts of a prince who sets out in search of the meaning of life and love, written in rhymed couplets.

title: Prometheus Bound
author: Aeschylus
blurb: For giving fire to mortals against the will of Zeus, the Titan Prometheus is nailed to a crag in the Scythian wastes by Strength and Force, while a reluctant Hephaestus does the work. Visited by the sea-nymphs, by Oceanus and by the wandering, cow-horned Io, he foretells the fall of Zeus, until Hermes comes to demand the secret and the rocks collapse upon him.

title: Prometheus Unbound
subtitle: A Lyrical Drama in Four Acts
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
blurb: Shelley's lyrical drama in four acts, in which the Titan chained to the Caucasus is freed when Jupiter is overthrown and love takes the place of tyranny.

title: Psalm of the West
author: Sidney Lanier
blurb: Lanier's long poem on the making of America, running from Columbus's night voyage and the Norse landing in Vinland through the Mayflower and Lexington.

title: Psyche
subtitle: or, The Legend of Love
author: Mary Tighe
blurb: Mary Tighe's retelling of the myth of Cupid and Psyche, from Apuleius, in six cantos of Spenserian stanzas.

sections.title: Dedicatory Sonnet, Addressed to My Mother

title: The Instruction of Ptah-hotep and the Instruction of Ke'gemni
subtitle: The Oldest Books in the World
author: Ptah-hotep
blurb: The oldest surviving Egyptian books of counsel, in which a vizier instructs his son in speech, manners and justice.

title: Punica
subtitle: The Second Punick War between Hannibal and the Romanes
author: Silius Italicus
blurb: Silius Italicus's Latin epic of the war between Rome and Hannibal, the longest surviving Latin epic, in seventeen books of heroic couplets by Thomas Ross.

title: The Purgatorio (Okey)
subtitle: Prose translation by Thomas Okey (Temple Classics)
author: Dante Alighieri
blurb: Dante's climb of the mountain of Purgatory in Thomas Okey's plain, literal prose for the Temple Classics, printed in 1901 as the facing English of the Italian text.

title: The Purple Island
subtitle: or, The Isle of Man
author: Phineas Fletcher
blurb: The body of man allegorised as an island, its anatomy described in Spenserian-derived stanzas, and the war of the virtues and vices for it in the last cantos.

title: Queen Hynde
author: James Hogg
blurb: Hogg's long romance in six parts, in tetrameter couplets, of a legendary Queen of Scotland in the age of St Columba, and the Norse suitors who beset her.

title: Queen Mary: A Drama
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
blurb: Tennyson's historical drama of the reign of Mary Tudor, from her triumphant entry into London and the Wyatt rebellion to her marriage to Philip of Spain, the burning of Cranmer, the loss of Calais and her death, with the throne passing to Elizabeth.

title: The Queen's Wake
subtitle: A Legendary Poem
author: James Hogg
blurb: Hogg's legendary poem of a minstrel contest at Holyrood, where the bards of Scotland sing before Mary, Queen of Scots, in the first weeks after her return from France. Twelve of the seventeen songs are given, among them Kilmeny and The Witch of Fife, together with the framing narrative divided into the Introduction, the three Nights, and the interludes between the songs.

title: The Quest of the Sangraal
author: Robert Stephen Hawker
blurb: Hawker's blank-verse narrative of King Arthur's knights setting out from Tintagel on the quest for the Holy Grail (the Sangraal), with Merlin's prophecy and the lots cast for the four quarters of the world.

title: The Institutio Oratoria
subtitle: The Education of an Orator
author: Quintilian
blurb: Quintilian's twelve-book education of the orator, from the first lessons of childhood to the ideal orator's character and style, with a celebrated survey of Greek and Roman authors.

title: The Raghuvamsa (The Story of Raghu's Line)
subtitle: Raghuvamsa
author: Kalidasa
blurb: Kalidasa's epic of the solar dynasty of Raghu, from King Dilipa's vow at the hermitage of Vasishtha through Rama's life and banishment of Sita to the decline of the line under the last king, Agnivarna.

title: Ralph Roister Doister
author: Nicholas Udall
blurb: The vain braggart Ralph Roister Doister, egged on by the parasite Matthew Merygreeke, sets out to win the rich widow Christian Custance, who is already promised to the merchant Gawyn Goodlucke. His love letter is read aloud with the punctuation turned so that it insults her, his mock funeral and his gifts come to nothing, and in the end Custance and her maids beat off his assault on her house. Often called the first English comedy, the play follows Plautus and Terence but is set among English townsfolk, with songs and a closing prayer for the Queen.

title: The Ramayana
subtitle: The Epic of Rama, Prince of India, Condensed into English Verse
author: Valmiki
blurb: Romesh Chunder Dutt's condensed English rendering of the Sanskrit epic of Rama, in twelve books of rhymed couplets, from the bridal of Sita to the sacrifice of the horse and the recognition of Lava and Kusa. Published by J. M. Dent and Co., London, 1899.

author: Valmiki
blurb: The Sanskrit epic of Rama, prince of Ayodhya: his exile, the abduction of Sita by the demon Ravana, the alliance with the monkey host and the war in Lanka, rendered into English verse by Ralph T. H. Griffith.
