title: The Rape of Helen
subtitle: Prose translation by A. W. Mair
author: Colluthus
blurb: A short epic retelling the judgement of Paris and the abduction of Helen from Sparta.

title: The Rape of Proserpine (Digges)
author: Claudian
blurb: The first English verse translation of Claudian's unfinished epic of Pluto's abduction of Proserpine, by Leonard Digges, the editor of Shakespeare's Poems (1640).

title: The Rape of the Bucket
subtitle: La Secchia Rapita, an heroi-comical poem in twelve cantos
author: Alessandro Tassoni
blurb: Tassoni's mock-heroic epic of the war between Modena and Bologna over a stolen wooden bucket, the first of its kind in Italian, in James Atkinson's English ottava rima.

title: The Rape of the Lock
subtitle: An Heroi-Comical Poem, in Five Cantos
author: Alexander Pope
blurb: A mock-epic on a society scandal — a lock of hair snipped in jest — blown up with the full machinery of Homeric epic, sylphs and all.

title: The Taill of Rauf Coilyear
subtitle: A Scots romance of Charlemagne and the collier
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Scots comic romance in thirteen-line stanzas. Caught in a storm on the way to Paris, Charlemagne takes shelter in the house of the collier Rauf, who knocks him down for his bad manners and makes him sit at his table; next day, at court, Rauf finds his surly guest is the king and is knighted for his pains.

title: Red Cotton Night-Cap Country; or, Turf and Towers
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A narrative in four parts, in blank verse, of a rich young Parisian's religious mania and fatal leap, based on a recent Normandy law case.

title: The Regement of Princes
subtitle: De Regimine Principum
author: Thomas Hoccleve
blurb: Sleepless at Chester's Inn, the clerk Hoccleve meets an old beggar who talks him into writing a book of counsel for Prince Henry: a verse mirror for princes on justice, mercy, patience, prudence, largesse and peace, in rhyme royal.

title: Remorse
subtitle: A Tragedy in Five Acts
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
blurb: Coleridge's tragedy was first played at Drury Lane Theatre on 23 January 1813 and ran for twenty nights. Don Alvar, thought dead, returns in disguise to Granada, where his younger brother Ordonio, who had arranged his murder, is courting Alvar's betrothed Teresa. Alvar's attempt to rouse his brother's conscience, played out amid the persecution of the Moors, ends in violence and reckoning. It is a reworking of Coleridge's earlier play Osorio.

title: The Return of the Druses: A Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A tragedy set on an islet of the Sporades in the fifteenth century. The Druses, exiles from Lebanon living under the Knights of Rhodes, believe their long-awaited prophet Hakeem is about to return and lead them home. Djabal, the man they hail as his incarnation, knows himself an impostor, and the play follows his unmasking amid a Venetian fleet, a Latin knight, and the woman who loves him.

title: The Return of Ulysses
subtitle: A Drama in Five Acts in a mixed manner
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Bridges's drama in five acts on the homecoming of Odysseus, first published in 1890. Athena brings Ulysses to Ithaca, where, in disguise, he meets Eumaeus and Telemachus and at last confronts the wooers of Penelope in his own hall; a chorus of the wooers sings between the speeches.

title: The Revenge: A Tragedy
author: Edward Young
blurb: Zanga, a Moorish prince taken captive in war, has been struck in the face by his master, the Spanish general Don Alonzo, and nurses his revenge in secret. Working on Alonzo's pride and his love for Leonora, he persuades him that his wife and his dearest friend, Don Carlos, have betrayed him. First staged at Drury Lane in 1721, the play was long a favourite vehicle for tragic actors.

title: Rhesus
author: Euripides
blurb: On the night after Hector's victory, the Trojan sentinels rouse their chief, a spy is sent into the Greek camp, and the Thracian king Rhesus arrives with his famous snow-white horses, only to be murdered in his sleep by Odysseus and Diomedes. Gilbert Murray renders the play, whose authorship has long been disputed, in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Rhesus
author: Euripides
blurb: On the night after Hector's victory, the Trojan sentinels rouse their chief, a spy is sent into the Greek camp, and the Thracian king Rhesus arrives with his famous snow-white horses, only to be murdered in his sleep by Odysseus and Diomedes. Arthur Way renders the play, whose authorship has long been disputed, in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Richard II banishes Bolingbroke and Mowbray, seizes the estate of the dying John of Gaunt, and sails for Ireland, only to find on his return that the exiled Bolingbroke has come home with an army. Deposed in Westminster Hall and imprisoned, Richard loses his crown to the man who becomes Henry IV. He is murdered at Pomfret Castle by Sir Pierce of Exton, and Henry is left to mourn the deed he wished for.

title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, plots his way to the crown through the deaths of his brother Clarence, the wooing of Lady Anne, the murder of the princes in the Tower and the use and discarding of Buckingham. On the eve of Bosworth the ghosts of his victims curse him in his sleep and bless his rival, and Richmond's victory begins the Tudor line as Henry VII.

title: Roderick, the Last of the Goths
subtitle: A Tragic Poem
author: Robert Southey
blurb: A blank-verse epic in twenty-five sections on the last Visigothic king of Spain, who after his defeat by the Moors lives on as a penitent and fights again beside Pelayo.

sections.title: IV. The Monastery of St. Felix
XXI. The Fountain in the Forest

title: Rokeby
subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: A verse romance of the English Civil War, set around Barnard Castle and the River Greta just after Marston Moor, whose outlaw songs — 'Brignall Banks' and 'Allen-a-Dale' among them — became favourites.

title: Roland and Vernagu
subtitle: The Auchinleck Charlemagne romance of the giant Saracen Vernagu
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle English tail-rhyme romance of Charlemagne's Spanish wars. Charles wins Spain for Christ, and the giant Saracen Vernagu, who cannot be wounded below the navel, is defeated by Roland in a two-day duel in which the two knights argue over the Trinity.

title: The Romaunt of the Rose
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
type: Allegorical dream vision (translation from Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun)
blurb: A dreamer enters the walled Garden of Love and sets his heart on a rosebud, helped and hindered by allegorical figures such as Fair Welcome, Danger and Reason, in the English version of the great French allegory.

title: The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: In Verona, the children of two feuding houses, Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet, fall in love at a masked ball and marry in secret with the help of Friar Lawrence. When Tybalt kills Mercutio and Romeo kills Tybalt, Romeo is banished, and Juliet, pressed to marry Paris, takes a sleeping potion that makes her seem dead. The message to Romeo goes astray, and both lovers die in the tomb, ending their parents' quarrel too late.

title: Rose Mary
author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
blurb: A ballad in three parts of the magic Beryl-stone, of the maiden Rose Mary who must read it, and of the spirits that dwell in it, with a Beryl-song between the parts.

title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
subtitle: Fifth Edition
author: Edward FitzGerald
translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1889), from Omar Khayyam
blurb: FitzGerald's free English version of the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, the fifth edition of 1889.

title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
subtitle: First Edition
author: Edward FitzGerald
translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1859), from Omar Khayyam
blurb: FitzGerald's free English version of the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, the first edition of 1859.

title: Rubáiyát of Doc Sifers
author: James Whitcomb Riley
blurb: A Hoosier country doctor, Doc Sifers, is sketched in numbered quatrain-stanzas in Indiana dialect, from his rounds on horseback and his fire-fighting to his plain-spoken kindness.

title: Salaman and Absal
subtitle: An Allegory
author: Jami
blurb: Jami's allegory of a king of Greece whose son Salaman, nursed and then seduced by the beautiful Absal, flees with her, is saved from a funeral pyre, and is finally freed from earthly love by the heavenly Venus, with the closing section explaining the story as the soul's journey.

title: The Conspiracy of Catiline
subtitle: De Coniuratione Catilinae, on the plot of 63 BC
author: Sallust
blurb: Sallust’s account of the conspiracy of Lucius Sergius Catiline, a ruined patrician who plotted to seize Rome in 63 BC, and of its exposure by the consul Cicero, with the speeches of Caesar and Cato on the fate of the conspirators and Catiline’s death in battle.

title: The Jugurthine War
subtitle: Bellum Iugurthinum, 112–105 BC
author: Sallust
blurb: Sallust’s history of the war Rome fought against Jugurtha, the Numidian prince who murdered his rivals, bribed Roman commanders and senators, and was finally betrayed by his father-in-law Bocchus, with the rise of Marius and Sulla, and Sallust’s reflections on the corruption of the Roman nobility.

title: Samson Agonistes
subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
author: John Milton
blurb: A tragedy on the Greek model — the blinded, captive Samson among the Philistines, moving toward his final act.

title: Sardanapalus
subtitle: A Tragedy
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's tragedy in five acts, first published in 1821, on the last king of Assyria. Sardanapalus, a pleasure-loving monarch who prefers peace and his Ionian slave Myrrha to war and empire, is roused too late when the Mede Arbaces and the priest Beleses rebel; after fighting bravely he builds a funeral pyre in his palace and dies upon it with Myrrha.

title: Ane Pleasant Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
subtitle: In Commendatioun of Vertew and Vituperatioun of Vyce
author: Sir David Lyndsay
blurb: A long Scots morality play in rhyme, first staged in 1552, in which the young King Humanitas, led astray by Wantonnes and Sensualitie, is brought to reform by Divyne Correctioun and Dame Veritie, while Johne the Common-weill and the poor man Pauper accuse the clergy, lords and merchants of the Thrie Estaitis.

title: The School of the Heart
author: Henry Alford
blurb: A long blank-verse poem in six lessons: a young man's meditation on love, nature, the Church and death, which the author later called a collection of detached passages of youthful feeling.

title: The Second Shepherds' Play
subtitle: Wakefield (Towneley) Cycle
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: Three Yorkshire shepherds, grumbling on a cold moor, are joined by the sheep-stealer Mak, who steals a lamb and hides it in a cradle at home, passing it off as his newborn son. When the shepherds find it, they toss Mak in a blanket; then an angel sings of Christ's birth, and they go to adore the true child in Bethlehem. The play is famous for its comic parody of the Nativity.

blurb: A Persian Sufi poem of 1311 in reply to fifteen questions about the mystic path, in Florence Lederer's selective English verse.

title: Sejanus His Fall
author: Ben Jonson
blurb: Jonson's Roman tragedy follows the rise and ruin of Aelius Sejanus, favourite of the emperor Tiberius. Sejanus poisons Drusus, the emperor's son, and schemes against the house of Germanicus, while the honest Romans Arruntius, Silius and Sabinus watch an age of flatterers and informers close over them. Tiberius, withdrawing to Capri, secretly raises Macro against his favourite and brings him down in the senate with a long, doubtful letter, and the mob tears Sejanus to pieces.

title: Apocolocyntosis
subtitle: The Pumpkinification of Claudius
author: Seneca
blurb: Seneca’s mock-deification of the dead emperor Claudius, a satire in prose and verse. Claudius labours to breathe his last, arrives at the gates of heaven stammering and lame, is argued over by the gods, and is at last condemned and sent below, to rattle dice for ever in a box with no bottom.

title: On Benefits
subtitle: De Beneficiis
author: Seneca
blurb: Seneca's seven books on how a benefit ought to be given, received and repaid: a Stoic treatise on generosity, gratitude and ingratitude, written for his friend Aebutius Liberalis.

title: The Seven Against Thebes
author: Aeschylus
blurb: Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices, doomed by their father's curse, face each other across the walls of Thebes. As a scout reports the seven champions of the Argive host, one to each gate, Eteocles assigns a defender to six of them, and then, learning that his own brother stands at the seventh, resolves to meet him in person. The brothers kill each other, and the play closes on the dirge for them and the defiance of Antigone.

title: The Shadowy Waters
author: W. B. Yeats
blurb: Forgael, a sea-king, sails the waste seas in search of the immortal love promised him by the birds of the otherworld, while his crew grow mutinous. They capture a ship and its royal passenger, Dectora, whom Forgael enchants with the music of his harp, so that she is drawn to follow him beyond the world. In the end she cuts the rope that binds them to the world, and the two drift together into the shadowy waters. Yeats prefaces the play with a verse dedication to Lady Gregory, written among the seven woods of Coole.

title: The Shahnama of Firdausi
subtitle: Done into English by Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner
author: Firdausi
translator: trans. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner (1905–1925)
blurb: The Warners' complete blank-verse English translation of Firdausi's Persian national epic; all nine volumes, from the creation of kingship under Gaiumart to the war with Mazandaran, Suhrab, Siyawush and the coming of Kai Khusrau, then Kai Khusrau's long wars with Turan (Piran, Kamus, the Khan of Chin, Bizhan and Manizha, the Twelve Rukhs, the fall of Afrasiyab) and the reign of Luhrasp, then the reign of Gushtasp (the coming of Zarduhsht, the wars with Arjasp, Asfandiyar's Seven Stages, the fight of Rustam and Asfandiyar, the death of Rustam), Bahman, Humai and Darab, and the last two reigns of the Kaianian line, Dara and Sikandar, the legend of Alexander; then the Sasanian dynasty, from the Ashkanians and the rise of Ardshir Papakan through the reigns of his successors, Bahram Gur's hunts and adventures, Nushirwan's justice with the tales of Buzurjmihr and Mahbud and the invention of chess, and Hurmuzd, to the long reign of Khusrau Parwiz (the revolt of Bahram Chubina, Khusrau's flight to Rum, Shirin, and his fall), then the brief reigns of his successors (the lament of Barbad, the death of Shirin, the women Shahs Purandukht and Azarmdukht), and last the reign of Yazdagird: the Arab conquest, the death of Rustam at Kadisiya, the flight to Khurasan and the murder of Yazdagird by the miller, ending with Firdausi's own closing words.

title: The Shah Nameh
subtitle: The Book of Kings (abridged)
author: Firdausi
blurb: James Atkinson's abridged English version of Firdausi's Persian national epic, alternating verse with prose summary, from Kaiumers to Firdausi's satire on Mahmud.

Barzú, and His Conflict with Rustem
Gushtásp, and the Faith of Zerdusht
Húmaí and the Birth of Dáráb

title: Shakuntala
subtitle: Shakuntala and the Ring of Recognition
author: Kalidasa
blurb: King Dushyanta, hunting in the forest, comes to the hermitage of the sage Kanva and falls in love with his foster-daughter Shakuntala; they marry by mutual consent, and he leaves her a signet ring. Cursed by the irascible Durvasas, the king forgets her, and rejects her when she comes to court, until a fisherman finds the lost ring and his memory returns. Years later, in the heavenly hermitage of Kashyapa, he is reunited with Shakuntala and their son Bharata.

title: The Shepheard’s Calender
subtitle: Twelve Æglogues Proportionable to the Twelve Monethes
author: Edmund Spenser
blurb: Spenser’s first major work: twelve eclogues, one for each month, mixing pastoral love-complaint, satire of the clergy, and elegy in a deliberately archaic English.

title: The Shepherd of Hermas
subtitle: Visions, Mandates and Parables (Similitudes)
author: Hermas
blurb: An early Christian book of five visions, twelve mandates and ten parables, written at Rome in the second century and widely read in the early Church.

title: The Shepherd's Week
subtitle: In Six Pastorals
author: John Gay
blurb: Gay's six burlesque pastorals, one for each day of the week, in which English rustics quarrel, court, mourn and get drunk in mock-Spenserian dialect, a parody of Ambrose Philips's pastoral manner

title: The Shield of Hercules
author: Hesiod
blurb: Elton’s blank-verse version of the poem traditionally, though doubtfully, attributed to Hesiod, on Heracles’ duel with Cycnus and the description of his shield.

title: The Shield of Heracles
author: Hesiod
blurb: An epic fragment on Heracles’ duel with the brigand Cycnus, built around a long description of the hero’s richly decorated shield and traditionally, though doubtfully, attributed to Hesiod.

title: The Shield of Heracles
author: Hesiod
blurb: A prose version of the poem on Herakles’ combat with Kyknos, son of Ares, built around a long description of the hero’s decorated shield; ancient tradition ascribed it to Hesiod, though its authorship is doubtful.

title: The Ship of Fools
subtitle: Translated out of Latin, French and Dutch by Alexander Barclay, 1509
author: Alexander Barclay
blurb: A shipload of fools of every kind, from the owner of unread books to the dishonest judge and the ill-matched bride, is rowed through a long series of rime-royal chapters, each closing with Barclay’s own warning, in the first English version of Brant’s great German satire.

title: The Shipwreck
subtitle: In Three Cantos
author: William Falconer
blurb: A narrative poem in heroic couplets of a merchant ship's voyage from Alexandria and its loss on the coast of Greece, drawn from the author's own experience at sea.

title: The Sibylline Oracles
subtitle: Translated from the Greek into English blank verse
author: The Sibylline Oracles
blurb: Twelve books of Greek hexameter prophecy put into the mouth of the pagan Sibyl by Jewish and Christian writers between the second century BC and the fifth century AD, from the creation and the flood to the fall of Rome and the last judgment.

title: The Psalms of David (Psalms 1–43)
subtitle: Metrical paraphrase from the Sidney Psalter, in the 1823 printed text
author: Sir Philip Sidney
blurb: Sir Philip Sidney's verse paraphrase of the first forty-three Psalms, each in a different metre and stanza form, begun in the early 1580s and completed by his sister Mary, Countess of Pembroke.

title: The Siege of Thebes
author: John Lydgate
blurb: Lydgate, as a Benedictine pilgrim newly arrived at Canterbury, is told by the Host to tell a tale on the road home, and he gives the story of Thebes: Oedipus, the Sphinx, the doomed rivalry of Eteocles and Polynices, and the Argive siege that ends in the brothers' death. A continuation of the Canterbury Tales in Chaucer's spirit, ending with a plea for peace.

title: The Siege of Valencia
subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
author: Felicia Hemans
blurb: Valencia, held by the Christian governor Alvar Gonzalez, a descendant of the Cid, lies under siege by the Moors. Abdullah, the Moorish chief, has taken two of Gonzalez’s sons prisoner and offers their lives in exchange for the city. Gonzalez refuses, and the play follows his wife Elmina, his daughter Ximena and the priest Hernandez through the city’s last days, to the deaths of the sons and of Gonzalez himself, as Castilian help arrives.

title: The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs
subtitle: In four books: Sigmund, Regin, Brynhild, Gudrun
author: William Morris
blurb: Morris's epic retelling of the Volsunga Saga in long anapaestic lines: the Volsung kings, Sigurd's slaying of Fafnir, his waking of Brynhild, the Niblungs' treachery, and the vengeance of Gudrun, in four books.

title: Sir Amadace
subtitle: A verse rendering
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: Sir Amadace, ruined by his own open-handedness, sets out with what money is left and finds a dead man refused burial because of his debts. He spends everything to lay the corpse in the ground, and the favour is repaid when a mysterious White Knight helps him win a princess and a kingdom, on one terrible condition.

title: Sir Eglamour of Artois
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of Sir Eglamour, who wins the love of Christabel, daughter of the Earl of Artois, by slaying a giant and a monstrous boar, and by killing a dragon at Rome. After long separation, their child, carried off by a griffin, grows up to be a knight and, unknowing, is wed to his own mother, until a token reveals the truth and the family is reunited.

title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
subtitle: A Middle-English Arthurian Romance
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: A green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's Christmas feast with an impossible challenge; Sir Gawain's answer sends him on a year-long quest that tests his courage, his courtesy, and his honesty alike.

title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
subtitle: A verse rendering
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: A green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's Christmas feast with an impossible challenge; Sir Gawain's answer sends him on a year-long quest that tests his courage, his courtesy, and his honesty alike. Here the poem is rendered in rhymed, bobbed-and-wheeled stanzas.

title: Sir Gawayne and the Grene Knyȝt (Middle English text)
subtitle: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
author: Gawain Poet
blurb: The original alliterative Middle English of the great Arthurian romance: a green-skinned knight rides into Camelot at Christmas, and Gawain's answer to his beheading game leads him through a year of trial to the castle of Bertilak, the temptations of the lady, and the green girdle.

title: Sir Isumbras
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of a proud and prosperous knight who is warned by a bird to choose penance in this life. He loses wealth, wife and three sons, serves as a smith and a palmer, and at last regains all by God's mercy and wins a Christian kingdom from the Saracens.

title: Launfal
subtitle: Sir Launfal
author: Thomas Chestre
blurb: A tail-rhyme Breton lay of about 1,040 lines, adapted from Marie de France's Lanval and the anonymous Graelent: a knight of Arthur's court, impoverished and slighted by Guinevere, is loved by the fairy Tryamour.

title: Sir Orpheo
subtitle: Sir Orfeo
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle English Breton lay of about 510 lines, the Orpheus story moved into fairyland: King Orpheo's queen Heurodis is carried off by the king of Faerie, and Orpheo gives up his crown to live as a harper in the wilderness, follows the fairy riders into their country, and wins her back with his playing.

title: Sir Perceval of Galles
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of the boy Perceval, reared in the wilds by his widowed mother, who rides to Arthur's court, avenges his father's death on the Red Knight and wins a lady's release from a Saracen sultan.

title: Sir Tristrem
subtitle: A verse rendering
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: Tristrem, son of Roland Riis and of Blancheflower, King Mark's sister, is brought up by the loyal Rohant and educated in the courtly arts before he comes to his uncle Mark in Cornwall. He kills the Irish champion Moraunt, is healed by Ysonde, wins her as Mark's bride, and shares with her a love that survives suspicion, banishment and exile.

title: Sister Songs
subtitle: An Offering to Two Sisters
author: Francis Thompson
blurb: Published in 1895, Sister Songs is Thompson’s offering to Monica and Madeline (Sylvia) Meynell, daughters of his patrons Wilfrid and Alice Meynell. It moves from a Proem addressed to Spring through two long parts to a closing Inscription.

title: Solomon and Saturn
subtitle: The poetic dialogues
author: Anonymous (Old English)
translator: trans. J. M. Kemble, The Dialogue of Salomon and Saturnus (Ælfric Society, 1848)
blurb: Old English verse dialogues in which the wise King Solomon answers the riddling questions of the Chaldean prince Saturn.

title: Solomon and Saturn (Old English)
subtitle: The poetic dialogues: Old English text
author: Anonymous (Old English)
blurb: Old English verse dialogues in which the wise King Solomon answers the riddling questions of the Chaldean prince Saturn.

title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
subtitle: A Poem in Three Books
author: Matthew Prior
blurb: Prior's longest poem: Solomon looks for happiness in knowledge, pleasure and power, and finds that all is vanity. Each book opens with the poet's prose argument.

title: The Song of Hiawatha
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: A trochaic epic drawing on Ojibwe legend, following the life of the hero Hiawatha — his childhood, wooing, feats, and eventual departure — in a rhythm modeled on the Finnish Kalevala.

sections.title: The Son of the Evening Star

title: The Song of the Merchant Kalashnikov
subtitle: A Song of the Tzar Ivan Vasilyevich, of the Young Oprichnik and of the Bold Merchant Kalashnikov
author: Mikhail Lermontov
blurb: In the Moscow of Ivan the Terrible, the merchant Kalashnikov fights and kills the Tsar's favourite oprichnik to avenge the insult to his wife, and pays for it on the block.

title: The Song of Los
author: William Blake
blurb: Los sings the long history of the laws and religions that bound Africa and Asia, until Orc's fires break out in Europe and America.

title: The Song of Roland
subtitle: La Chanson de Roland
author: Anonymous (Old French)
blurb: Betrayed by his stepfather Ganelon, Charlemagne's nephew Roland holds the pass at Roncevaux against the Saracens, refuses to sound his horn until too late, and dies a martyr; the Emperor then avenges him.

title: The Song of Roland
subtitle: La Chanson de Roland
author: Anonymous (Old French)
blurb: John O'Hagan's version renders the epic of Roland's last stand at Roncevaux in rhymed octosyllabic couplets, divided into three Parts and numbered laisses, with scene headings of his own.

sections.title: Part I: The Treason of Ganelon
Part II: The Prelude of the Great Battle (Laisses LXXXIII–CXLVII)
Part II: The Great Battle Continued (Laisses CXLVIII–CXCVII)

title: The Song of Songs
subtitle: Authorized Version of the Song of Solomon.
author: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
blurb: An anthology of Hebrew love lyrics, traditionally ascribed to Solomon.

title: Sordello
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Browning's long narrative poem in six books follows the thirteenth-century Mantuan troubadour Sordello through the Guelf and Ghibelline wars of northern Italy, and is chiefly a study of the growth and failure of a poet's soul.

title: A Soul's Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A two-part drama set in the Italian town of Faenza. In the verse first act, "the poetry of Chiappino's life", the blustering republican Chiappino quarrels with his friend Luitolfo and strikes down the tyrannical Provost. In the prose second act the people make him Provost in turn, and the Pope's Legate Ogniben quietly takes his measure.

title: The Romaunce of the Sowdone of Babylone and of Ferumbras His Sone Who Conquerede Rome
subtitle: The Sowdone of Babylone
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle English romance in rhymed quatrains. The Saracen Soudan Laban of Babylon sacks Rome; his son Ferumbras is defeated and converted, and his daughter Floripas helps the imprisoned peers of Charlemagne win their freedom before Charles himself defeats Laban in Spain. Preserved in a single manuscript.

title: The Spanish Gypsy
author: George Eliot
blurb: A dramatic poem of fifteenth-century Spain, in five books. Fedalma, a Gypsy foundling brought up in the household of the Duke Silva, is about to marry him when her father Zarca, chief of the Zincali, claims her for the cause of his people. She renounces her love, and after her father's death sails with the exiled Gypsies for Africa. It mixes narrative blank verse, dramatic dialogue with named speakers, and songs.

title: The Spanish Student
subtitle: A Play in Three Acts
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: A verse play set in Spain. The student Victorian loves Preciosa, a gypsy dancer of Madrid, whom the profligate Count of Lara also pursues. Her gypsy guardian, jealousies and a slandering plot divide the lovers, and the story passes from Madrid to the Guadarrama mountains, with serenades and gypsy songs set within the dialogue, before her true parentage is revealed.

title: The Spanish Tragedy
subtitle: Containing the lamentable end of Don Horatio and Bel-imperia, with the pitiful death of old Hieronimo
author: Thomas Kyd
blurb: The ghost of the Spanish courtier Don Andrea, slain in battle, is led back from the underworld by Revenge to watch his killer Balthazar punished. Instead he sees Andrea's friend Horatio murdered in his father's arbour and Hieronimo, the Knight-Marshall of Spain, driven half mad by grief as he seeks justice from a corrupt court. Hieronimo at last stages a play before the court in which the real deaths are carried out.

title: The Spirit of Discovery by Sea
subtitle: A Descriptive and Historical Poem
author: William Lisle Bowles
blurb: A blank-verse poem in five books on the history of maritime discovery, from the Ark to the voyages of the eighteenth century.

title: The Historie of Squyer Meldrum
author: Sir David Lyndsay
blurb: Lyndsay's verse romance of William Meldrum of Cleish and Binns, a Fife laird: a gallant, fighting, loving squire who defends a lady from robbers, wins a tournament in Ireland and a wife at home, and dies in his bed, leaving a Testament that is part mock-heroic, part valediction.

sections.title: The Historie of Squyer William Meldrum, of Cleische and Bynnis
The Testament of the Nobill and Vailyeand Squyer William Meldrum of the Bynnis

title: The Squyr of Lowe Degre
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A romance of about 1,130 lines in rhymed couplets: a squire of low degree loves the king of Hungary's daughter. She bids him win fame in arms abroad, the king's steward betrays him, and after seven years of mourning over a body she wrongly takes to be his, the princess finds him alive and they are married.

title: Le Morte Arthur
subtitle: The stanzaic Morte Arthur
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: An English verse romance of about 1400 in eight-line stanzas, telling the last days of King Arthur: the love of Lancelot and Guinevere, the Maid of Ascolot, the war between Arthur and Lancelot, Mordred's treason, the passing of Arthur and the deaths of Lancelot and Guinevere. It was a main source of Malory's last books.

title: The Story of Rimini
author: Leigh Hunt
blurb: Hunt's retelling of the story of Paolo and Francesca, from Dante's Inferno, in four cantos of heroic couplets: the bride fetched to Rimini, her journey, the fatal passion and its end.

title: Strafford: A Tragedy
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Browning's first play, written for the actor Macready. Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, King Charles I's chief minister, returns from Ireland to face the Parliamentary party led by his old friend John Pym. Betrayed by the weak King he serves, Strafford is impeached and condemned, and the play ends with their last meeting before his execution.

title: Such Stuff as Dreams Are Made Of
subtitle: A drama taken from Calderón's La Vida es Sueño
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: Basilio, King of Poland, confines his son Segismund from birth because of a prophecy, then drugs him and lets him wake in the palace for a day to test it. FitzGerald's free version of La vida es sueño, whose title he turns into a joke on the stolen phrase.

title: The Lives of the Twelve Caesars
subtitle: With the Lives of the Grammarians, Rhetoricians and Poets
author: Suetonius
translator: trans. Alexander Thomson, revised by T. Forester (1855)
blurb: Suetonius's lives of the Caesars from Julius to Domitian, with his surviving short Lives of grammarians, rhetoricians and poets, in Alexander Thomson's translation (1796) as revised by T. Forester for Bohn's Classical Library (1855). Thomson's own essays on the history and literature of each period are omitted.

title: The Suppliant Maidens
author: Aeschylus
blurb: The fifty daughters of Danaus flee Egypt to escape forced marriage to their cousins, the sons of Aegyptus, and beg sanctuary at Argos. King Pelasgus must choose between sheltering them and war; the Argive assembly votes to protect them, and the Egyptian herald's threats are turned back as the maidens give thanks.

title: The Suppliants
author: Euripides
blurb: After the failed assault on Thebes, the mothers of the fallen Argive champions come as suppliants to Eleusis, begging Theseus to recover their sons’ unburied bodies. Persuaded by his mother Aethra, Theseus faces down Thebes’ herald, wins the battle, and returns the dead for burial, while Evadne leaps onto her husband’s pyre; Athena closes the play with an oath binding Argos to Athens.

title: The Suppliants
author: Euripides
blurb: After the failed assault of the Seven against Thebes, the mothers of the fallen Argive chiefs come to Eleusis and beg Theseus to win back the unburied bodies of their sons. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

title: Oedipus Tyrannus; or, Swellfoot the Tyrant
subtitle: A Tragedy in Two Acts, Translated from the Original Doric
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
blurb: Shelley's Aristophanic farce transforms the Queen Caroline affair into a Theban comedy: King Swellfoot and his ministers scheme to put Iona Taurina, the Queen, on trial, while the Swinish Multitude of the people grunts in her defence. Written at Pisa in 1819 as George IV sought to divorce his wife, it was published anonymously in 1820 and suppressed within days.

title: Sylvia; or, The May Queen
subtitle: A Lyrical Drama
author: George Darley
blurb: A lyrical drama set in the Apennines. The traveller Romanzo falls in love with Sylvia, May Queen of a glen shared between the fairy queen Morgana and Ararach, king of the fiends. The fiends plot to seize Sylvia and to torment Romanzo with a phantom show, while the comic servant Andrea, transformed by the fiends, blunders between the two parties, until the fairy host drives off the fiends and the lovers are reunited. Blank verse, songs and comic prose.

title: Syphilis
subtitle: A Poetical History of the French Disease
author: Girolamo Fracastoro
blurb: Fracastoro's Latin didactic poem on the origin, nature and cure of the new disease that gave syphilis its name, in Nahum Tate's English couplets.

title: The Life and Death of Julius Agricola
subtitle: Church and Brodribb translation, 1876
author: Tacitus
translator: trans. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1876)
blurb: Tacitus's memoir of his father-in-law Gnaeus Julius Agricola, governor of Britain, from his boyhood in Gaul through the campaigns against the Caledonians to his death under Domitian, in Church and Brodribb's English prose of 1876.

sections.title: The Life and Death of Julius Agricola

title: The Annals
subtitle: Church and Brodribb translation, 1876
author: Tacitus
translator: trans. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1876)
blurb: Tacitus's annals of the Roman Empire from the death of Augustus through the reigns of Tiberius, Claudius and Nero, in the surviving books (I–VI and XI–XVI), in Church and Brodribb's English prose of 1876.

title: A Dialogue on Oratory
subtitle: Church and Brodribb translation, 1877
author: Tacitus
translator: trans. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1877)
blurb: A conversation set in the reign of Vespasian among the orators Marcus Aper, Julius Secundus, Vipstanus Messalla and the poet Curiatius Maternus on why eloquence has declined since the age of Cicero, in Church and Brodribb's English prose of 1877.

title: Germania
subtitle: The Origin and Situation of the Germans
author: Tacitus
translator: trans. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1876)
blurb: Tacitus's short ethnography of the Germanic peoples beyond the Rhine and Danube, their land, customs, government, war and religion, and the tribe-by-tribe survey that follows, in Church and Brodribb's English prose of 1876.

title: The History
subtitle: Church and Brodribb translation, 1864
author: Tacitus
translator: trans. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1864)
blurb: Tacitus's account of the civil wars of AD 69 and the Flavian accession: Galba, Otho and Vitellius, the rise of Vespasian and the revolt of Civilis on the Rhine, in the English prose of Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1864). The surviving books end mid-narrative.

title: The Histories
subtitle: Fyfe translation, 1912
author: Tacitus
blurb: Tacitus's account of the civil wars of AD 69 and the Flavian accession: Galba, Otho and Vitellius, the rise of Vespasian, the revolt of Civilis on the Rhine and the siege of Jerusalem, in W. Hamilton Fyfe's English prose of 1912. The surviving books end mid-narrative.

title: The Táin
subtitle: Táin Bó Cúailnge, the Cattle-Raid of Cooley, in English verse
author: Anonymous (Old Irish)
blurb: The central epic of the Ulster cycle in Mary Hutton's English blank verse: Queen Maev of Connaught and King Ailill gather the Four Fifths of Ireland to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley, and the boy-hero Cúchulainn (her Cucullin) holds the Ulster border alone until Ulster rises. It opens with the tale of how the poets recovered the lost Táin from the ghost of Fergus.

title: The Taking of Ilios
subtitle: Prose translation by A. W. Mair
author: Tryphiodorus
blurb: A short late-antique epic on the last night of the Trojan War, from the building of the wooden horse to the sacrifice of Polyxena.

title: A Tale of Eternity
subtitle: The Haunted Hurst
author: Gerald Massey
blurb: Gerald Massey's long narrative poem of haunting and the afterlife, in seven parts, first published in 1870.

title: The Tale of Gamelyn
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A younger son, Gamelyn, is cheated of his inheritance and kept in servitude by his elder brother. He wrestles his way to fame, escapes his bonds, and becomes king of the outlaws in the greenwood. When his brother has him arraigned, Gamelyn returns, takes the judge's seat and hangs the corrupt justice, the sheriff and the jury. The story is the source of Shakespeare's As You Like It.

title: A Tale of Paraguay
subtitle: Dedication, Proem and four cantos (1825)
author: Robert Southey
blurb: Southey's Spenserian tale of the Guarani Indian pair Quiara and Monnema, left alone by a plague of smallpox, and of their son Yeruti and daughter Mooma, whom the Jesuit missionary Dobrizhoffer receives into the mission of St Joachin; written in 1824-25 and dedicated to his daughter Edith May.

title: Tamburlaine the Great: Part 1
author: Christopher Marlowe
blurb: Marlowe's first great play, in blank verse, follows the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine from his seizure of the Persian crown to his triumph over Bajazeth, the Soldan of Egypt and the city of Damascus.

title: Tamburlaine the Great: Part 2
author: Christopher Marlowe
blurb: The sequel in blank verse follows Tamburlaine through the death of Zenocrate, the killing of his faint-hearted son Calyphas and the burning of Babylon, to his own death.

title: The Taming of the Shrew
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: A tinker, Christopher Sly, is tricked by a Lord into believing he is a nobleman, and a company of players performs the play-within-a-play for him. In Padua, Baptista will not let his gentle younger daughter Bianca marry until his sharp-tongued elder daughter Katherina has a husband, so the fortune-hunting Petruchio woos Katherina and sets about taming her by contradiction and deprivation. While Bianca's suitors scheme and exchange disguises, Petruchio wins a wager at the final feast when Katherina alone obeys her husband's summons.

title: Tartuffe; or, The Hypocrite
author: Molière
blurb: Orgon, a prosperous Parisian householder, has taken the pious Tartuffe into his home and fallen wholly under his spell, promising him his daughter's hand and his fortune. Orgon's family, led by the sharp-tongued maid Dorine and his wife Elmire, try to open his eyes to the impostor, who is in fact scheming to seize the house and seduce Elmire. Molière's comedy of religious hypocrisy was banned for five years after its first performance in 1664.

title: Temora: An Ancient Epic Poem
subtitle: In Eight Books
author: James Macpherson
blurb: Ossian's epic of Cairbar's murder of King Cormac and Fingal's expedition to Ireland to restore the throne, ending in the battle with Cathmor, in measured prose.

title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Prospero, the usurped Duke of Milan, has lived twelve years on an enchanted island with his daughter Miranda, served by the spirit Ariel and the savage Caliban. When his enemies sail past, he raises a storm and wrecks their ship, and through illusion, music and a courtship between Miranda and Ferdinand he brings them to repentance. In the end he forgives his brother, frees Ariel, and abjures his magic.

title: The Temple of Nature
subtitle: or, The Origin of Society
author: Erasmus Darwin
blurb: Darwin's last poem, published after his death, traces in four cantos the progress of life from its first stirrings in the ocean to the rise of mind, society and morality. Written in heroic couplets, it versifies his evolutionary speculations in the mysteries of an ancient temple.

sections.title: Canto III. Progress of the Mind
Canto IV. Of Good and Evil

title: Adelphi
subtitle: The Brothers
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's last comedy: two brothers, one strict and one indulgent, raise two sons between them, and a scandal, a stolen music-girl and a clever slave test both methods of upbringing, in Riley's literal prose.

title: Andria
subtitle: The Fair Andrian
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's first comedy: a young Athenian's secret love for a girl from Andros, a father's pretended wedding plans, and a clever slave, in Riley's literal prose.

title: Eunuchus
subtitle: The Eunuch
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's most popular comedy: a courtesan, a boastful captain, a disguised young man and a parasite, in Riley's literal prose.

title: Heautontimorumenos
subtitle: The Self-Tormentor
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's play of two fathers and their sons: a harsh old man punishes himself with farm labour for driving his son abroad, while his neighbour's son and a scheming slave run up a courtesan's bills, in Riley's literal prose.

title: Hecyra
subtitle: The Mother-in-Law
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's most reversed play, twice driven from the stage: a young husband's secret guilt, a wife in hiding and a wrongly blamed mother-in-law, in Riley's literal prose.

title: Phormio
subtitle: The Scheming Parasite
author: Terence
blurb: Terence's most celebrated comedy of intrigue: a parasite weds a penniless girl to a young Athenian by a trick at law, and two old brothers are caught out by a secret that Phormio holds, in Riley's literal prose.

title: The Testament of Beauty
subtitle: A Poem in Four Books
author: Robert Bridges
blurb: Published on Bridges's eighty-fifth birthday, in his last year as Poet Laureate, this long meditative poem in loose Alexandrines sets out his philosophy of beauty as the meeting-point of instinct and spirit in the mind of man. It is in four books: Introduction, Selfhood, Breed and Ethick.

title: Thalaba the Destroyer
author: Robert Southey
blurb: An Arabian romance in twelve books, in irregular unrhymed verse: the orphan Thalaba is chosen to destroy the sorcerers of the Domdaniel caverns that murdered his family.

title: The Apostle
subtitle: Az apostol
author: Sándor Petőfi
blurb: Petőfi's long poem of democratic faith: the foundling Szilveszter, raised in cruelty, grows up to become a wandering preacher of liberty and brotherhood, here in twenty parts in English verse by William N. Loew.

title: The Bride's Prelude
author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
blurb: An unfinished narrative poem begun in 1848: on the morning of Aloyse's wedding she tells her sister Amelotte the story of her lost love.

title: The Bridge
subtitle: A Poem
author: Hart Crane
blurb: Hart Crane’s long poem of America, taking the Brooklyn Bridge as its emblem: from Columbus’s landfall in Ave Maria through the Pocahontas section, Cutty Sark, the Whitmanic Cape Hatteras, the Three Songs, Quaker Hill and The Tunnel, to the closing hymn of Atlantis.

sections.title: II. Powhatan’s Daughter: 1. The Harbor Dawn
V. Three Songs: 2. National Winter Garden

title: The Cenci
subtitle: A Tragedy in Five Acts
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
blurb: Shelley's blank-verse tragedy of the Roman nobleman Francesco Cenci, whose cruelty to his family drives his daughter Beatrice to plot his murder; she is tried and executed for the deed. Based on a sixteenth-century Roman crime, it was written in 1819.

title: The Doctor
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series: 1
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: The longest of the Fo'c's'le Yarns: a seaman's tale in rhymed Manx dialect of the Doctor and the people around him, told to a forecastle audience that suspects him of spinning stories.

title: The Excursion
author: William Wordsworth
blurb: Wordsworth's nine-book blank-verse poem follows the poet, the Wanderer, the Solitary and the Pastor through a Lake District excursion in which grief and despondency are met with reflections on nature, faith, human suffering and the moral life.

sections.title: Book Sixth: The Church-yard among the Mountains
Book Seventh: The Church-yard among the Mountains (continued)
Book Ninth: Discourse of the Wanderer, and an Evening Visit to the Lake

title: The Golden Violet
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: A frame poem of a two-day minstrel contest in Provence for the prize of the Golden Violet, in which each minstrel sings his or her own tale.

sections.title: The Broken Spell: The First Provençal Minstrel's Lay
The Falcon: The Lay of the Norman Knight
The Dream: The Lay of the Scottish Minstrel
The Child of the Sea: The Lay of the Second Provençal Bard
The Ring: The German Minnesinger's Tale
The Queen of Cyprus: The Provençal Lady's Lay
The Rose: The Italian Minstrel's Tale
The Haunted Lake: The Irish Minstrel's Legend
The Wreath: Tale of the Moorish Bard
Sir Walter Manny at His Father's Tomb: The English Knight's Ballad

title: The Improvisatrice
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: An Italian poet-improvisatrice tells her own story of art, song and an unhappy love for Lorenzo, with the songs and tales she sings along the way as their own sections.

sections.title: Song (Farewell! we shall not meet again)

title: The Indiaman
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Third Series: 3
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A seaman's dialect yarn of Fanny Graeme, who caught her frock boarding at the Prince's dock, and of Peter Young, whom she married.

title: The Inn Album
author: Robert Browning
blurb: A blank-verse tale in eight parts of a young man, an older cardsharp and the woman between them, set in the parlour of a country inn.

title: The Jacquerie
subtitle: A Fragment
author: Sidney Lanier
blurb: Lanier's unfinished early narrative poem about the French peasant revolt known as the Jacquerie, left in five chapters.

title: The King's Tragedy
subtitle: James I. of Scots, 20th February 1437
author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
blurb: A ballad in which Catherine Douglas, called Kate Barlass, tells the murder of King James I of Scotland in 1437.

title: The Lost Pleiad
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: A story from the stars: the legend of the Pleiad that left her sisters, and what it costs a heavenly love to touch the earth.

title: The Manx Witch
subtitle: A Story of the Laxdale Mines
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A dialect-verse story of the Laxdale mines, in which a witch's spells trouble Nessy Brew and the miners who court her.

title: The Passing Bell
author: John S. B. Monsell
blurb: A meditation in five parts on the old custom of tolling the church bell for a dying soul, each part turning its warning on a different temptation: the man of business, the domestic man, the young and giddy, the sinful, and the pastor.

title: The Prelude
subtitle: or Growth of a Poet's Mind
author: William Wordsworth
blurb: Wordsworth's blank-verse autobiography traces the growth of his imagination from boyhood in the Lake District through Cambridge, London and revolutionary France to the recovery of his poetic vocation.

sections.title: Book I: Introduction — Childhood and School-time
Book VI: Cambridge and the Alps
Book VIII: Retrospect — Love of Nature Leading to Love of Man
Book XII: Imagination and Taste, How Impaired and Restored
Book XIII: Imagination and Taste, How Impaired and Restored (concluded)

title: The Princess
subtitle: A Medley
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
blurb: Tennyson's blank-verse medley of a prince who woos Princess Ida, founder of a women's university, framed by a summer fete at Vivian-place and broken by its famous songs, among them 'Tears, idle tears' and 'The splendour falls'.

title: The Ring and the Book
author: Robert Browning
blurb: Browning's twelve-book epic retells a seventeenth-century Roman murder trial through the conflicting voices of the town, the lawyers, the killer, his victim and the Pope.

sections.title: I. The Ring and the Book
VIII. Dominus Hyacinthus de Archangelis, Pauperum Procurator
IX. Juris Doctor Johannes-Baptista Bottinius, Fisci et Rev. Cam. Apostol. Advocatus
XII. The Book and the Ring

title: The Russiadde
subtitle: A Fragment of an Ancient Epic Poem, Supposed to Have Been Written by Gilbert Hume, a Sutor of Selkirk
author: James Hogg
blurb: Hogg's burlesque fragment of an epic, in two books, supposedly by a Selkirk cobbler.

title: The Schoolmasters
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series: 3
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A shorter dialect yarn on the three schools of the parish and their masters, told by the speaker of the earlier Christmas Rose.

title: The Seasons
author: James Thomson
blurb: Thomson's blank-verse poem on the four seasons of the year, with a closing hymn, a landmark of eighteenth-century nature poetry.

title: The Task
subtitle: A Poem, in Six Books
author: William Cowper
blurb: Begun as a joke on the subject of a sofa, The Task grew into Cowper’s masterpiece — a long, ruminative blank-verse walk through rural retirement, nature, solitude, and faith.

sections.title: Book V: The Winter Morning Walk
Book VI: The Winter Walk at Noon

title: The Temple of Glass
author: John Lydgate
blurb: A Chaucerian dream vision in which the poet, carried in sleep to a temple of glass, overhears a lady and her knightly lover lament and console each other in unrequited love — modelled closely on Chaucer's House of Fame and Parliament of Fowls.

title: The Troubadour
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: A verse romance in four cantos of the troubadour Raymond, set in Provence, with songs and tales worked into the story.

title: The Venetian Bracelet
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
blurb: A tale of Venice in fourteen numbered parts, centred on a serpent bracelet and the doomed love of Amenaide.

title: The Wanderer
subtitle: A Vision, in Five Cantos
author: Richard Savage
blurb: A visionary meditation in heroic couplets, in which a wanderer in retirement weighs the still life against the active and finds that misfortune can refine the mind.

title: Thebaid
author: Statius
blurb: Statius’s epic of the war of the Seven against Thebes, in twelve books, from the quarrel of Oedipus’s sons to the burial of the dead.

title: The First Book of Statius's Thebais
author: Statius
blurb: Pope's youthful heroic-couplet version of the first book of Statius's epic of the war of the Seven against Thebes, from the curse of Oedipus to the hymn to Apollo at the court of Adrastus.

title: The Theogony
author: Hesiod
blurb: Elton’s blank-verse version of Hesiod’s account of the birth of the gods, from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the victory of Zeus.

title: Theogony
author: Hesiod
blurb: Hesiod’s account of the birth of the gods, from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the victory of Zeus, opened by his own story of being called to poetry by the Muses on Mount Helicon.

title: Theogony
author: Hesiod
blurb: A prose version of Hesiod’s account of the origin of the gods, opening with the Muses of Helikon and tracing the line from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the rule of Zeus and the unions of gods with mortals.

title: The Characters
author: Theophrastus
translator: trans. Charles E. Bennett and William A. Hammond (1902)
blurb: Thirty brief sketches of human failings, from the Dissembler and the Flatterer to the Late Learner and the Vicious Man, drawn with a few bold strokes.

title: The City of Dreadful Night
author: James Thomson (B.V.)
blurb: James Thomson's poem of a nocturnal city of despair, in twenty-one numbered sections, with an epigraph from Dante, one from Leopardi and a Proem.

title: Three Judgments at a Blow
author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
blurb: In the Aragon of Pedro IV, a quarrel between two noble houses and a blow struck in the dark bring three sentences down together on the House of Urrea and the King's Minister. The title is Calderón's own riddle, answered in the closing lines: three judgments summed up in a single blow.

title: The History of the Grecian War
subtitle: The war between Athens and Sparta, 431–404 BC, in eight books
author: Thucydides
blurb: Thucydides' unfinished account of the war between Athens and Sparta, in the first English translation made directly from the Greek, by the philosopher Thomas Hobbes, in the seventeenth-century English of the 1843 Molesworth edition.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War
subtitle: The war between Athens and Sparta, 431–404 BC, in eight books
author: Thucydides
blurb: Thucydides' unfinished account of the twenty-seven years' war between Athens and Sparta, including Pericles' Funeral Oration and the Melian Dialogue, in Richard Crawley's translation.

title: Thyestes
author: Seneca
blurb: The ghost of Tantalus and a Fury drive the house of Pelops to a new crime. King Atreus, pretending reconciliation, lures his exiled brother Thyestes home to share the throne. Atreus slaughters Thyestes’ sons, and at a banquet serves their flesh to their father, who learns what he has eaten only when the severed heads are shown to him. The play ends in Thyestes’ helpless curse upon his brother.

title: Tiriel
author: William Blake
blurb: The blind and aged king Tiriel curses his sons, wanders to the vales of Har, and dies at last before the feet of his gentle, childlike parents.

title: The Tragedy of Titus Andronicus
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Titus Andronicus, returning to Rome after a war against the Goths, has Tamora's eldest son put to death in sacrifice and kills his own son Mutius, and Tamora, made empress, takes revenge through her sons Chiron and Demetrius, who rape Lavinia, Titus's daughter, and cut off her hands and tongue. Two more of Titus's sons are executed on a false charge, and Titus loses a hand to a false bargain for their lives. Titus kills Chiron and Demetrius, bakes them in a pie served to Tamora, then kills Lavinia and Tamora; Saturninus kills Titus and is killed in turn, leaving Lucius to rule Rome and Aaron to be buried to the chest and left to starve.

title: Tommy Big-Eyes
subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, First Series: IV
author: Thomas Edward Brown
blurb: A dialect yarn about Tommy Gellin, a shy man with a head of his own, and how he won his darling little wife.

title: Torrent of Portyngale
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A Middle English verse romance in tail-rhyme stanzas. Torrent, the son of a Portuguese earl, loves the king's daughter Desonell, is sent to fight giants and a dragon, and after many adventures is crowned emperor of Rome. Preserved in a single fifteenth-century manuscript.

title: Towards Democracy
subtitle: Complete Edition in Four Parts
author: Edward Carpenter
blurb: Carpenter's long free-verse chant in the manner of Whitman, begun in 1881: a single continuing poem of freedom, simplicity and comradeship, followed by three further parts of shorter poems on the city, nature, love and the coming of a new social life.

title: The Trachinian Maidens
author: Sophocles
blurb: Deianira, fearing she is losing Heracles to the captive princess Iole, sends him a robe smeared with what she believes is the centaur Nessus' love-charm. It is a poison, and Heracles is carried home in agony to die on a pyre on Mount Oeta, while Deianira takes her own life.

title: Trachiniae
author: Sophocles
blurb: Left alone for fifteen months while Heracles is away at war, Deianeira learns that he has sent home a captive princess, Iole, as his new love. To win him back she smears a robe with what the dying centaur Nessus told her was a love-charm, and sends it to him. It is a deadly poison. Jebb's plain, close English prose follows the Greek of Sophocles.

title: The Tragedy of Man
subtitle: A dramatic poem in fifteen scenes
author: Imre Madách
blurb: Adam and Eve, newly cast out of Eden, are shown by Lucifer in a series of dreams the future course of humankind, from Egypt, Athens and Rome to the medieval church, Renaissance Prague, revolutionary Paris, a mechanised London and a frozen end of the world. In each dream Adam takes up a new ideal and sees it fail. Waking from the last, he is ready to end his life, until Eve tells him she is to bear a child and God bids him to strive and to trust.

title: The Tragedie of Mariam, the Faire Queene of Jewry
author: Elizabeth Cary, Viscountess Falkland
blurb: Herod, King of Judaea, is reported dead at Rome, and his wife Mariam, who has long hated him for the murder of her brother and grandfather, finds she cannot rejoice. Her mother Alexandra and Herod's sister Salome quarrel over her, while Salome plots to be rid of her husband Constabarus so that she may marry the Arabian Silleus. Herod returns alive, a cup of poison is falsely charged against Mariam, and on Salome's scheming she is beheaded. Too late, Herod is struck with a frantic remorse. The play is the first original tragedy in English to be published by a woman, and each act ends with a Chorus.

title: Trial by Jury
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: In a London court of justice, Angelina sues Edwin for breach of promise of marriage. The jury is sympathetic to the plaintiff, the defendant pleads youthful inconstancy, and the Learned Judge, once a briefless barrister who won his place by marrying a rich attorney's elderly daughter, settles the matter by proposing to Angelina himself. Gilbert's first collaboration with Sullivan to reach the stage as a one-act comic opera.

title: The Tristia
subtitle: Ovid's Lament from Exile, Books I–V, prose translation by Henry T. Riley
author: Ovid
blurb: Ovid's five books of elegies written after Augustus banished him to Tomi on the Black Sea, in Riley's prose: the voyage into exile, letters to his wife and friends, pleas for mercy, and the long autobiographical elegy of Book IV.

title: Tristram of Lyonesse
author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
blurb: Swinburne's retelling of the Arthurian love story of Tristram and Iseult in rhymed heroic couplets: a Prelude and nine cantos, from the sailing of the Swallow to the lovers' death and the sailing of the Swan.

sections.title: I. The Sailing of the Swallow
IX. The Sailing of the Swan

title: Tristram
subtitle: A Poem
author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
blurb: Blank-verse narrative in ten parts, the last of Robinson's Arthurian poems: the love of Tristram and Isolt of Ireland, the Cornish court of King Mark, and Isolt of the white hands in Brittany.

title: The Triumphs
subtitle: Petrarch's Triumphs, in the Bohn Petrarch
author: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
translator: trans. Henry Boyd (1807), with Anna Hume (1644) and Macgregor (in Bohn, 1879)
blurb: Petrarch's allegorical procession in terza rima, in which Love, Chastity, Death, Fame, Time and Eternity each triumph in turn.

subtitle: The Tryumphes of Fraunces Petrarcke
author: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
blurb: Petrarch's visionary Trionfi, in which Love is conquered by Chastity, Chastity by Death, Death by Fame, Fame by Time, and Time by Eternity, in the rhymed English of Lord Morley's Tudor translation.

title: Trivia
subtitle: Or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London
author: John Gay
blurb: Gay's mock-georgic on London on foot — shoes, coats, weather signs, the dangers of day and night — in three books of couplets, with the tale of Cloacina and the origin of the shoeblack.

title: Troades
subtitle: The Trojan Women
author: Seneca
blurb: Troy has fallen and the Greek fleet waits on the shore for a wind. The ghost of Achilles demands the sacrifice of the princess Polyxena, and the prophet Calchas declares that Hector’s little son Astyanax must die before the Greeks can sail. Hecuba and Andromache, captives awaiting their allotment to Greek masters, are made to watch as the boy is torn from his hiding-place in Hector’s tomb and the girl is led to her death.

title: Troilus and Cressida
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Seven years into the siege of Troy, the young prince Troilus, sick with love, enlists Cressida's uncle Pandarus to bring him to her bed, and the two swear eternal faith. Almost at once Cressida is traded to the Greek camp in exchange for the captured Antenor, where she yields to Diomedes while Troilus looks on. Around this affair the Greek leaders quarrel, Akhilleus sulks in his tent with Patroclus, Ajax is puffed up as a champion, and Thersites rails at the whole war. Hector is killed by Akhilleus' Myrmidons, and the play closes on Troy's coming fall and Pandarus' bitter epilogue.

title: Troilus and Criseyde
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: In rime royal, Chaucer tells how the Trojan prince Troilus wins the love of Criseyde through her uncle Pandarus, and then loses her to the Greek camp, in the original Middle English.

title: Twelfth Night; or, What You Will
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Shipwrecked on the coast of Illyria, Viola disguises herself as the page Cesario and enters the service of Duke Orsino, who loves the Countess Olivia, who in turn falls for the disguised Viola. Meanwhile Olivia's kinsmen and servants gull her pompous steward Malvolio with a forged love letter, while Viola's twin brother Sebastian, believed drowned, turns up to untangle the confusions of identity and desire. Feste the fool sings the songs that frame the play's wistful mirth.

title: The Two Foscari
subtitle: An Historical Tragedy
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's historical tragedy in five acts, written at Ravenna in June and July 1821. It dramatises the downfall of Francesco Foscari, Doge of Venice, whose son Jacopo is tortured and condemned to exile by the Council of Ten, in the presence of his wife Marina. The play is set in the Ducal Palace and keeps to the unities of time and place.

title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Valentine leaves Verona for the court at Milan, where he falls in love with Silvia, the Duke's daughter. His friend Proteus, who has abandoned his own beloved Julia, follows him there, betrays Valentine to the Duke and presses his suit on Silvia. Valentine is banished and becomes captain of a band of outlaws, until Proteus's treachery is exposed in the forest, friendship is renewed, and Julia, who has followed in the disguise of a page, wins back her faithless lover.

title: Vala, or The Four Zoas
subtitle: The Death and Judgement of the Ancient Man: a Dream of Nine Nights
author: William Blake
blurb: Blake's unfinished first epic, in nine Nights, on the fall of Albion, the Ancient Man, into the strife of the Four Zoas and his redemption.

title: The Vespers of Palermo
subtitle: A Tragedy, in Five Acts
author: Felicia Hemans
blurb: Sicily, 1282, under the yoke of Charles of Anjou. The exiled Count di Procida returns in disguise and plots a rising with the nobleman Montalba. His son Raimond, who loves Constance, the sister of the French viceroy Eribert, is drawn into the conspiracy, while Eribert presses his suit on Vittoria, widow-in-grief of the murdered Conradin. At the signal of the Vesper-bell the Sicilians rise and massacre their oppressors. Raimond, bound by an oath, must choose between his love and his country, and the play ends in tragedy.

title: A Vision of Judgement
subtitle: In twelve parts (1821)
author: Robert Southey
blurb: Southey's dream-vision of the Last Judgment of King George III, written in English hexameters for the death of the king in 1820: the trial before the gate of Heaven, the accusers and absolvers, and the king's welcome among the worthies of the Georgian age. Byron's parody of the same title is a different poem.

sections.title: X. The Worthies of the Georgian Age

title: The Vision of Sir Launfal
author: James Russell Lowell
blurb: A knight sets out in search of the Holy Grail and learns, on his return home destitute, that true charity is found in what is shared rather than what is given.

title: Visions of the Daughters of Albion
author: William Blake
blurb: Oothoon, ravished by Bromion and spurned by Theotormon, pleads for the freedom of love against the jealousy of the law.

title: The New Life (La Vita Nuova)
subtitle: Translated by Dante Gabriel Rossetti
author: Dante Alighieri
blurb: Dante's account of his love for Beatrice, told in short prose chapters and thirty-one sonnets, ballate and canzoni, in Rossetti's translation.

title: The Ten Books on Architecture
subtitle: De architectura
author: Vitruvius
blurb: Vitruvius’s only surviving work and the one complete architectural treatise of antiquity, addressed to Augustus: the education of the architect, city sites, materials, temples, public and private buildings, water, clocks and machines, in the English translation of Morris Hicky Morgan.

title: Volpone; or, The Fox
author: Ben Jonson
blurb: The Venetian magnifico Volpone feigns a mortal illness so that the greedy Voltore, Corbaccio and Corvino will compete to be named his heir, each loading him with gifts, while his parasite Mosca plays them against one another. When Volpone's lust for Corvino's virtuous wife Celia and Mosca's own ambition tip the scheme out of control, the two cheats are hauled before the Venetian magistrates and punished for their trickery.

title: The Voyage of Columbus
author: Samuel Rogers
blurb: Rogers's unfinished narrative of the first Atlantic crossing, set out as translated fragments in twelve cantos, from the mutinous voyage to the discoverer's last days.

title: The Voyage of St. Brendan
subtitle: A.D. 545
author: Denis Florence MacCarthy
blurb: MacCarthy’s poem on the legendary sea voyage of St. Brendan of Clonfert to the western isles, in six parts.

title: A Voyage to the Isle of Love
author: Aphra Behn
blurb: Lisander's verse letter to his friend Lysidas, telling of his voyage to the Isle of Love, his happiness with Aminta, her death, and his lonely exile.

sections.title: An Account from Lisander to Lysidas his Friend

title: The Wallace
subtitle: The Life and Acts of Sir William Wallace of Ellerslie
author: Blind Hary
blurb: Blind Hary's Older Scots epic in eleven bukes, in rhyming couplets, on the life, battles and betrayal of the Scottish champion Sir William Wallace.

title: Wat o' the Cleuch
subtitle: A parody of Walter Scott
author: James Hogg
blurb: Hogg's parody of Walter Scott's border romances, in three cantos, from The Poetic Mirror, in which he imitated the principal living poets of Britain.

title: Werner
subtitle: Or, The Inheritance: A Tragedy
author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: Byron's five-act tragedy, written between December 1821 and January 1822 and published in November 1822. It is adapted from Harriet Lee's tale Kruitzner in her Canterbury Tales. Werner, an impoverished exile whose inheritance is at stake, robs the nobleman Stralenheim, who is his rival for the family estates, and his son Ulric's secret act brings the family to ruin; the action is set at the close of the Thirty Years' War.

title: The White Devil
author: John Webster
blurb: Vittoria Corombona, a Venetian beauty, and Brachiano, Duke of Brachiano, are lovers, and her brother Flamineo arranges the murders of her husband Camillo and the Duke's wife Isabella to clear their way. Vittoria is arraigned for the crimes by Cardinal Monticelso and, though she defies her accusers, is condemned to a house of convertites. Brachiano carries her off, but Isabella's brother, the Duke of Florence, plots revenge through the banished Count Lodovico, who poisons the Duke. In the last act the lovers and Flamineo are shot down by disguised assassins, and Giovanni, Brachiano's son, orders justice on the murderers.

title: The Texts of the White Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā)
author: The Rishis of the Yajur Veda
blurb: The sacrificial liturgy of the Adhvaryu priests in forty books, from the New and Full Moon rites to the Horse Sacrifice (Books XXII–XXV, XXIX), closing with the Isa Upanishad (Book XL).

title: Who Can Be Happy and Free in Russia?
subtitle: Verse translation
author: Nikolay Nekrasov
blurb: Seven peasants, freed from serfdom in 1861, wander Russia asking who lives happily and at ease: the priest, the landowner, the merchant or the Tsar.

title: William Tell
subtitle: A Play in Five Acts
author: Friedrich Schiller
blurb: In the Swiss cantons oppressed by the Austrian bailiffs, Werner Stauffacher, Walter Furst and Arnold of Melchthal bind the men of Schwytz, Uri and Unterwald in a league of liberation at the Rutli. Wilhelm Tell, who keeps clear of conspiracy, is forced by the tyrant Gessler to shoot an apple from his own son's head; afterwards he waits in a hollow way near Kussnacht and kills Gessler with his crossbow. The cantons rise and break the castles, and Tell is hailed as their deliverer.

title: The Winter’s Tale
author: William Shakespeare
blurb: Leontes, King of Sicilia, is seized by a sudden jealousy and accuses his pregnant queen, Hermione, of adultery with his oldest friend, Polixenes of Bohemia. He casts out the newborn Perdita, defies the oracle of Apollo, and loses both his son and, as he believes, his wife. Sixteen years pass, announced by the figure of Time, and Perdita, raised by shepherds in Bohemia, falls in love with Prince Florizel amid a sheep-shearing feast enlivened by the rogue Autolycus and his songs. The lovers flee to Sicilia, where the truth comes out and a statue of Hermione, in Paulina’s house, comes to life.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
blurb: Elton’s rhymed-couplet version of Hesiod’s poem of advice to his brother Perses, with the myths of Pandora and the Five Ages, farming lore and a calendar of days.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
blurb: Hesiod’s poem of advice to his idle brother Perses, mixing the myths of Pandora and the Five Ages with farming lore, moral counsel and a calendar of lucky and unlucky days.

title: Works and Days
author: Hesiod
blurb: A prose version of Hesiod’s poem of counsel to his brother Perses, with the tales of Prometheus, Pandora and the five ages of men, the praise of honest labour, a farmer’s and sailor’s calendar, and a list of lucky and unlucky days.

title: Anabasis
subtitle: The March of the Ten Thousand, in seven books
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's own account of how ten thousand Greek mercenaries marched into Persia with Cyrus the Younger, lost their leader at Cunaxa, and fought their way back to the sea.

title: Anabasis
subtitle: The March of the Ten Thousand, in seven books
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's own account of how ten thousand Greek mercenaries marched into Persia with Cyrus the Younger, lost their leader at Cunaxa, and fought their way back to the sea.

title: The Apology
subtitle: Socrates' Defence to the Jury
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's account of why Socrates, on trial for his life, chose to speak as he did and to welcome death as better than a long old age.

title: Cyropaedia: The Education of Cyrus
subtitle: The education and rule of Cyrus the Great, in eight books
author: Xenophon
translator: trans. Henry Graham Dakyns, rev. F. M. Stawell (1914)
blurb: Xenophon's romance-like life of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian empire: his Persian upbringing, his campaigns, and his ideal of the ruler who wins willing obedience.

title: The Economist
subtitle: Oeconomicus: a Treatise on the Science of the Household, in the Form of a Dialogue
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's dialogue on the management of a household and estate: Socrates and Critobulus discuss wealth and farming, and Socrates recalls the model gentleman Ischomachus, his methods and his instruction of his young wife.

title: Hellenica
subtitle: A history of Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BC, in seven books
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's continuation of Thucydides: the closing years of the Peloponnesian War, the Spartan ascendancy, and the rise and fall of Theban power down to the battle of Mantinea.

title: Hellenica
subtitle: A history of Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BC, in seven books
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's continuation of Thucydides: the closing years of the Peloponnesian War, the Spartan ascendancy, and the rise and fall of Theban power down to the battle of Mantinea.

title: Memorabilia
subtitle: Recollections of Socrates, in four books
author: Xenophon
blurb: Xenophon's recollections of Socrates in word and deed, written to answer the charges on which Athens put him to death and to show him as the best and happiest of men.

title: The Symposium
subtitle: The Banquet
author: Xenophon
blurb: A dinner given by the wealthy Callias for the youth Autolycus, at which Socrates and his friends each say what they most prize, and the evening closes with a mimed wedding of Dionysus and Ariadne.

title: The Yashts
subtitle: Hymns to the yazatas, from the Zend-Avesta, Part II
author: The Avesta
blurb: The twenty-two Yashts of the Younger Avesta, hymns of praise to Ahura Mazda and the yazatas, from Mithra and Anahita to the Fravashis, in James Darmesteter’s prose translation of 1883.

title: The Yeomen of the Guard
subtitle: Or, The Merryman and His Maid
author: W. S. Gilbert
blurb: In the Tower of London, Colonel Fairfax, condemned to death for sorcery, is secretly married to the strolling singer Elsie Maynard so that he may keep his estate from his enemy, while Sergeant Meryll's children scheme to save him by disguise. Jack Point, the jester who loves Elsie, finds his own part in the plot ending in a tragedy that is unusually dark for a comic opera.

title: Yusuf and Zulaikha
subtitle: Verse translation
author: Jami
blurb: Jami's Persian romance of the Qur'anic story of Yusuf (Joseph) and Zulaikha, the wife of the Egyptian vizier who falls in love with him, followed from her dreams and long pining, through his temptation, imprisonment and rise, to her repentance and the restoring of her youth.

title: Yvain, or the Knight with the Lion
subtitle: Yvain, ou Le Chevalier au lion
author: Chrétien de Troyes
blurb: Yvain wins a widow's love, forfeits it by neglect, and earns it back with the aid of a grateful lion.

title: Ywaine and Gawin
subtitle: Ywain and Gawain
author: Anonymous (Middle English)
blurb: A northern Middle English verse romance of about 4,000 lines in couplets, adapted from Chretien de Troyes: Ywain wins the Lady of the Fountain, loses her by forgetting his promise, and regains her with a lion at his side.

title: Zapolya
subtitle: A Christmas Tale, in Two Parts
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
blurb: Coleridge's dramatic poem, written at Calne in 1815 and published in 1817, is modelled on Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale; he calls the first part a Prelude rather than an act, with an interval of twenty years before the second. In Illyria the usurper Emerick seizes the throne and drives out Queen Zapolya, who escapes with her infant son. Twenty years later the young Prince Andreas, raised as a mountaineer's son, returns to claim his inheritance.

title: Zophiel, a Poem (Canto I, 1825)
author: Maria Gowen Brooks
blurb: A fallen spirit, Zophiel, loves the Hebrew maiden Egla in this Romantic narrative poem of angels and mortals, written in Cuba and first printed in Boston in 1825.
